entry.title: Semi-truck fire shuts down SW Pratt Whitney Road near South Fork High School
entry.summary: A semi tractor-trailer fire has forced a closure of a major roadway in Stuart, affecting traffic flow and school access Wednesday morning. SW Pratt Whitney Road is completely closed from just south of SW Bulldog Way to Bridge Road as emergency crews respond to the incident. The closure is impacting access to South Fork High School, with only students and staff able to reach the campus from the northern approach. No injuries have been reported at this time, and the cause of the fire remains under investigation. Motorists are urged to avoid the area entirely and seek alternate routes. The closure is expected to remain in effect until the scene is cleared and the roadway is deemed safe for travel.

entry.title: Woman arrested after stealing Broward Sheriff's cruiser, fleeing to St. Lucie County
entry.summary: A Fort Lauderdale woman was arrested Tuesday night after allegedly stealing a marked Broward County Sheriff's Office patrol car and abandoning it on Interstate 95 in St. Lucie County. The incident began at 9:30 p.m. when authorities issued a BOLO alert for the stolen Dodge Charger, which was traveling northbound on I-95. At around 9:40 p.m., deputies with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Patrol Operations Bureau, along with officers from the Port St. Lucie Police Department and troopers from the Florida Highway Patrol, responded to I-95 after receiving information about the stolen patrol vehicle near Gatlin Boulevard. Within minutes, FHP located the abandoned patrol vehicle on the I-95 northbound exit ramp to SW Gatlin Boulevard at mile marker 118. During the response, St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office deputies found Shannon Marie Dillon, 42, in the area wearing an outer ballistic vest displaying Broward Sheriff's Office insignia. Dillon now faces charges in St. Lucie County including grand theft of law enforcement equipment, unlawful use of a police badge or law enforcement vehicle, unlawful possession of four or fewer identification items, possession or use of drug paraphernalia, possession of a weapon or ammunition by a convicted felon, driving while license suspended and resisting an officer without violence. She also faces charges out of Broward County for grand theft of law enforcement equipment from an authorized emergency vehicle and grand theft. The northbound I-95 exit ramp to SW Gatlin Boulevard was temporarily closed while crime scene investigators processed the scene. The ramp reopened at 12:45 a.m. Wednesday morning.

entry.summary: A nonprofit based in Palm Beach County that sends care packages to our military men and women stationed around the world is asking for your help. Forgotten Soldiers Outreach tells me it's running critically low on donated supplies. WATCH BELOW: Nonprofit running low on supplies for military care packages Non-profit needs donations to send to military members They send monthly care packages to more than 5,200 active duty military units. I connected with the organization's leadership at its headquarters in Lake Worth earlier this year and have even brought my own family to prepare the packages. The executive director tells me that extended deployments due to the war in Iran and new units requesting packages are dwindling their supplies.             A detailed list of needed items is available on the Forgotten Soldiers Outreach website .

entry.title: The cost is steep in 2026 to insure new teen drivers in Florida
entry.summary: The cost of adding a new young driver to your auto insurance policy this year isn't pretty. New data from MoneyGeek shows Florida is the most expensive state to insure a 16-year-old driver. Families should prepare to shell out $651 a month, or $7,812 a year. It's the highest amount in the nation and nine times more than what families in Hawaii spend at $72 a month. WATCH: The cost is steep in 2026 to insure new teen drivers in Florida The cost is steep in 2026 to insure new teen drivers in Florida Florida ranked the worst state in the country for a new driver, with a score of 67.9 out of 100. The metrics used in the rankings include monthly premiums, licensing laws and overall local conditions. Twelve of the 15 worst states considered costly or dangerous to insure new teen drivers are in the South or West. The study focused on drivers from 15 to 20-years-old. entry.title: ‘We’re about to fight’: Teens, dad clash at Indiantown bus stop over pizza and bullying - WPBF
entry.summary: ‘We’re about to fight’: Teens, dad clash at Indiantown bus stop over pizza and bullying    WPBF
entry.article_text: A confrontation between teenagers at an Indiantown school bus stop escalated into a man pulling a gun on two teens, according to a Martin County Sheriff’s Office report. The incident happened Friday morning near Southwest 174th Court and Southwest 175th Court as students were preparing to board a bus headed to South Fork High School. The sheriff’s office ultimately determined that no criminal charges would be filed as investigators believe the man who displayed the gun was legally allowed to defend himself under Florida’s Stand Your Ground Law. Sheriff John Budensiek said detectives spent the entire day Friday investigating the incident, interviewing students who were on the bus and the people involved. He said the investigation found the father had gone to the bus stop after his 16-year-old son reported being bullied by a 14-year-old student on the bus the day before. "The misinformation is of zero value. Actually, it's counterproductive to the safety of our citizens of Martin County," Budensiek said. According to the sheriff, the initial dispute happened Thursday when the 16-year-old got on the bus carrying a pizza. Budensiek said a 14-year-old student began asking the teen for pizza, eventually threatening him and hitting him in the head after he refused to give him some. The 16-year-old then went home and told his father what happened. Budensiek said the father returned to the bus stop that afternoon and spoke with the female bus driver, who told him she would try to address the situation. Confrontation at the bus stop The next morning, on Friday, the father drove his son to the bus stop. Budensiek said the 14-year-old involved in the previous day's incident was already on the bus when they arrived. As the 16-year-old got on the bus, his father began speaking with the driver again. According to the sheriff, that is when the 14-year-old got off the bus and confronted the father. "Now you have students on the bus that are yelling. You have the 14-year-old boy that came off the bus that's yelling, screaming at the dad," Budensiek said. Budensiek said other students on the bus then called another teenager to come to the scene. There were actually two 16-year-olds involved, according to the sheriff: the father's son, whom he described as the victim, and another 16-year-old who was already suspended from school and was not on the bus that morning. That second 16-year-old came to the bus stop after being summoned by students on the bus, Budensiek said. "So now you have two young men who look like grown men that are happening upon the dad, going at the dad and yelling at the dad," Budensiek said. The sheriff said the father initially held his hand up and repeatedly told the teenagers to stay back. "They got all the way up on him before he pulled out a concealed weapon and told them to get back, which he's legally allowed to do," Budensiek said. He said both teenagers backed away, the father put the gun away and the confrontation ended. The father then drove around the corner, flagged down a deputy and immediately explained what had happened. Dad drives right around the corner, flags down a deputy, says, 'This is what happened, this is what I did, this is why I did it,'" Budensiek said. No criminal charges Budensiek said detectives interviewed students who witnessed the incident, including students on the bus and the two teenagers who approached the father. He said investigators found the accounts were consistent. "Everybody said the consistent story," Budensiek said. The sheriff said investigators would have sought warrants for the 14-year-old and the other 16-year-old who approached the father if the father had wanted to pursue charges. "We would have filed for warrants on the 14-year-old and the 16-year-old that went after the dad, except for the fact that the dad did not want to press charges," Budensiek said. The sheriff said the father's actions may not have been how he would have handled it, but investigators determined he did not break the law. "While it may not have been how I would have handled it, did not do anything illegal. You are allowed to stand your ground whether the person coming after you is 16 or 24 or 34," Budensiek said. Budensiek also said the father is a security guard and was legally carrying a concealed firearm. It's my understanding that he was a security guard and was carrying the gun," Budensiek said. He emphasized that the weapon was concealed before the confrontation. Budensiek said the father has since pulled his son out of school and plans to homeschool him. "He just was going to protect himself and his son at all costs," the sheriff said. Teenagers dispute sheriff's account The two teenagers who were in the video told WPBF 25 News a different version of what happened, disputing the sheriff’s narrative and saying they were frightened when the gun was pointed at them. RJ McIntyre and Trevor Ivory spoke with WPBF 25 News about what they say happened. McIntyre said he was walking to the bus stop Friday morning when someone called him and told him there was "an old man here looking for you." He said that when he got closer, he saw the man near the bus. McIntyre said he boarded the bus and noticed the father pointing toward him through the window. He said a back-and-forth exchange then began between him and the father's son, who had been involved in the pizza dispute the previous day. McIntyre said the bus driver eventually told both teenagers they needed to get off the bus. He said they dropped their backpacks and appeared ready to fight. "We dropped our backpacks. We're about to fight," McIntyre said, recalling the confrontation. Ivory said he was not originally at the bus stop but received a call from his younger brother. "My brother called me and he was like, 'There's a grown men at the bus stop. He's looking for somebody,'" Ivory said. Ivory said he went to the bus stop because he felt responsible for his younger brother. "I'm supposed to look after him," Ivory said. He said he spoke with the adult man before the teenagers got off the bus. "I was like, 'What's up with you? Like, who are you looking for?'" Ivory said. He said he eventually saw McIntyre and the man's son come off the bus. He said he could tell they were fighting and told the man to give them space. "I'm telling the dad, I'm like, 'No, just let them two fade,'" Ivory said. Seconds later, Ivory said a gun was drawn. "And the next thing you know, he put his son behind him, and he pulled a gun out on us," he told WPBF. McIntyre said he remembers what was going through his head when he saw the gun. "I can't process anything. I'm just like, am I going to make it home? It's life or death right now. It's a gun," McIntyre said. McIntyre said he grew up in the area and had never experienced anything like it. Ivory said he was also stunned. "In the moment, I was just like, it's crazy," Ivory said. Both teens put their hands up as they backed away. The dispute the day before McIntyre acknowledged he had interacted with the other student the previous day, but disputed the sheriff's characterization of that interaction as bullying. He said the encounter started when the other teen brought pizza onto the bus. McIntyre said he asked if he could buy a slice for a dollar. Instead, he said, the other student responded disrespectfully. "He screamed in my face," McIntyre said. McIntyre said he continued trying to talk to the student about the interaction during the ride home. He acknowledged that he used profanity and said he could have handled the situation differently. I think, like, when I was asking for pizza and he told me, you know, the first time, I think I should have left it there," McIntyre said. Questions over the gun The teenagers said they believe the father should be held accountable for bringing a firearm to the bus stop. McIntyre said the presence of the gun was particularly concerning because there were other children nearby. "I feel like under any circumstance, however you felt, no firearms should be displayed at a bus stop where there's a bunch of kids on a bus looking forward to going to school," McIntyre said. He said students on the bus could be heard reacting to the incident. "As you all can hear in the video, 'Oh Lord, please Lord, I hope they don't get shot,'" McIntyre said. The sheriff, however, said the father did not pull the gun until after the teenagers had approached him despite repeated warnings to stay back. He said the incident would not have happened if the 14-year-old had remained on the bus. "If he had stayed on the bus and kept his mouth shut and everybody had not called the other friend over there, there would have been no issues," Budensiek said. Sheriff blasts social media video The sheriff also criticized the spread of a partial video of the confrontation on social media. He said the video did not show the entire context leading up to the firearm being displayed. "There was a video that was put out on social media that was a half of a video and a half of a fraction of the story that actually took place and that grew legs and got spread around, and that's extremely counterproductive," he said. Budensiek said the social media posts created confusion in the community and questioned the work of investigators. "It unsettles the community. It undermines our law enforcement job that we're out there investigating it," Budensiek told WPBF. The sheriff said his agency conducted a thorough investigation and would have arrested the two teenagers if the father had wanted to press charges. "We did a thorough investigation, and you are allowed to stand your ground," Budensiek said. The sheriff ultimately characterized the father as the victim in the incident and said there will be no criminal charges. "To recap it, the individual with the gun was the victim in this case," Budensiek said. He said the father has since taken his son out of school to be homeschooled. "He did not want to press charges. He just wants to be left alone. He wants his son to be left alone," he said. McIntyre and Ivory, meanwhile, maintain they were not the aggressors and question why the father came to their bus stop armed. This is a developing story. entry.title: Crosswalk coming to Haverhill Road near Greenacres Elementary School after safety study
entry.summary: A crosswalk is coming to Haverhill Road near Greenacres Elementary School after a county pedestrian safety study confirmed it's needed. Palm Beach County Engineering and Public Works is working to agree on the exact location either at Haverhill and Carver or Haverhill and 4th before submitting the design to the City of Greenacres. Once the crosswalk is installed, a crossing guard will be placed there. The city tells WPTV's Christy Waite they will allocate for the crossing guard(s). Waite has been investigating safety conditions along Haverhill Road across from Greenacres Elementary School for nearly a month. Brandon and Lynn Pote are among the parents who raised concerns about the stretch of road. 'Right here on Haverhill there's no school zone and it's 40 mph,' Pote said. The City of Greenacres tells WPTV: iWe have been in touch with PBC and are happy to hear they conducted a study and will be moving forward with the crosswalk. Being Haverhill is a county road, the review and permitting will be solely done by Palm Beach County rather than here at the city. When referencing the city, it is possible they will send a design to us as a courtesy which would just be a quick administrative review/feedback. We did have discussion with Palm Beach County and agreed to allocate a crossing guard(s). As this is not a identified 'school zone' and may not include flashing beacons, we did request some type of flashers to increase visibility for the safety of the students and crossing guards. The city will not be financially responsible for the project other than the crossing guards/i. Waite reached out to the Palm Beach County School District about the area being a school zone. The district said in a statement: iGreenacres Elementary School resides in a school zone, where traffic speeds are limited to 20 miles per hour along Jackson Avenue during arrival and dismissal times. With school in session, we remind drivers to allow extra commute time and exercise caution near schools. Please remain highly alert for students, school buses, and heavier traffic./i The crosswalk is expected to be completed early next year. entry.title: New midterm polling gives Democrats an edge in battleground states
entry.summary: With the midterm elections just 41 days away, a wave of polling released this week suggests Democrats may have an advantage in several key races. In Texas, where a Democrat has not won a statewide election since 1994, James Talarico is leading current state Attorney General Ken Paxton by 6 points in a Marist poll. RELATED STORY | Trump claims Iran is waiting until after midterm elections to strike deal In the battleground state of Michigan, Democratic challenger Abdul El-Sayed leads former Republican Rep. Mike Rogers by 7 points. In Alaska, former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola is edging Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan by 4 points. And in Iowa, Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson trails Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek by 8 points. Democrats need to flip four Senate seats to control the Senate. Despite the polling momentum, Democrats continue to face financial challenges heading into the final stretch of the campaign. RELATED STORY | 'Pretend that I'm on the ballot': Trump courts Republicans at unusual GOP midterm convention Federal Election Commission filings show Republicans outraised Democrats in July and have roughly eight times as much cash on hand. Democrats are also carrying about $18 million in debt.

entry.summary: The U.S. Department of Justice unsealed an indictment that charges a Postal Service employee in Utah with allegedly disposing of hundreds of mail-in ballots. Damon Matai Seei was arrested Tuesday and indicted a day later after officials said he 'did unlawfully secrete, destroy, and delay mail entrusted to him and which came into his possession.' Seei entered a not guilty plea and was released on his own recognizance. entry.title: CROS Ministries hosts Hustle to End Hunger 5K as food insecurity rises in Palm Beach County
entry.summary: CROS Ministries is preparing for its annual Hustle to End Hunger 5K as the nonprofit warns food insecurity continues to rise across Palm Beach County. During WPTVs 'Shining A Light' segment Wednesday morning, executive director Ruth Mageria said more than 200,000 people in Palm Beach County do not have enough to eat. WATCH BELOW: Hustle to End Hunger 5K helps families facing food insecurity Hustle to End Hunger 5K helps families facing food insecurity 'The numbers are up in terms of who's food insecure,' Mageria said. '(About) 200,000 individuals here in Palm Beach County don't have enough to eat.' The Hustle to End Hunger 5K will take place Saturday, Oct. 3, at John Prince Park near Lake Worth Beach. The event raises money for CROS Ministries food assistance programs serving Palm Beach and Martin counties. Mageria encouraged community members to participate in the race or volunteer to support the organizations mission. 'What you can do to help is come to the Hustle to End Hunger 5K on Saturday, October 3rd at John Prince Park,' Mageria said. Registration for the event is available online, and viewers can receive a 15% discount using the code 'WPTV' or 'FOX29' in all capital letters, according to organizers. Volunteers spent the morning packing race bags and organizing supplies inside the CROS Ministries warehouse in Lake Worth Beach. The race is also drawing support from local community groups, including Pineapple Grove Run Club. 'Were bringing the two communities together to raise awareness for hunger, and were excited,' said Rob Cordoba, a founder of Pineapple Grove Run Club and CROS board member. CROS Ministries operates food pantries, meal programs and produce recovery initiatives throughout the region. The nonprofit has reported growing demand for food assistance amid rising grocery and housing costs. The organization also encourages residents to volunteer. Students can also receive volunteer service hours through the organization, according to volunteers at the event.

entry.title: Woman arrested after stealing Broward Sheriff's cruiser, fleeing to St. Lucie County
entry.summary: A Fort Lauderdale woman was arrested Tuesday night after allegedly stealing a marked Broward County Sheriff's Office patrol car and abandoning it on Interstate 95 in St. Lucie County. The incident began at 9:30 p.m. when authorities issued a BOLO alert for the stolen Dodge Charger, which was traveling northbound on I-95. WATCH BELOW: Shannon Marie Dillon makes her first appearance Fort Lauderdale woman arrested after stealing Broward Sheriff's patrol car, abandoning it on I-95 At around 9:40 p.m., deputies with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Patrol Operations Bureau, along with officers from the Port St. Lucie Police Department and troopers from the Florida Highway Patrol, responded to I-95 after receiving information about the stolen patrol vehicle near Gatlin Boulevard. Within minutes, FHP located the abandoned patrol vehicle on the I-95 northbound exit ramp to SW Gatlin Boulevard at mile marker 118. During the response, St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office deputies found Shannon Marie Dillon, 42, in the area wearing an outer ballistic vest displaying Broward Sheriff's Office insignia. Dillon now faces charges in St. Lucie County including grand theft of law enforcement equipment, unlawful use of a police badge or law enforcement vehicle, unlawful possession of four or fewer identification items, possession or use of drug paraphernalia, possession of a weapon or ammunition by a convicted felon, driving while license suspended and resisting an officer without violence. She also faces charges out of Broward County for grand theft of law enforcement equipment from an authorized emergency vehicle and grand theft. The northbound I-95 exit ramp to SW Gatlin Boulevard was temporarily closed while crime scene investigators processed the scene. The ramp reopened at 12:45 a.m. Wednesday morning.

entry.title: Cybersecurity expert finds card skimmer on Fort Pierce gas pump - WPEC
entry.summary: Cybersecurity expert finds card skimmer on Fort Pierce gas pump    WPEC
entry.article_text: A man with decades of experience in cybersecurity found a credit card skimmer on a gas pump at a Fort Pierce 7-Eleven , and police are now investigating. Arlo Bess said he was stopping for gas at the 7-Eleven on the south side of Orange Avenue near Interstate 95 before heading back to Palm Bay when he found the device. Bess said he has worked in cybersecurity on and off for about 25 years. He said that background made him cautious at the pump. For years, he has tugged on the outside of the card reader every time he pays with a card at a gas station. He said this was the first time one came loose. "I was quite surprised when I went in there and pulled on it, just like I normally do, half not expecting anything to come out, and out pops this," Bess said. Bess said skimmers take almost no time to put on. "It literally takes about two to three seconds to put one in place and about the same amount of time to pull one out," Bess said. Bess said skimmers like this one are often held on with double-sided tape. A small chip inside reads the data on a card's magnetic stripe as it goes in. He said thieves usually leave a device in place for about a week and collect card numbers, expiration dates, and often security codes. They can then sell that information on the dark web or copy it onto other cards to make purchases at places like self-checkout kiosks or online. Bess took the device inside and showed it to the store manager, who called police. He said officers arrived a few minutes later and took a report, and they checked every pump at the station with him for more skimmers. Bess said neither the manager nor the responding officer had ever seen a skimmer in person. He said the manager also reported it to her supervisor with the company. The Fort Pierce Police Department confirmed it is investigating. Bess said you can't reliably spot a skimmer just by looking. "By looking at it visually, you can't tell the difference between a pump that's got a skimmer on it and one that doesn't," Bess said. See also: Is it illegal to drive with hazard lights on in the rain? It depends; here's the law The one he found looked newer and shinier than the scuffed readers on the other pumps. Still, he said the best check is a firm pull on the card reader with your hands, without using tools. He also said newer skimmers can sit inside the card slot, where they can't be seen at all. "My advice would be to tap your card, go inside and pay. It's much harder to put these skimming devices on card readers inside the store," Bess said. He also recommends not using a debit card at the pump. He said fraud protections for debit cards are different from those for credit cards, so it can take weeks to get stolen money back from a checking account. If you need to use a debit or ATM card, Bess suggests using a machine inside a bank lobby. He said outdoor machines, including drive-thru ATMs, are easier targets because thieves are less likely to be seen. We'll have an update on the investigation from the Fort Pierce Police Department, and we'll give you the details when they become available.

entry.title: ‘We’re about to fight’: Teens, dad clash at Indiantown bus stop over pizza and bullying - WPBF
entry.summary: ‘We’re about to fight’: Teens, dad clash at Indiantown bus stop over pizza and bullying    WPBF
entry.article_text: A confrontation between teenagers at an Indiantown school bus stop escalated into a man pulling a gun on two teens, according to a Martin County Sheriff’s Office report. The incident happened Friday morning near Southwest 174th Court and Southwest 175th Court as students were preparing to board a bus headed to South Fork High School. The sheriff’s office ultimately determined that no criminal charges would be filed as investigators believe the man who displayed the gun was legally allowed to defend himself under Florida’s Stand Your Ground Law. Sheriff John Budensiek said detectives spent the entire day Friday investigating the incident, interviewing students who were on the bus and the people involved. He said the investigation found the father had gone to the bus stop after his 16-year-old son reported being bullied by a 14-year-old student on the bus the day before. "The misinformation is of zero value. Actually, it's counterproductive to the safety of our citizens of Martin County," Budensiek said. According to the sheriff, the initial dispute happened Thursday when the 16-year-old got on the bus carrying a pizza. Budensiek said a 14-year-old student began asking the teen for pizza, eventually threatening him and hitting him in the head after he refused to give him some. The 16-year-old then went home and told his father what happened. Budensiek said the father returned to the bus stop that afternoon and spoke with the female bus driver, who told him she would try to address the situation. Confrontation at the bus stop The next morning, on Friday, the father drove his son to the bus stop. Budensiek said the 14-year-old involved in the previous day's incident was already on the bus when they arrived. As the 16-year-old got on the bus, his father began speaking with the driver again. According to the sheriff, that is when the 14-year-old got off the bus and confronted the father. "Now you have students on the bus that are yelling. You have the 14-year-old boy that came off the bus that's yelling, screaming at the dad," Budensiek said. Budensiek said other students on the bus then called another teenager to come to the scene. There were actually two 16-year-olds involved, according to the sheriff: the father's son, whom he described as the victim, and another 16-year-old who was already suspended from school and was not on the bus that morning. That second 16-year-old came to the bus stop after being summoned by students on the bus, Budensiek said. "So now you have two young men who look like grown men that are happening upon the dad, going at the dad and yelling at the dad," Budensiek said. The sheriff said the father initially held his hand up and repeatedly told the teenagers to stay back. "They got all the way up on him before he pulled out a concealed weapon and told them to get back, which he's legally allowed to do," Budensiek said. He said both teenagers backed away, the father put the gun away and the confrontation ended. The father then drove around the corner, flagged down a deputy and immediately explained what had happened. Dad drives right around the corner, flags down a deputy, says, 'This is what happened, this is what I did, this is why I did it,'" Budensiek said. No criminal charges Budensiek said detectives interviewed students who witnessed the incident, including students on the bus and the two teenagers who approached the father. He said investigators found the accounts were consistent. "Everybody said the consistent story," Budensiek said. The sheriff said investigators would have sought warrants for the 14-year-old and the other 16-year-old who approached the father if the father had wanted to pursue charges. "We would have filed for warrants on the 14-year-old and the 16-year-old that went after the dad, except for the fact that the dad did not want to press charges," Budensiek said. The sheriff said the father's actions may not have been how he would have handled it, but investigators determined he did not break the law. "While it may not have been how I would have handled it, did not do anything illegal. You are allowed to stand your ground whether the person coming after you is 16 or 24 or 34," Budensiek said. Budensiek also said the father is a security guard and was legally carrying a concealed firearm. It's my understanding that he was a security guard and was carrying the gun," Budensiek said. He emphasized that the weapon was concealed before the confrontation. Budensiek said the father has since pulled his son out of school and plans to homeschool him. "He just was going to protect himself and his son at all costs," the sheriff said. Teenagers dispute sheriff's account The two teenagers who were in the video told WPBF 25 News a different version of what happened, disputing the sheriff’s narrative and saying they were frightened when the gun was pointed at them. RJ McIntyre and Trevor Ivory spoke with WPBF 25 News about what they say happened. McIntyre said he was walking to the bus stop Friday morning when someone called him and told him there was "an old man here looking for you." He said that when he got closer, he saw the man near the bus. McIntyre said he boarded the bus and noticed the father pointing toward him through the window. He said a back-and-forth exchange then began between him and the father's son, who had been involved in the pizza dispute the previous day. McIntyre said the bus driver eventually told both teenagers they needed to get off the bus. He said they dropped their backpacks and appeared ready to fight. "We dropped our backpacks. We're about to fight," McIntyre said, recalling the confrontation. Ivory said he was not originally at the bus stop but received a call from his younger brother. "My brother called me and he was like, 'There's a grown men at the bus stop. He's looking for somebody,'" Ivory said. Ivory said he went to the bus stop because he felt responsible for his younger brother. "I'm supposed to look after him," Ivory said. He said he spoke with the adult man before the teenagers got off the bus. "I was like, 'What's up with you? Like, who are you looking for?'" Ivory said. He said he eventually saw McIntyre and the man's son come off the bus. He said he could tell they were fighting and told the man to give them space. "I'm telling the dad, I'm like, 'No, just let them two fade,'" Ivory said. Seconds later, Ivory said a gun was drawn. "And the next thing you know, he put his son behind him, and he pulled a gun out on us," he told WPBF. McIntyre said he remembers what was going through his head when he saw the gun. "I can't process anything. I'm just like, am I going to make it home? It's life or death right now. It's a gun," McIntyre said. McIntyre said he grew up in the area and had never experienced anything like it. Ivory said he was also stunned. "In the moment, I was just like, it's crazy," Ivory said. Both teens put their hands up as they backed away. The dispute the day before McIntyre acknowledged he had interacted with the other student the previous day, but disputed the sheriff's characterization of that interaction as bullying. He said the encounter started when the other teen brought pizza onto the bus. McIntyre said he asked if he could buy a slice for a dollar. Instead, he said, the other student responded disrespectfully. "He screamed in my face," McIntyre said. McIntyre said he continued trying to talk to the student about the interaction during the ride home. He acknowledged that he used profanity and said he could have handled the situation differently. I think, like, when I was asking for pizza and he told me, you know, the first time, I think I should have left it there," McIntyre said. Questions over the gun The teenagers said they believe the father should be held accountable for bringing a firearm to the bus stop. McIntyre said the presence of the gun was particularly concerning because there were other children nearby. "I feel like under any circumstance, however you felt, no firearms should be displayed at a bus stop where there's a bunch of kids on a bus looking forward to going to school," McIntyre said. He said students on the bus could be heard reacting to the incident. "As you all can hear in the video, 'Oh Lord, please Lord, I hope they don't get shot,'" McIntyre said. The sheriff, however, said the father did not pull the gun until after the teenagers had approached him despite repeated warnings to stay back. He said the incident would not have happened if the 14-year-old had remained on the bus. "If he had stayed on the bus and kept his mouth shut and everybody had not called the other friend over there, there would have been no issues," Budensiek said. Sheriff blasts social media video The sheriff also criticized the spread of a partial video of the confrontation on social media. He said the video did not show the entire context leading up to the firearm being displayed. "There was a video that was put out on social media that was a half of a video and a half of a fraction of the story that actually took place and that grew legs and got spread around, and that's extremely counterproductive," he said. Budensiek said the social media posts created confusion in the community and questioned the work of investigators. "It unsettles the community. It undermines our law enforcement job that we're out there investigating it," Budensiek told WPBF. The sheriff said his agency conducted a thorough investigation and would have arrested the two teenagers if the father had wanted to press charges. "We did a thorough investigation, and you are allowed to stand your ground," Budensiek said. The sheriff ultimately characterized the father as the victim in the incident and said there will be no criminal charges. "To recap it, the individual with the gun was the victim in this case," Budensiek said. He said the father has since taken his son out of school to be homeschooled. "He did not want to press charges. He just wants to be left alone. He wants his son to be left alone," he said. McIntyre and Ivory, meanwhile, maintain they were not the aggressors and question why the father came to their bus stop armed. This is a developing story. entry.title: Tri-Rail fares set to increase 10% on Oct. 1
entry.summary: Tri-Rail fares will increase by 10% beginning Oct. 1, the South Florida Regional Transportation Authority (SFRTA) announced Wednesday. The fare adjustment was approved by the SFRTA Governing Board following a public hearing held on June 26, SFRTA stated in a press release. WATCH BELOW: Tri-Rail funding crisis threatens service for South Florida commuters Tri-Rail funding crisis threatens service for South Florida commuters The increase comes weeks after WPTV's Samantha Gutierrez reported that Tri-Rail is facing a severe funding crisis that threatens to disrupt or eliminate services. The commuter rail line is counting on $60 million in state funding that is currently stalled, leaving the future of the system uncertain despite a record-breaking year of 4.5 million passenger rides. SFRTA said the fare adjustment will help sustain long-term financial sustainability of the system. Tri-Rail continues to provide an important and affordable transportation option for residents, commuters and visitors traveling throughout the region, Diane Hernandez Del Calvo, SFRTA deputy executive director, said in the release. This fare adjustment is just one of the components to help sustain service and support the long-term financial sustainability of the system. The adjustment will apply to applicable fare products, including one-way fares and passes. Discounted fares will continue to be available for eligible passengers in accordance with Tri-Rails fare policies, SFRTA said. Tri-Rail remains committed to providing an affordable alternative to driving and connecting communities throughout Palm Beach, Broward and Miami-Dade counties. The system also provides connections to the regions major airports and other transportation services. Passengers and members of the public are encouraged to familiarize themselves with the new fare structure by visiting Tri-Rails website www.tri-rail.com , or calling 1-800-874-7245.

entry.title: West Palm Beach advances Downtown Master Plan as residents seek balance between growth and livability
entry.summary: When residents and visitors walk through downtown West Palm Beach, it's hard to miss the transformation. Construction cranes tower over city blocks, development projects are taking shape in nearly every direction and city leaders are trying to determine how future growth should unfold. 'A lot of growth happening. Just take a couple strolls down a few blocks and you'll see that there's construction going on everywhere,' said Mark Alpaugh, who works downtown. 'As a young professional like myself, it's exciting to see.' For longtime residents and newcomers alike, the changing skyline is impossible to ignore. 'It's a completely different city,' said downtown resident Gabriella Biondo, reflecting on the changes since she was a student at Palm Beach Atlantic University. The city Master Plan moved forward through the downtown action committee at the beginning of the month. And while many welcome the growth, city officials acknowledge it comes with challenges. Last week, the West Palm Beach Planning Board unanimously recommended approval of comprehensive plan amendments tied to the Downtown Master Plan update, a document that could help shape how downtown grows over the next several decades. The recommendation is not the final step. Additional public meetings and hearings are still planned before the City Commission makes final decisions. City leaders: Growth is happening regardless Throughout the discussion, city leaders and planning consultants repeatedly emphasized one key message: 'Development is coming whether we like it or not,' said consultant Bernard Zyscovich during the Downtown Master Plan presentation. Officials argued the city has two choices: proactively plan for growth or allow development to occur under existing regulations and state laws. Zyscovich said the city is trying to stay ahead of development pressures before they become more difficult to manage. 'There is no way to stop some of these things if we don't get ahead of it,' Zyscovich said. entry.article_text: When residents and visitors walk through downtown West Palm Beach, it's hard to miss the transformation.Construction cranes tower over city blocks, development projects are taking shape in nearly every direction and city leaders are trying to determine how future growth should unfold."A lot of growth happening. Just take a couple strolls down a few blocks and you'll see that there's construction going on everywhere," said Mark Alpaugh, who works downtown. "As a young professional like myself, it's exciting to see."For longtime residents and newcomers alike, the changing skyline is impossible to ignore."It's a completely different city," said downtown resident Gabriella Biondo, reflecting on the changes since she was a student at Palm Beach Atlantic University.The city Master Plan moved forward through the downtown action committee at the beginning of the month.And while many welcome the growth, city officials acknowledge it comes with challenges.Last week, the West Palm Beach Planning Board unanimously recommended approval of comprehensive plan amendments tied to the Downtown Master Plan update, a document that could help shape how downtown grows over the next several decades.The recommendation is not the final step. Additional public meetings and hearings are still planned before the City Commission makes final decisions.Throughout the discussion, city leaders and planning consultants repeatedly emphasized one key message:"Development is coming whether we like it or not," said consultant Bernard Zyscovich during the Downtown Master Plan presentation.Officials argued the city has two choices: proactively plan for growth or allow development to occur under existing regulations and state laws.Zyscovich said the city is trying to stay ahead of development pressures before they become more difficult to manage."There is no way to stop some of these things if we don't get ahead of it," Zyscovich said.Planning Board Chairman Steven Mayans said many of the issues residents are experiencing today are the result of West Palm Beach becoming a more desirable place to live."The problems are an outgrowth of success, and hopefully the growth is going to happen. Hopefully we're learning to manage it well," Mayans.One of the proposed changes centers on affordable housing.Under the plan, developers seeking additional building height and density would face stronger affordable housing requirements.Planning Director Anna Maria Ponte told board members:"The intention is to have every new project downtown basically support the construction of affordable housing," Ponte.The proposal would allow developers to build larger projects in certain districts, but only if they provide additional affordable housing or contribute toward affordable housing goals.For Biondo, that is one of the most important parts of the discussion.When asked what she hopes comes from the master plan, she said:"I would love less traffic, more affordable housing. All that sounds great," said Biondo. "It's not really affordable I would say to live downtown in West Palm Beach. I spend a lot of money for the convenience."City leaders also want to direct more development into transit-oriented areas near Brightline and Tri-Rail instead of pushing growth deeper into existing neighborhoods.Officials said those areas have stronger transportation options and are better suited to accommodate future development.The goal, they said, is to concentrate density where transit access is strongest while preserving the character of established neighborhoods.While affordable housing generated discussion, traffic remained the dominant concern throughout the meeting.City officials presented data showing Okeechobee Boulevard is operating at roughly 98% to 99% of planning capacity between Australian and Rosemary avenues.Residents and board members repeatedly raised concerns about congestion downtown and whether infrastructure can keep pace with new development.Alpaugh said traffic frustrations are already part of daily life."Okeechobee can sometimes get backed up, which can be frustrating," Alpaugh.One proposed solution would reduce the number of parking spaces developers are required to provide by about 25% in certain transit-oriented districts.Supporters argue fewer parking spaces could encourage greater use of public transportation, walking and biking.Planning Director Anna Maria Ponte defended the strategy during the meeting."If the concern is congestion, the solution is not to allow everybody to drive because we are never going to be able to have enough road for everybody," Ponte. "We're not restricting it. If you want to drive, you will be able to drive. We're not going to say you're not. But we offer other options for different alternatives and create certain friction. So the (best option is not always drive."Planning Board member Sam Fisch agreed saying, "The only way to have less traffic with more people is to have less cars."Several residents argued that future development isn't the biggest issue. Instead, they pointed to the impacts of projects already underway.Speakers described traffic detours, construction noise, dust, vibration and quality-of-life concerns.In response, city officials said they're evaluating stronger construction-management requirements, including regulations governing traffic plans, truck routes, staging areas, worker parking and enforcement measures.While many residents said they are not opposed to growth, several argued the city should move more carefully and ensure infrastructure can handle future development.One of the strongest comments came from resident Mark Hyman."Will it remain a livable city with a strong sense of community and an excellent quality of life? Growth is not the enemy, though. Poorly planned growth is."That statement captured much of the concern voiced by residents who say they want development but believe it must be managed carefully.The Planning Board's vote does not finalize the Downtown Master Plan.A public meeting is scheduled for Oct. 6 at Flagler Gallery at City Hall, followed by additional Planning Board discussions on Oct. City commissioners are expected to begin reviewing the plan later this fall.For now, the debate continues over how West Palm Beach should grow, and what kind of city it hopes to become in the years ahead.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Port St. Lucie HOA tells residents to replace dead trees, homeowners push back - WPEC
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie HOA tells residents to replace dead trees, homeowners push back    WPEC
entry.article_text: Some residents in Port St. Lucie and their homeowners' association are at odds over dead trees. People who live in Cadence at Tradition received a letter dated Sept. 1 from Campbell Property Management on behalf of Cadence at Tradition Homeowners Association Inc., saying the dead tree or dead trees on their property need to be replaced. The letter says: "Your assistance and cooperation are requested regarding the following: Landscaping-Dead Tree- The deceased tree(s) on your property is in need of attention." Residents say the trees are on the easement, the strip of grass between the sidewalk and the street, and the trees were killed during a cold snap. Because the dead trees are on the easement, some residents say it should be the HOA 's job to replace them at the HOA's expense, not the homeowners. The letter goes on to say: "We kindly request you address this matter by 9/30/26 to avoid escalation." See also: Stolen Broward deputy's car found on I-95 in St. Lucie County, woman arrested The letter does not say what action will be taken if a homeowner does not replace the dead trees. Some residents say now is not the best time to replace the dead trees. They say if new trees need to be planted, it should be done in April, at the start of the growing season. Some say if new trees are planted now, they could be wiped out by a freeze in the months ahead.

entry.title: ‘Is this going to be the real one?’ Martin County families react after fourth bomb threat - WPEC
entry.summary: ‘Is this going to be the real one?’ Martin County families react after fourth bomb threat    WPEC
entry.article_text: Students returned to class as usual Wednesday after a 15-year-old Martin County High School student was accused of making a false bomb threat Tuesday, marking the fourth threat tied to the Stuart school in just over a week as parents voice growing concern. Families express concern after repeated threats: The repeated threats are taking a toll on some students and parents. CBS12 News spoke with freshman Maya and her mother, Liz, during school drop-off Wednesday morning. Maya described the response to one of the previous threats as frightening. The last bomb threat, it was crazy because, like a cop in Building Two, the alarm didn’t even go off, Maya said. A police officer had to go door to door and come get us and tell us to get out of the building. So, it was kind of like scary. Her mother said the string of threats has left her questioning what could happen each time she drops her daughter off at school. It is very concerning, Liz said. Every morning it’s like, should I bring her to school today? Is it going to be another one? Is this going to be the real one? District officials told CBS12 News counselors are readily available to support students if they are nervous from the ongoing issue. Student arrested in latest threat: The latest threat was reported Tuesday morning. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office said 15-year-old sophomore Noah Taylor used FortifyFL, Florida’s school safety reporting system, to submit a report claiming bombs were inside a boys bathroom and would go off during third period. The school resource deputy determined the threat was not credible. Investigators said surveillance video and interviews with students led them to Taylor. Deputies said Taylor later admitted making the false report because Taylor wanted to get out of his third-period class. Taylor was arrested and charged with making a false report concerning the planting of a bomb, a second-degree felony. Sheriff John Budensiek said Taylor is not believed to be connected to the three previous threats involving Martin County High School. Three earlier threats still under investigation: The Sheriff’s Office continues to investigate the other three threats. Budensiek said investigators traced the first threat to someone in Russia. The other two investigations remain active. The sheriff has warned students that false threats can carry serious and lasting consequences, including criminal charges and possible school discipline. For families such as Maya and Liz, the concern now is whether the threats will stop. The advice I give to my daughter is to stay calm. She’s very smart and quick to think, and I tell her to do what God is telling her right away. Follow the rules and what the teachers tell you, but you have to react how you feel in that moment. I know they’re not allowed to use their phones, but I really don’t care if you need to make a phone call in an emergency, just do it," said Liz. Maya said what initially felt unusual has started to feel more routine after so many incidents. A lot of people were screaming and calling their parents. Then, when they got home, they were looking on Facebook because Facebook has everything. We all talked about it and who we think is doing it. Everyone was saying it was Russia or something, but I don’t know," said Maya. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office continues working to determine who is responsible for the three unresolved threats. Martin County High School released the following statement: The safety and security of our students and staff remains our top priority. We appreciate the swift response and coordination of the Martin County Sheriff's Office, our School Resource Officers, and the District's Safety and Security Team, whose efforts allowed yesterday's false FortifyFL report involving Martin County High School to be quickly investigated, determined to be unfounded, and ultimately resolved with an arrest. Because the report was confirmed to be false, there is no additional law enforcement presence on campus related to this incident. Our two School Resource Officers remain on campus, and additional patrols continue as part of our normal daily safety operations. We also want to be clear: false threats and false reports are not pranks. They create fear, disrupt the educational environment, divert critical law enforcement resources, and carry serious disciplinary and criminal consequences. Individuals who make false reports should expect to be held fully accountable, exactly as how it unfolded yesterday. We understand these threats can cause fear and distress, and when we talk about student safety, we want them to feel safe as well. We will be providing additional services and staff during the school day, including School Social Service Workers and School Counselors, and we encourage students who need support to talk with them. We continue to encourage students, staff, and families to report legitimate safety concerns. Every report is taken seriously and investigated thoroughly because protecting our students and staff will always come first.

entry.title: Woman arrested after stealing Broward Sheriff's cruiser, fleeing to St. Lucie County - wflx.com
entry.summary: Woman arrested after stealing Broward Sheriff's cruiser, fleeing to St. Lucie County    wflx.com
entry.article_text: A Fort Lauderdale woman was arrested Tuesday night after allegedly stealing a marked Broward County Sheriff’s Office patrol car and abandoning it on Interstate 95 in St. The incident began at 9:30 p.m. when authorities issued a BOLO alert for the stolen Dodge Charger, which was traveling northbound on I-95. At around 9:40 p.m., deputies with the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office Patrol Operations Bureau, along with officers from the Port St. Lucie Police Department and troopers from the Florida Highway Patrol, responded to I-95 after receiving information about the stolen patrol vehicle near Gatlin Boulevard. Within minutes, FHP located the abandoned patrol vehicle on the I-95 northbound exit ramp to SW Gatlin Boulevard at mile marker 118. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office deputies found Shannon Marie Dillon, 42, in the area wearing an outer ballistic vest displaying Broward Sheriff’s Office insignia. Dillon now faces charges in St. Lucie County including grand theft of law enforcement equipment, unlawful use of a police badge or law enforcement vehicle, unlawful possession of four or fewer identification items, possession or use of drug paraphernalia, possession of a weapon or ammunition by a convicted felon, driving while license suspended and resisting an officer without violence. She also faces charges out of Broward County for grand theft of law enforcement equipment from an authorized emergency vehicle and grand theft. The northbound I-95 exit ramp to SW Gatlin Boulevard was temporarily closed while crime scene investigators processed the scene. The ramp reopened at 12:45 a.m.

entry.summary: Former NFL star wide receiver Antonio Brown plans to accept a plea deal on an attempted murder charge in Miami that avoids prison, his lawyer said Wednesday. Brown is scheduled to appear in court next Wednesday to make the deal final. He could face up to 30 years in prison if convicted of the current attempted murder charge. RECENT NFL NEWS| Stafford passes Philip Rivers on all-time TD list in Rams win Brown is accused of grabbing a handgun from a security staffer after a celebrity boxing match in Miami on May 16, 2025, and firing two shots at a man he had gotten into a fistfight with earlier, according to an arrest warrant. Zul-Qarnain Kwame Nantambu told investigators that one of the bullets grazed his neck. Brown spent 12 years in the NFL and was an All-Pro wide receiver who last played in 2021 for Tampa Bay, including a Super Bowl championship with quarterback Tom Brady. He spent much of his career with Pittsburgh. entry.title: ‘We’re about to fight’: Teens, dad clash at Indiantown bus stop over pizza and bullying - wpbf.com
entry.summary: ‘We’re about to fight’: Teens, dad clash at Indiantown bus stop over pizza and bullying    wpbf.com
entry.article_text: A confrontation between teenagers at an Indiantown school bus stop escalated into a man pulling a gun on two teens, according to a Martin County Sheriff’s Office report. The incident happened Friday morning near Southwest 174th Court and Southwest 175th Court as students were preparing to board a bus headed to South Fork High School. The sheriff’s office ultimately determined that no criminal charges would be filed as investigators believe the man who displayed the gun was legally allowed to defend himself under Florida’s Stand Your Ground Law. Sheriff John Budensiek said detectives spent the entire day Friday investigating the incident, interviewing students who were on the bus and the people involved. He said the investigation found the father had gone to the bus stop after his 16-year-old son reported being bullied by a 14-year-old student on the bus the day before. "The misinformation is of zero value. Actually, it's counterproductive to the safety of our citizens of Martin County," Budensiek said. According to the sheriff, the initial dispute happened Thursday when the 16-year-old got on the bus carrying a pizza. Budensiek said a 14-year-old student began asking the teen for pizza, eventually threatening him and hitting him in the head after he refused to give him some. The 16-year-old then went home and told his father what happened. Budensiek said the father returned to the bus stop that afternoon and spoke with the female bus driver, who told him she would try to address the situation. Confrontation at the bus stop The next morning, on Friday, the father drove his son to the bus stop. Budensiek said the 14-year-old involved in the previous day's incident was already on the bus when they arrived. As the 16-year-old got on the bus, his father began speaking with the driver again. According to the sheriff, that is when the 14-year-old got off the bus and confronted the father. "Now you have students on the bus that are yelling. You have the 14-year-old boy that came off the bus that's yelling, screaming at the dad," Budensiek said. Budensiek said other students on the bus then called another teenager to come to the scene. There were actually two 16-year-olds involved, according to the sheriff: the father's son, whom he described as the victim, and another 16-year-old who was already suspended from school and was not on the bus that morning. That second 16-year-old came to the bus stop after being summoned by students on the bus, Budensiek said. "So now you have two young men who look like grown men that are happening upon the dad, going at the dad and yelling at the dad," Budensiek said. The sheriff said the father initially held his hand up and repeatedly told the teenagers to stay back. "They got all the way up on him before he pulled out a concealed weapon and told them to get back, which he's legally allowed to do," Budensiek said. He said both teenagers backed away, the father put the gun away and the confrontation ended. The father then drove around the corner, flagged down a deputy and immediately explained what had happened. Dad drives right around the corner, flags down a deputy, says, 'This is what happened, this is what I did, this is why I did it,'" Budensiek said. No criminal charges Budensiek said detectives interviewed students who witnessed the incident, including students on the bus and the two teenagers who approached the father. He said investigators found the accounts were consistent. "Everybody said the consistent story," Budensiek said. The sheriff said investigators would have sought warrants for the 14-year-old and the other 16-year-old who approached the father if the father had wanted to pursue charges. "We would have filed for warrants on the 14-year-old and the 16-year-old that went after the dad, except for the fact that the dad did not want to press charges," Budensiek said. The sheriff said the father's actions may not have been how he would have handled it, but investigators determined he did not break the law. "While it may not have been how I would have handled it, did not do anything illegal. You are allowed to stand your ground whether the person coming after you is 16 or 24 or 34," Budensiek said. Budensiek also said the father is a security guard and was legally carrying a concealed firearm. It's my understanding that he was a security guard and was carrying the gun," Budensiek said. He emphasized that the weapon was concealed before the confrontation. Budensiek said the father has since pulled his son out of school and plans to homeschool him. "He just was going to protect himself and his son at all costs," the sheriff said. Teenagers dispute sheriff's account The two teenagers who were in the video told WPBF 25 News a different version of what happened, disputing the sheriff’s narrative and saying they were frightened when the gun was pointed at them. RJ McIntyre and Trevor Ivory spoke with WPBF 25 News about what they say happened. McIntyre said he was walking to the bus stop Friday morning when someone called him and told him there was "an old man here looking for you." He said that when he got closer, he saw the man near the bus. McIntyre said he boarded the bus and noticed the father pointing toward him through the window. He said a back-and-forth exchange then began between him and the father's son, who had been involved in the pizza dispute the previous day. McIntyre said the bus driver eventually told both teenagers they needed to get off the bus. He said they dropped their backpacks and appeared ready to fight. "We dropped our backpacks. We're about to fight," McIntyre said, recalling the confrontation. Ivory said he was not originally at the bus stop but received a call from his younger brother. "My brother called me and he was like, 'There's a grown men at the bus stop. He's looking for somebody,'" Ivory said. Ivory said he went to the bus stop because he felt responsible for his younger brother. "I'm supposed to look after him," Ivory said. He said he spoke with the adult man before the teenagers got off the bus. "I was like, 'What's up with you? Like, who are you looking for?'" Ivory said. He said he eventually saw McIntyre and the man's son come off the bus. He said he could tell they were fighting and told the man to give them space. "I'm telling the dad, I'm like, 'No, just let them two fade,'" Ivory said. Seconds later, Ivory said a gun was drawn. "And the next thing you know, he put his son behind him, and he pulled a gun out on us," he told WPBF. McIntyre said he remembers what was going through his head when he saw the gun. "I can't process anything. I'm just like, am I going to make it home? It's life or death right now. It's a gun," McIntyre said. McIntyre said he grew up in the area and had never experienced anything like it. Ivory said he was also stunned. "In the moment, I was just like, it's crazy," Ivory said. Both teens put their hands up as they backed away. The dispute the day before McIntyre acknowledged he had interacted with the other student the previous day, but disputed the sheriff's characterization of that interaction as bullying. He said the encounter started when the other teen brought pizza onto the bus. McIntyre said he asked if he could buy a slice for a dollar. Instead, he said, the other student responded disrespectfully. "He screamed in my face," McIntyre said. McIntyre said he continued trying to talk to the student about the interaction during the ride home. He acknowledged that he used profanity and said he could have handled the situation differently. I think, like, when I was asking for pizza and he told me, you know, the first time, I think I should have left it there," McIntyre said. Questions over the gun The teenagers said they believe the father should be held accountable for bringing a firearm to the bus stop. McIntyre said the presence of the gun was particularly concerning because there were other children nearby. "I feel like under any circumstance, however you felt, no firearms should be displayed at a bus stop where there's a bunch of kids on a bus looking forward to going to school," McIntyre said. He said students on the bus could be heard reacting to the incident. "As you all can hear in the video, 'Oh Lord, please Lord, I hope they don't get shot,'" McIntyre said. The sheriff, however, said the father did not pull the gun until after the teenagers had approached him despite repeated warnings to stay back. He said the incident would not have happened if the 14-year-old had remained on the bus. "If he had stayed on the bus and kept his mouth shut and everybody had not called the other friend over there, there would have been no issues," Budensiek said. Sheriff blasts social media video The sheriff also criticized the spread of a partial video of the confrontation on social media. He said the video did not show the entire context leading up to the firearm being displayed. "There was a video that was put out on social media that was a half of a video and a half of a fraction of the story that actually took place and that grew legs and got spread around, and that's extremely counterproductive," he said. Budensiek said the social media posts created confusion in the community and questioned the work of investigators. "It unsettles the community. It undermines our law enforcement job that we're out there investigating it," Budensiek told WPBF. The sheriff said his agency conducted a thorough investigation and would have arrested the two teenagers if the father had wanted to press charges. "We did a thorough investigation, and you are allowed to stand your ground," Budensiek said. The sheriff ultimately characterized the father as the victim in the incident and said there will be no criminal charges. "To recap it, the individual with the gun was the victim in this case," Budensiek said. He said the father has since taken his son out of school to be homeschooled. "He did not want to press charges. He just wants to be left alone. He wants his son to be left alone," he said. McIntyre and Ivory, meanwhile, maintain they were not the aggressors and question why the father came to their bus stop armed. This is a developing story. entry.title: Port St. Lucie HOA tells residents to replace dead trees, homeowners push back - WPEC
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie HOA tells residents to replace dead trees, homeowners push back    WPEC
entry.article_text: Some residents in Port St. Lucie and their homeowners' association are at odds over dead trees. People who live in Cadence at Tradition received a letter dated Sept. 1 from Campbell Property Management on behalf of Cadence at Tradition Homeowners Association Inc., saying the dead tree or dead trees on their property need to be replaced. The letter says: "Your assistance and cooperation are requested regarding the following: Landscaping-Dead Tree- The deceased tree(s) on your property is in need of attention." Residents say the trees are on the easement, the strip of grass between the sidewalk and the street, and the trees were killed during a cold snap. Because the dead trees are on the easement, some residents say it should be the HOA 's job to replace them at the HOA's expense, not the homeowners. The letter goes on to say: "We kindly request you address this matter by 9/30/26 to avoid escalation." See also: Stolen Broward deputy's car found on I-95 in St. Lucie County, woman arrested The letter does not say what action will be taken if a homeowner does not replace the dead trees. Some residents say now is not the best time to replace the dead trees. They say if new trees need to be planted, it should be done in April, at the start of the growing season. Some say if new trees are planted now, they could be wiped out by a freeze in the months ahead.

entry.title: Delray Beach school zone cameras issue nearly 5,000 speeding tickets
entry.summary: New school zone speed cameras in Delray Beach have issued nearly 5,000 violations since enforcement began on Aug. 10, but a timing malfunction at one elementary school has prompted officials to dismiss and refund some of the $100 fines. entry.title: Amendment 3 could shift property-tax costs onto Florida renters, report warns
entry.summary: A tax break for Florida homeowners could bring a bigger bill for renters next door, according to a new report examining Amendment 3. The report released by the Florida Housing Coalition estimates that if local governments raise property-tax rates to replace revenue lost under the amendment, annual taxes would increase by an average of $406 per apartment and $1,081 per single-family rental home in 2028. Watch more from Forrest Saunders on the report Amendment 3 could shift property-tax costs onto Florida renters, report warns Much of that expense could ultimately be passed on to tenants through higher rents, said Jared Walczak, the tax-policy analyst who wrote the report. Renters pay taxes, they just don't write the check, Walczak said. Amendment 3 would increase the homestead exemption for non-school property taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, with inflation adjustments beginning in 2029. The exemption reduces the property value on which taxes are calculated for qualifying primary residences. School district property taxes would remain unchanged. Rental properties do not qualify for the homestead exemption. Local governments facing lost revenue could respond by cutting spending, increasing property-tax rates, raising other taxes or fees, or combining those approaches. Walczaks analysis models rate increases intended to replace lost revenue, subject to existing limits on those rates. While landlords would write the check, most of the burden would ultimately be borne by renters in the form of higher rent, he said. The estimates represent average increases in property-tax bills. How much of that cost reaches tenants would depend on rental-market conditions and local budget decisions. By 2031, the report estimates the additional annual property-tax burden would reach $544 per apartment and $1,471 per single-family rental home under the same approach. The amendment also includes a provision benefiting rental and other non-homestead properties: It would lower the annual cap on increases in assessed value from 10% to 5%. That limits assessment growth, while allowing local tax rates to rise. Walczaks report concludes that the benefit of the lower assessment cap would be outweighed by the modeled tax shift. Ron DeSantis supports Amendment 3 and says future lawmakers will pursue targeted state grants to help maintain essential services. Democrat David Jolly and Republican Byron Donalds spoke in back-to-back 30-minute panel discussions, but were kept separate throughout the event. entry.title: West Palm Beach advances Downtown Master Plan as residents seek balance between growth and livability
entry.summary: When residents and visitors walk through downtown West Palm Beach, it's hard to miss the transformation. entry.article_text: When residents and visitors walk through downtown West Palm Beach, it's hard to miss the transformation.Construction cranes tower over city blocks, development projects are taking shape in nearly every direction and city leaders are trying to determine how future growth should unfold.WATCH BELOW: Downtown Master Plan: How West Palm residents can weigh in"A lot of growth happening. Just take a couple strolls down a few blocks and you'll see that there's construction going on everywhere," said Mark Alpaugh, who works downtown. "As a young professional like myself, it's exciting to see."For longtime residents and newcomers alike, the changing skyline is impossible to ignore."It's a completely different city," said downtown resident Gabriella Biondo, reflecting on the changes since she was a student at Palm Beach Atlantic University.The city Master Plan moved forward through the downtown action committee at the beginning of the month.And while many welcome the growth, city officials acknowledge it comes with challenges.Last week, the West Palm Beach Planning Board unanimously recommended approval of comprehensive plan amendments tied to the Downtown Master Plan update, a document that could help shape how downtown grows over the next several decades.The recommendation is not the final step. Additional public meetings and hearings are still planned before the City Commission makes final decisions.Throughout the discussion, city leaders and planning consultants repeatedly emphasized one key message:"Development is coming whether we like it or not," said consultant Bernard Zyscovich during the Downtown Master Plan presentation.Officials argued the city has two choices: proactively plan for growth or allow development to occur under existing regulations and state laws.Zyscovich said the city is trying to stay ahead of development pressures before they become more difficult to manage."There is no way to stop some of these things if we don't get ahead of it," Zyscovich said.Planning Board Chairman Steven Mayans said many of the issues residents are experiencing today are the result of West Palm Beach becoming a more desirable place to live."The problems are an outgrowth of success, and hopefully the growth is going to happen. Hopefully we're learning to manage it well," Mayans.One of the proposed changes centers on affordable housing.Under the plan, developers seeking additional building height and density would face stronger affordable housing requirements.Planning Director Anna Maria Ponte told board members:"The intention is to have every new project downtown basically support the construction of affordable housing," Ponte.The proposal would allow developers to build larger projects in certain districts, but only if they provide additional affordable housing or contribute toward affordable housing goals.For Biondo, that is one of the most important parts of the discussion.When asked what she hopes comes from the master plan, she said:"I would love less traffic, more affordable housing. All that sounds great," said Biondo. "It's not really affordable I would say to live downtown in West Palm Beach. I spend a lot of money for the convenience."City leaders also want to direct more development into transit-oriented areas near Brightline and Tri-Rail instead of pushing growth deeper into existing neighborhoods.Officials said those areas have stronger transportation options and are better suited to accommodate future development.The goal, they said, is to concentrate density where transit access is strongest while preserving the character of established neighborhoods.While affordable housing generated discussion, traffic remained the dominant concern throughout the meeting.City officials presented data showing Okeechobee Boulevard is operating at roughly 98% to 99% of planning capacity between Australian and Rosemary avenues.Residents and board members repeatedly raised concerns about congestion downtown and whether infrastructure can keep pace with new development.Alpaugh said traffic frustrations are already part of daily life."Okeechobee can sometimes get backed up, which can be frustrating," Alpaugh.One proposed solution would reduce the number of parking spaces developers are required to provide by about 25% in certain transit-oriented districts.Supporters argue fewer parking spaces could encourage greater use of public transportation, walking and biking.Planning Director Anna Maria Ponte defended the strategy during the meeting."If the concern is congestion, the solution is not to allow everybody to drive because we are never going to be able to have enough road for everybody," Ponte. "We're not restricting it. If you want to drive, you will be able to drive. We're not going to say you're not. But we offer other options for different alternatives and create certain friction. So the (best option is not always drive."Planning Board member Sam Fisch agreed saying, "The only way to have less traffic with more people is to have less cars."Several residents argued that future development isn't the biggest issue. Instead, they pointed to the impacts of projects already underway.Speakers described traffic detours, construction noise, dust, vibration and quality-of-life concerns.In response, city officials said they're evaluating stronger construction-management requirements, including regulations governing traffic plans, truck routes, staging areas, worker parking and enforcement measures.While many residents said they are not opposed to growth, several argued the city should move more carefully and ensure infrastructure can handle future development.One of the strongest comments came from resident Mark Hyman."Will it remain a livable city with a strong sense of community and an excellent quality of life? Growth is not the enemy, though. Poorly planned growth is."That statement captured much of the concern voiced by residents who say they want development but believe it must be managed carefully.The Planning Board's vote does not finalize the Downtown Master Plan.A public meeting is scheduled for Oct. 6 at Flagler Gallery at City Hall, followed by additional Planning Board discussions on Oct. City commissioners are expected to begin reviewing the plan later this fall.For now, the debate continues over how West Palm Beach should grow, and what kind of city it hopes to become in the years ahead.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI.
