entry.title: Port St. Lucie HOA tells residents to replace dead trees, homeowners push back - WPEC
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie HOA tells residents to replace dead trees, homeowners push back    WPEC
entry.article_text: Some residents in Port St. Lucie and their homeowners' association are at odds over dead trees. People who live in Cadence at Tradition received a letter dated Sept. 1 from Campbell Property Management on behalf of Cadence at Tradition Homeowners Association Inc., saying the dead tree or dead trees on their property need to be replaced. The letter says: "Your assistance and cooperation are requested regarding the following: Landscaping-Dead Tree- The deceased tree(s) on your property is in need of attention." Residents say the trees are on the easement, the strip of grass between the sidewalk and the street, and the trees were killed during a cold snap. Because the dead trees are on the easement, some residents say it should be the HOA 's job to replace them at the HOA's expense, not the homeowners. The letter goes on to say: "We kindly request you address this matter by 9/30/26 to avoid escalation." See also: Stolen Broward deputy's car found on I-95 in St. Lucie County, woman arrested The letter does not say what action will be taken if a homeowner does not replace the dead trees. Some residents say now is not the best time to replace the dead trees. They say if new trees need to be planted, it should be done in April, at the start of the growing season. Some say if new trees are planted now, they could be wiped out by a freeze in the months ahead.

entry.article_text: A Fort Lauderdale woman is in the St. Lucie County Jail after a stolen Broward Sheriff's Office patrol vehicle was found abandoned on an Interstate 95 off-ramp Tuesday night, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office. The sheriff's office said deputies, Port St. Lucie police officers and Florida Highway Patrol troopers went to I-95 at about 9:40 p.m. They had received information that a stolen Broward Sheriff's Office patrol vehicle was heading north near Gatlin Boulevard. The response was coordinated with the Broward Sheriff's Office. When units arrived, they found the patrol vehicle abandoned on the Gatlin Boulevard off-ramp, the sheriff's office said. Deputies then saw a woman nearby wearing an outer ballistic vest with Broward Sheriff's Office insignia on it. They stopped her and identified her as Shannon Marie Dillon, 42, of Fort Lauderdale. Lucie County, Dillon faces charges of grand theft of law enforcement equipment, unlawful use of a police badge or law enforcement vehicle, unlawful possession of four or fewer identification items, possession or use of drug paraphernalia, possession of a weapon or ammunition by a convicted felon, driving while license suspended, and resisting an officer without violence. See also: Can Florida police pull you over for a license plate frame? What the new law says She also faces charges in Broward County of grand theft of law enforcement equipment from an authorized emergency vehicle and grand theft, according to the sheriff's office. Investigators with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office and the Broward Sheriff's Office are still working the case. The sheriff's office said it will release more information when it becomes available.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie HOA tells residents to replace dead trees, homeowners push back - WPEC
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie HOA tells residents to replace dead trees, homeowners push back    WPEC
entry.article_text: Some residents in Port St. Lucie and their homeowners' association are at odds over dead trees. People who live in Cadence at Tradition received a notice dated Sept. 1 from Campbell Property Management on behalf of Cadence at Tradition Homeowners Association Inc., saying the dead tree or dead trees on their property need to be replaced. The notice says: "Your assistance and cooperation are requested regarding the following: Landscaping-Dead Tree- The deceased tree(s) on your property is in need of attention." Residents say the trees are on the swale, the strip of grass between the sidewalk and the street, and numerous trees were killed during a cold snap. Because the dead trees are on the swale, some residents say it should be the HOA 's job to replace them at the HOA's expense, not the homeowners. "It's just a little bit frustrating and disappointing that we, as homeowners, have to endure this from the HOA," said Keyla Peguero, a homeowner at Cadence at Tradition. Recently the HOA has removed many of the dead trees, leaving holes in the ground where residents are supposed to put in new trees, at the homeowners' expense. But homeowners such as Chip Collison say the dead trees were in common areas, not their yards, so they want the HOA to pay for new trees in the swales. "You think the swale is a common area?" we asked Collison. "Based on the documentation I've read? The notice sent to homeowners goes on to say: "We kindly request you address this matter by 9/30/26 to avoid escalation." See also: Stolen Broward deputy's car found on I-95 in St. Lucie County, woman arrested The letter does not say what action will be taken if a homeowner does not replace the dead trees. Some residents say now is not the best time to replace the dead trees. They say if new trees need to be planted, it should be done in April, at the start of the growing season. Some say if new trees are planted now, they could be wiped out by a freeze in the months ahead. "We're well into hurricane season now. If we plant new trees, no one can predict the future. These trees could be freshly planted. We get a strong hurricane come through, they're all gone, and they're gonna have to be redone again," Collison said. Peguero says she replaced a dead tree in the swale in front of her house, at a total cost of $300 to remove the dead tree, haul it away and replace it with a new tree. She says she's not willing to do it again and shouldn't have had to do it in the first place. A public relations firm for The Cadence at Tradition HOA sent us this written statement: Currently, the HOA is replacing thousands of dead trees and shrubs in the common areas that have yet to recover from the last freeze. In the limited common areas, such as the rights of way immediately adjacent to and between individual lots, including areas containing sidewalks and driveway aprons, residents are responsible for replacing trees and maintaining these areas. Because the HOA is currently purchasing and installing trees in bulk, we’ve invited residents to participate in the program. This allows homeowners to share in the cost savings while ensuring that tree replacements around their homes are selected and installed professionally.

entry.summary: Florida's two gubernatorial nominees offered sharply different visions for the state's economy Wednesday at the WLRN Sunshine Economy Summit in downtown Fort Lauderdale, where affordability, property taxes, and hurricane insurance dominated the conversation. Democrat David Jolly and Republican Byron Donalds spoke in back-to-back 30-minute panel discussions, but were kept separate throughout the event. Donalds said he supports the measure. 'I think voters need relief. I think the property owners need relief,' Donalds said. 'I anticipate I will vote against Amendment 3,' Jolly told the audience. 'I don't think the math works, and I think we know that because even Ron DeSantis now won't campaign for Amendment 3, and our sheriffs have come out and said, 'Please don't do this. It's going to defund services.'' Hurricane insurance Disaster relief and insurance costs also emerged as a major point of contrast. 'We are not going to solve this without government taking on a larger role in backing this. Otherwise, people are going to be priced out of their homes,' Jolly said. Donalds said that plan won't work. He is instead calling for the elimination of a premium surcharge that contributes to the state's catastrophic fund. 'We get through this hurricane season, the Cat Fund is estimated to have somewhere between 13 and 13-and-a-half billion dollars. entry.title: Crosswalk coming to Haverhill Road near Greenacres Elementary School after safety study
entry.summary: A crosswalk is coming to Haverhill Road near Greenacres Elementary School after a county pedestrian safety study confirmed it's needed. Palm Beach County Engineering and Public Works is working to agree on the exact location either at Haverhill and Carver or Haverhill and 4th before submitting the design to the City of Greenacres. Once the crosswalk is installed, a crossing guard will be placed there. WATCH BELOW: Crosswalk coming to Haverhill Road near this school Crosswalk coming to Haverhill Road near Greenacres Elementary School after safety study The city tells WPTV's Christy Waite they will allocate for the crossing guard(s). Waite has been investigating safety conditions along Haverhill Road across from Greenacres Elementary School for nearly a month. Brandon and Lynn Pote are among the parents who raised concerns about the stretch of road. 'Right here on Haverhill there's no school zone and it's 40 mph,' Pote said. The City of Greenacres tells WPTV: iWe have been in touch with PBC and are happy to hear they conducted a study and will be moving forward with the crosswalk. Being Haverhill is a county road, the review and permitting will be solely done by Palm Beach County rather than here at the city. When referencing the city, it is possible they will send a design to us as a courtesy which would just be a quick administrative review/feedback. We did have discussion with Palm Beach County and agreed to allocate a crossing guard(s). As this is not a identified 'school zone' and may not include flashing beacons, we did request some type of flashers to increase visibility for the safety of the students and crossing guards. The city will not be financially responsible for the project other than the crossing guards/i. Waite reached out to the Palm Beach County School District about the area being a school zone. The district said in a statement: iGreenacres Elementary School resides in a school zone, where traffic speeds are limited to 20 miles per hour along Jackson Avenue during arrival and dismissal times. With school in session, we remind drivers to allow extra commute time and exercise caution near schools. Please remain highly alert for students, school buses, and heavier traffic./i The crosswalk is expected to be completed early next year. entry.title: Woman arrested after stealing Broward Sheriff's cruiser, fleeing to St. Lucie County
entry.summary: A Fort Lauderdale woman was arrested Tuesday night after allegedly stealing a marked Broward County Sheriff's Office patrol car and abandoning it on Interstate 95 in St. Lucie County. Woman who stole BSO patrol car found in ballistic vest in St. Lucie County, makes bizarre request to judge The incident began at 9:30 p.m. when authorities issued a BOLO alert for the stolen Dodge Charger, which was traveling northbound on I-95. WATCH BELOW: Shannon Marie Dillon makes her first appearance Fort Lauderdale woman arrested after stealing Broward Sheriff's patrol car, abandoning it on I-95 At around 9:40 p.m., deputies with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Patrol Operations Bureau, along with officers from the Port St. Lucie Police Department and troopers from the Florida Highway Patrol, responded to I-95 after receiving information about the stolen patrol vehicle near Gatlin Boulevard. Within minutes, FHP located the abandoned patrol vehicle on the I-95 northbound exit ramp to SW Gatlin Boulevard at mile marker 118. During the response, St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office deputies found Shannon Marie Dillon, 42, in the area wearing an outer ballistic vest displaying Broward Sheriff's Office insignia. Dillon now faces charges in St. Lucie County including grand theft of law enforcement equipment, unlawful use of a police badge or law enforcement vehicle, unlawful possession of four or fewer identification items, possession or use of drug paraphernalia, possession of a weapon or ammunition by a convicted felon, driving while license suspended and resisting an officer without violence. She also faces charges out of Broward County for grand theft of law enforcement equipment from an authorized emergency vehicle and grand theft. The northbound I-95 exit ramp to SW Gatlin Boulevard was temporarily closed while crime scene investigators processed the scene. The ramp reopened at 12:45 a.m. Wednesday morning.

entry.title: Gubernatorial Candidate Byron Donalds talks costs, insurance at Martin County roundtable - WPEC
entry.summary: Gubernatorial Candidate Byron Donalds talks costs, insurance at Martin County roundtable    WPEC
entry.article_text: With just six weeks until Florida voters choose their next governor, Republican gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds brought his campaign to Martin County on Wednesday for a roundtable discussion focused on affordability and other issues facing residents. For about an hour inside a small meeting room at the Martin County Chamber of Commerce in Stuart, Rep. Donalds took questions from about a dozen Martin county voters, including insurance agents, realtors and homeowners. Rather than deliver a formal speech, Donalds encouraged an open discussion with community members. "Let's go around, introduce yourself and let's just have a dialogue," Donalds said at the start of the event. Questions centered largely on the rising cost of living, including homeowners insurance and healthcare costs. One homeowner asked Donalds what could be done about rising insurance costs. "What about homeowner's insurance because it's literally pricing people out of staying in their homes," the woman said. See also: Brightline may file Chapter 11 bankruptcy as soon as this week, reports say Donalds said higher construction costs have played a role in rising insurance premiums and outlined proposals he says would help lower costs for Floridians. The congressman also discussed his support for reducing property insurance premiums by 20% to 25% and his long-term goal of eliminating homestead property taxes. When another attendee raised concerns about increasing application fees and other costs imposed by local governments, Donalds said local officials should review their budgets and identify areas where spending can be cut. Throughout the discussion, Donalds emphasized making Florida more affordable for families, highlighting issues including insurance, housing and healthcare. "In healthcare, it's making sure we deal with stuff like dealing with in-network, out-of-network, prior authorizations," Donalds said. In an exclusive one-on-one interview with CBS12 News, Donalds was also asked about recent changes to his campaign website that removed prominent references to President Donald Trump's endorsement. "We're not distancing ourselves from President Trump," Donalds said. "We've been planning on making website changes for about two months now coming out of the primary. We wanted the website to be purely on the issues that we're campaigning on." Donalds added that he remains grateful for Trump's endorsement. Ron DeSantis has also endorsed Donalds in the race for governor. Donalds will face Democrat David Jolly in the November general election.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie HOA tells residents to replace dead trees, homeowners push back - cw34.com
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie HOA tells residents to replace dead trees, homeowners push back    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Some residents in Port St. Lucie and their homeowners' association are at odds over dead trees. People who live in Cadence at Tradition received a notice dated Sept. 1 from Campbell Property Management on behalf of Cadence at Tradition Homeowners Association Inc., saying the dead tree or dead trees on their property need to be replaced. The notice says: "Your assistance and cooperation are requested regarding the following: Landscaping-Dead Tree- The deceased tree(s) on your property is in need of attention." Residents say the trees are on the swale, the strip of grass between the sidewalk and the street, and numerous trees were killed during a cold snap. Because the dead trees are on the swale, some residents say it should be the HOA 's job to replace them at the HOA's expense, not the homeowners. "It's just a little bit frustrating and disappointing that we, as homeowners, have to endure this from the HOA," said Keyla Peguero, a homeowner at Cadence at Tradition. Recently the HOA has removed many of the dead trees, leaving holes in the ground where residents are supposed to put in new trees, at the homeowners' expense. But homeowners such as Chip Collison say the dead trees were in common areas, not their yards, so they want the HOA to pay for new trees in the swales. "You think the swale is a common area?" we asked Collison. "Based on the documentation I've read? The notice sent to homeowners goes on to say: "We kindly request you address this matter by 9/30/26 to avoid escalation." See also: Stolen Broward deputy's car found on I-95 in St. Lucie County, woman arrested The letter does not say what action will be taken if a homeowner does not replace the dead trees. Some residents say now is not the best time to replace the dead trees. They say if new trees need to be planted, it should be done in April, at the start of the growing season. Some say if new trees are planted now, they could be wiped out by a freeze in the months ahead. "We're well into hurricane season now. If we plant new trees, no one can predict the future. These trees could be freshly planted. We get a strong hurricane come through, they're all gone, and they're gonna have to be redone again," Collison said. Peguero says she replaced a dead tree in the swale in front of her house, at a total cost of $300 to remove the dead tree, haul it away and replace it with a new tree. She says she's not willing to do it again and shouldn't have had to do it in the first place. A public relations firm for The Cadence at Tradition HOA sent us this written statement: Currently, the HOA is replacing thousands of dead trees and shrubs in the common areas that have yet to recover from the last freeze. In the limited common areas, such as the rights of way immediately adjacent to and between individual lots, including areas containing sidewalks and driveway aprons, residents are responsible for replacing trees and maintaining these areas. Because the HOA is currently purchasing and installing trees in bulk, we’ve invited residents to participate in the program. This allows homeowners to share in the cost savings while ensuring that tree replacements around their homes are selected and installed professionally.

entry.title: ‘We’re about to fight’: Teens, dad clash at Indiantown bus stop over pizza and bullying - WPBF
entry.summary: ‘We’re about to fight’: Teens, dad clash at Indiantown bus stop over pizza and bullying    WPBF
entry.article_text: A confrontation between teenagers at an Indiantown school bus stop escalated into a man pulling a gun on two teens, according to a Martin County Sheriff’s Office report. The incident happened Friday morning near Southwest 174th Court and Southwest 175th Court as students were preparing to board a bus headed to South Fork High School. The sheriff’s office ultimately determined that no criminal charges would be filed as investigators believe the man who displayed the gun was legally allowed to defend himself under Florida’s Stand Your Ground Law. Sheriff John Budensiek said detectives spent the entire day Friday investigating the incident, interviewing students who were on the bus and the people involved. He said the investigation found the father had gone to the bus stop after his 16-year-old son reported being bullied by a 14-year-old student on the bus the day before. "The misinformation is of zero value. Actually, it's counterproductive to the safety of our citizens of Martin County," Budensiek said. According to the sheriff, the initial dispute happened Thursday when the 16-year-old got on the bus carrying a pizza. Budensiek said a 14-year-old student began asking the teen for pizza, eventually threatening him and hitting him in the head after he refused to give him some. The 16-year-old then went home and told his father what happened. Budensiek said the father returned to the bus stop that afternoon and spoke with the female bus driver, who told him she would try to address the situation. Confrontation at the bus stop The next morning, on Friday, the father drove his son to the bus stop. Budensiek said the 14-year-old involved in the previous day's incident was already on the bus when they arrived. As the 16-year-old got on the bus, his father began speaking with the driver again. According to the sheriff, that is when the 14-year-old got off the bus and confronted the father. "Now you have students on the bus that are yelling. You have the 14-year-old boy that came off the bus that's yelling, screaming at the dad," Budensiek said. Budensiek said other students on the bus then called another teenager to come to the scene. There were actually two 16-year-olds involved, according to the sheriff: the father's son, whom he described as the victim, and another 16-year-old who was already suspended from school and was not on the bus that morning. That second 16-year-old came to the bus stop after being summoned by students on the bus, Budensiek said. "So now you have two young men who look like grown men that are happening upon the dad, going at the dad and yelling at the dad," Budensiek said. The sheriff said the father initially held his hand up and repeatedly told the teenagers to stay back. "They got all the way up on him before he pulled out a concealed weapon and told them to get back, which he's legally allowed to do," Budensiek said. He said both teenagers backed away, the father put the gun away and the confrontation ended. The father then drove around the corner, flagged down a deputy and immediately explained what had happened. Dad drives right around the corner, flags down a deputy, says, 'This is what happened, this is what I did, this is why I did it,'" Budensiek said. No criminal charges Budensiek said detectives interviewed students who witnessed the incident, including students on the bus and the two teenagers who approached the father. He said investigators found the accounts were consistent. "Everybody said the consistent story," Budensiek said. The sheriff said investigators would have sought warrants for the 14-year-old and the other 16-year-old who approached the father if the father had wanted to pursue charges. "We would have filed for warrants on the 14-year-old and the 16-year-old that went after the dad, except for the fact that the dad did not want to press charges," Budensiek said. The sheriff said the father's actions may not have been how he would have handled it, but investigators determined he did not break the law. "While it may not have been how I would have handled it, did not do anything illegal. You are allowed to stand your ground whether the person coming after you is 16 or 24 or 34," Budensiek said. Budensiek also said the father is a security guard and was legally carrying a concealed firearm. It's my understanding that he was a security guard and was carrying the gun," Budensiek said. He emphasized that the weapon was concealed before the confrontation. Budensiek said the father has since pulled his son out of school and plans to homeschool him. "He just was going to protect himself and his son at all costs," the sheriff said. Teenagers dispute sheriff's account The two teenagers who were in the video told WPBF 25 News a different version of what happened, disputing the sheriff’s narrative and saying they were frightened when the gun was pointed at them. RJ McIntyre and Trevor Ivory spoke with WPBF 25 News about what they say happened. McIntyre said he was walking to the bus stop Friday morning when someone called him and told him there was "an old man here looking for you." He said that when he got closer, he saw the man near the bus. McIntyre said he boarded the bus and noticed the father pointing toward him through the window. He said a back-and-forth exchange then began between him and the father's son, who had been involved in the pizza dispute the previous day. McIntyre said the bus driver eventually told both teenagers they needed to get off the bus. He said they dropped their backpacks and appeared ready to fight. "We dropped our backpacks. We're about to fight," McIntyre said, recalling the confrontation. Ivory said he was not originally at the bus stop but received a call from his younger brother. "My brother called me and he was like, 'There's a grown men at the bus stop. He's looking for somebody,'" Ivory said. Ivory said he went to the bus stop because he felt responsible for his younger brother. "I'm supposed to look after him," Ivory said. He said he spoke with the adult man before the teenagers got off the bus. "I was like, 'What's up with you? Like, who are you looking for?'" Ivory said. He said he eventually saw McIntyre and the man's son come off the bus. He said he could tell they were fighting and told the man to give them space. "I'm telling the dad, I'm like, 'No, just let them two fade,'" Ivory said. Seconds later, Ivory said a gun was drawn. "And the next thing you know, he put his son behind him, and he pulled a gun out on us," he told WPBF. McIntyre said he remembers what was going through his head when he saw the gun. "I can't process anything. I'm just like, am I going to make it home? It's life or death right now. It's a gun," McIntyre said. McIntyre said he grew up in the area and had never experienced anything like it. Ivory said he was also stunned. "In the moment, I was just like, it's crazy," Ivory said. Both teens put their hands up as they backed away. The dispute the day before McIntyre acknowledged he had interacted with the other student the previous day, but disputed the sheriff's characterization of that interaction as bullying. He said the encounter started when the other teen brought pizza onto the bus. McIntyre said he asked if he could buy a slice for a dollar. Instead, he said, the other student responded disrespectfully. "He screamed in my face," McIntyre said. McIntyre said he continued trying to talk to the student about the interaction during the ride home. He acknowledged that he used profanity and said he could have handled the situation differently. I think, like, when I was asking for pizza and he told me, you know, the first time, I think I should have left it there," McIntyre said. Questions over the gun The teenagers said they believe the father should be held accountable for bringing a firearm to the bus stop. McIntyre said the presence of the gun was particularly concerning because there were other children nearby. "I feel like under any circumstance, however you felt, no firearms should be displayed at a bus stop where there's a bunch of kids on a bus looking forward to going to school," McIntyre said. He said students on the bus could be heard reacting to the incident. "As you all can hear in the video, 'Oh Lord, please Lord, I hope they don't get shot,'" McIntyre said. The sheriff, however, said the father did not pull the gun until after the teenagers had approached him despite repeated warnings to stay back. He said the incident would not have happened if the 14-year-old had remained on the bus. "If he had stayed on the bus and kept his mouth shut and everybody had not called the other friend over there, there would have been no issues," Budensiek said. Sheriff blasts social media video The sheriff also criticized the spread of a partial video of the confrontation on social media. He said the video did not show the entire context leading up to the firearm being displayed. "There was a video that was put out on social media that was a half of a video and a half of a fraction of the story that actually took place and that grew legs and got spread around, and that's extremely counterproductive," he said. Budensiek said the social media posts created confusion in the community and questioned the work of investigators. "It unsettles the community. It undermines our law enforcement job that we're out there investigating it," Budensiek told WPBF. The sheriff said his agency conducted a thorough investigation and would have arrested the two teenagers if the father had wanted to press charges. "We did a thorough investigation, and you are allowed to stand your ground," Budensiek said. The sheriff ultimately characterized the father as the victim in the incident and said there will be no criminal charges. "To recap it, the individual with the gun was the victim in this case," Budensiek said. He said the father has since taken his son out of school to be homeschooled. "He did not want to press charges. He just wants to be left alone. He wants his son to be left alone," he said. McIntyre and Ivory, meanwhile, maintain they were not the aggressors and question why the father came to their bus stop armed. This is a developing story. entry.summary: Gubernatorial Candidate Byron Donalds talks costs, insurance at Martin County roundtable    WPEC
entry.article_text: With just six weeks until Florida voters choose their next governor, Republican gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds brought his campaign to Martin County on Wednesday for a roundtable discussion focused on affordability and other issues facing residents. For about an hour inside a small meeting room at the Martin County Chamber of Commerce in Stuart, Rep. Donalds took questions from about a dozen Martin county voters, including insurance agents, realtors and homeowners. Rather than deliver a formal speech, Donalds encouraged an open discussion with community members. "Let's go around, introduce yourself and let's just have a dialogue," Donalds said at the start of the event. Questions centered largely on the rising cost of living, including homeowners insurance and healthcare costs. One homeowner asked Donalds what could be done about rising insurance costs. "What about homeowner's insurance because it's literally pricing people out of staying in their homes," the woman said. See also: Brightline may file Chapter 11 bankruptcy as soon as this week, reports say Donalds said higher construction costs have played a role in rising insurance premiums and outlined proposals he says would help lower costs for Floridians. The congressman also discussed his support for reducing property insurance premiums by 20% to 25% and his long-term goal of eliminating homestead property taxes. When another attendee raised concerns about increasing application fees and other costs imposed by local governments, Donalds said local officials should review their budgets and identify areas where spending can be cut. Throughout the discussion, Donalds emphasized making Florida more affordable for families, highlighting issues including insurance, housing and healthcare. "In healthcare, it's making sure we deal with stuff like dealing with in-network, out-of-network, prior authorizations," Donalds said. In an exclusive one-on-one interview with CBS12 News, Donalds was also asked about recent changes to his campaign website that removed prominent references to President Donald Trump's endorsement. "We're not distancing ourselves from President Trump," Donalds said. "We've been planning on making website changes for about two months now coming out of the primary. We wanted the website to be purely on the issues that we're campaigning on." Donalds added that he remains grateful for Trump's endorsement. Ron DeSantis has also endorsed Donalds in the race for governor. Donalds will face Democrat David Jolly in the November general election.

entry.title: Cybersecurity expert finds card skimmer on Fort Pierce gas pump - WPEC
entry.summary: Cybersecurity expert finds card skimmer on Fort Pierce gas pump    WPEC
entry.article_text: A man with decades of experience in cybersecurity found a credit card skimmer on a gas pump at a Fort Pierce 7-Eleven , and police are now investigating. Arlo Bess said he was stopping for gas at the 7-Eleven on the south side of Orange Avenue near Interstate 95 before heading back to Palm Bay when he found the device. Bess said he has worked in cybersecurity on and off for about 25 years. He said that background made him cautious at the pump. For years, he has tugged on the outside of the card reader every time he pays with a card at a gas station. He said this was the first time one came loose. "I was quite surprised when I went in there and pulled on it, just like I normally do, half not expecting anything to come out, and out pops this," Bess said. Bess said skimmers take almost no time to put on. "It literally takes about two to three seconds to put one in place and about the same amount of time to pull one out," Bess said. Bess said skimmers like this one are often held on with double-sided tape. A small chip inside reads the data on a card's magnetic stripe as it goes in. He said thieves usually leave a device in place for about a week and collect card numbers, expiration dates, and often security codes. They can then sell that information on the dark web or copy it onto other cards to make purchases at places like self-checkout kiosks or online. Bess took the device inside and showed it to the store manager, who called police. He said officers arrived a few minutes later and took a report, and they checked every pump at the station with him for more skimmers. Bess said neither the manager nor the responding officer had ever seen a skimmer in person. He said the manager also reported it to her supervisor with the company. The Fort Pierce Police Department confirmed it is investigating. Bess said you can't reliably spot a skimmer just by looking. "By looking at it visually, you can't tell the difference between a pump that's got a skimmer on it and one that doesn't," Bess said. See also: Is it illegal to drive with hazard lights on in the rain? It depends; here's the law The one he found looked newer and shinier than the scuffed readers on the other pumps. Still, he said the best check is a firm pull on the card reader with your hands, without using tools. He also said newer skimmers can sit inside the card slot, where they can't be seen at all. "My advice would be to tap your card, go inside and pay. It's much harder to put these skimming devices on card readers inside the store," Bess said. He also recommends not using a debit card at the pump. He said fraud protections for debit cards are different from those for credit cards, so it can take weeks to get stolen money back from a checking account. If you need to use a debit or ATM card, Bess suggests using a machine inside a bank lobby. He said outdoor machines, including drive-thru ATMs, are easier targets because thieves are less likely to be seen. We'll have an update on the investigation from the Fort Pierce Police Department, and we'll give you the details when they become available.

entry.title: From parks bonds to trash pickup: Local questions facing Palm Beach, Treasure Coast voters - cw34.com
entry.summary: From parks bonds to trash pickup: Local questions facing Palm Beach, Treasure Coast voters    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Voters in Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast will decide eight local ballot questions on Nov. 3, ranging from hundreds of millions of dollars in bonds to trash pickup, mosquito control and the future of public land. The questions are separate from candidate races and the three statewide constitutional amendments . Some apply countywide, while others are limited to Stuart, Port St. Palm Beach County Palm Beach County voters will consider three countywide funding questions. The first would authorize up to $280 million in general-obligation bonds , repaid through property taxes over no more than 20 years. The money would modernize aging parks, recreation facilities and botanical gardens; expand sports complexes; improve beach access and trail connections; and help develop new regional parks. A second question would authorize up to $175 million in general-obligation bonds for the Palm Beach County Library District. The money would be used to acquire, build, renovate, expand, improve and equip library facilities. The bonds would be repaid through property taxes within the library district over no more than 20 years. The third question asks voters to continue the School District of Palm Beach County’s existing 1-mill property-tax levy from July 1, 2027, through June 30, 2031. One mill equals $1 for every $1,000 of taxable value. The levy would fund school safety and police, mental-health services, teachers in arts, music, physical education and career and choice programs, and improved teacher pay. An independent citizens-and-experts committee would oversee spending. Martin County Martin County’s local ballot questions are limited to Stuart voters. One proposed charter amendment would require voter approval before the City Commission could sell, convey or lease for more than one year any city-owned property containing recreational ballfields. The second question concerns an undeveloped 1.97-acre city parcel on U.S. 1 opposite North River Shores Boulevard. Voters would decide whether to rescind a 2011 referendum requiring the city to commercially lease the land to fund maintenance of the Haney Creek Preserve. If approved, the city could convert the parcel to conservation land and add it to the preserve. Lucie County has three local issues, although they do not all apply to every voter. The countywide question would extend the existing half-cent infrastructure sales surtax for 10 years, from Jan. The current tax is set to expire in 2028. See also: Dead rodent in kitchen, 260 droppings & no hand-washing: 7 South Florida restaurants shut Revenue would continue to fund capital projects such as road improvements, traffic-congestion relief, drainage, flood control, sidewalks and water-quality work. Lucie voters also will see a nonbinding straw poll asking whether the city should change from once-a-week to twice-a-week trash pickup for an added fee . The city previously estimated the second pickup day would cost about $131 a year. The vote would not itself change collection service or rates. It is intended to gauge residents’ preferences before the City Council decides whether to pursue the change. Lucie County issue is a binding referendum on expanding the St. Lucie County Mosquito Control District by about 95,000 acres. The referendum is not countywide or citywide. Only qualified voters living in the area proposed for addition to the district will vote on it. If approved, those properties would be added to the district and become subject to its property-tax levy. Indian River and Okeechobee counties No countywide, municipal or special-district ballot question has been identified in the currently available Nov. 3 election materials for Indian River or Okeechobee counties. Voters there will still decide statewide constitutional amendments and candidate races, but there are no known local bonds, referendums or advisory questions to add to the local ballot-issues list.

entry.title: Drought conditions ease in parts of the Treasure Coast and Palm Beaches - WPEC
entry.summary: Drought conditions ease in parts of the Treasure Coast and Palm Beaches    WPEC
entry.article_text: Drought Monitor update shows improvement across portions of the Treasure Coast and Palm Beaches, although dry conditions have not disappeared entirely especially farther inland. The map, released Thursday and based on conditions through Tuesday morning, compares the latest drought picture with last week’s update. It does not measure rainfall alone. The weekly analysis also considers soil moisture, streamflow, groundwater and longer-term precipitation trends, so improvement after a wet stretch can take time to show up. Palm Beach County sees the clearest improvement The most noticeable change is across much of eastern and central Palm Beach County. Areas that were classified in moderate drought last week are now shown as abnormally dry in the latest update. That is a step in the right direction, but it does not mean the area is completely free of dryness. Moderate drought continues across parts of western Palm Beach County, including areas closer to the Lake Okeechobee agricultural region. Those locations will need more sustained rainfall to see additional improvement. Okeechobee County remains a mixed picture Okeechobee County also shows some improvement, with more of the county now classified as abnormally dry rather than moderate drought. However, a pocket of severe drought remains in the southwestern part of the county. That means water resources and agricultural interests there remain especially sensitive to an extended dry period. Treasure Coast conditions hold steady to improve slightly Indian River, St. Lucie and Martin counties continue to show a mix of abnormally dry conditions and areas that are not in drought. The latest map keeps much of the remaining dryness focused away from the immediate coast, while coastal sections have either held steady or seen modest improvement from last week. For residents, abnormally dry is the lowest level on the Drought Monitor scale and is not the same as an official drought designation. Still, it is a signal that rainfall and water conditions are running below where they should be. Moderate and severe drought categories indicate a greater and more persistent moisture deficit. The recent run of showers and thunderstorms has helped, and the changing weather pattern may bring additional opportunities for rain before drier air becomes more established. Even so, the update shows that one wet week does not erase a longer-term rainfall shortfall overnight. The main takeaway: drought conditions are trending in a better direction for parts of the Palm Beaches and Treasure Coast, particularly east of Lake Okeechobee, but inland areas will need more consistent rainfall to keep that improvement going.

entry.article_text: A year after WPTV first investigated a contentious legal battle over the future of Fisherman's Wharf, newly released environmental testing is raising fresh questions about a key argument in the dispute: contamination.The city of Fort Pierce previously told developer Chris Shelli that the waterfront property at the center of his lawsuit was "likely contaminated" and suggested the cost of remediation could essentially eliminate his claim for damages.But the city made that assertion before the Florida Department of Environmental Protection had completed its testing.Those results are now in.According to site assessments obtained by WPTV, FDEP found arsenic above state residential cleanup targets in two soil samples on city-owned land sold to Shelli. However, both samples were less than twice the residential cleanup target, and an environmental researcher who reviewed the findings for WPTV said the results on the development property did not appear particularly alarming."I don't think it's necessarily something to be too concerned with," said Jordon Beckler, an associate research professor at Florida Atlantic University’s Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institute.Shelli purchased approximately 3.2 acres around Fisherman’s Wharf with plans to transform the waterfront into a new destination.But WPTV Investigates previously uncovered a significant complication with the deal.Roughly half of the property was subject to a state right-of-reverter restriction, meaning the land could revert to the state if it were sold for private development.Emails obtained by WPTV in our first investigation showed Fort Pierce commissioners did not learn until 2023 — about two years after the sale — that removing the restriction could cost nearly $2 million.Shelli ultimately sued the city for breach of contract.In 2025, an attorney for the city sent Shelli a letter arguing the property was "likely contaminated" and that the cost of "remediation" essentially "eliminates" his damages claim.At the time, however, FDEP's environmental investigation was still underway.The environmental concerns extend beyond the Fisherman’s Wharf property itself.Land immediately north of Fisherman’s Wharf was once home to a citrus packing house. Lucie County purchased that property in 2018 and designated it as a brownfield site — a designation used for property where redevelopment may be complicated by actual or perceived environmental contamination.FDEP's site assessment found several soil samples at the former citrus packing house contained arsenic above Florida's residential and industrial cleanup targets.Beckler said those findings were consistent with the property's historical industrial use."Personally, there's not really much in the report that alarmed me," Beckler said. "I think the findings are consistent with the past industrial uses of the site."One sample, however, stood out.FDEP found an arsenic concentration roughly 148 times Florida's residential cleanup target at a location along the northern portion of the former citrus packing house property.But that hot spot was not on the land sold to Shelli.Shelli's proposed development property sits across the street.FDEP did send letters to seven surrounding property owners warning about possible off-site contamination. One of those letters went to the city of Fort Pierce and identified arsenic above the residential cleanup target in two soil samples on city-owned property sold to Shelli.Those exceedances, however, were far smaller than the hot spot found at the former packing house. Both were less than twice the residential cleanup target.Beckler also noted that environmental cleanup standards are intentionally conservative and that naturally occurring arsenic is present in Florida soils."The vast majority of those samples, while, yes, they were above that residential standard, they weren't that high above it," Beckler said.The distinction could become important in Shelli's lawsuit.FDEP identified remediation plans for five parcels included in its assessment, but those parcels are associated with the former citrus packing house property.The agency did not identify a remediation plan for the waterfront development property sold to Shelli.That is notable because the city's earlier letter specifically cited "remediation" when arguing that contamination would essentially eliminate Shelli's damages.Government law attorney Glen Torcivia, who is not involved in the lawsuit, reviewed the dispute for WPTV and said the new information does not necessarily resolve the legal fight.Instead, he said questions could remain over what the city knew — or should have known — and what responsibility Shelli had to investigate the property before the purchase."You're still going to have a dispute over whether the city knew or should have known that there were issues, and the city would argue from the developer standpoint, he should have done some due diligence," Torcivia said.Shelli told WPTV that the city has not provided FDEP's findings to him or his legal team.The lawsuit has potentially significant financial implications for Fort Pierce taxpayers.In March, commissioners were presented with a $6 million settlement offer from Shelli.During a public meeting, the city attorney warned commissioners that if they rejected the offer and Shelli later recovered at least $7.5 million, the city could also potentially become responsible for attorney's fees and other expenses under Florida's proposal-for-settlement rules.Commissioners took no action, and the offer was later deemed rejected."Maybe it's in everybody's best interests if they go to mediation," Torcivia said.WPTV reached out to the city for answers about its contamination claims and the status of the litigation. A spokesperson said the city does not comment on pending litigation.For Mike Jenkins, the dispute has consequences beyond the courtroom.Jenkins and his family own the property beneath 12A Buoy, a restaurant at Fisherman's Wharf. He said his family has owned the property for roughly 50 years.Jenkins said he was shocked when WPTV told him last year that contamination had become part of the city's legal argument."This place was clean," Jenkins said, adding that environmental testing had been conducted in the area decades ago.He worries that simply associating Fisherman's Wharf with contamination could affect surrounding property owners."You throw a word out like that — contaminated — that's going to scare everybody, scare all the landowners," Jenkins said. "I shouldn't have been in this situation."Shelli's lawsuit against Fort Pierce remains pending as the city also navigates turnover within its legal department.And while FDEP's testing did identify arsenic contamination in the broader area — including two exceedances on the city-owned property sold to Shelli — Beckler said the results he reviewed do not lead him to believe Fisherman’s Wharf is unsafe for recreational use.For now, the testing answers one question that has hung over Fisherman's Wharf for more than a year: what is actually in the soil.What it means for the multimillion-dollar legal battle over the waterfront — however — remains unresolved.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

entry.title: Witnesses tell police a parking dispute led to shooting at Pollo Tropical in Port St. Lucie
entry.summary: WPTV is learning more details about what led up to a shooting at a Pollo Tropical in Port St. Lucie last weekend. According to the incident report, the shooting stemmed from a dispute over a parking space. Multiple witnesses provided accounts of the incident to responding officers. One witness told police he was sitting at a high-top table inside the restaurant when he heard a verbal argument between two men outside. The witness said he observed Christopher Harris, 37, push another man and after continuing the verbal argument, the witness said he saw the man discharge a firearm, shooting Harris in the chest. Harris, listed as a victim in the report, then came back inside and asked someone to call 911. One witness told police he was sitting at a high-top table inside the restaurant when he heard a verbal argument between two men outside. The witness said he observed Christopher Harris, 37, push another man and after continuing the verbal argument, the witness said he saw the man discharge a firearm, shooting Harris in the chest. Harris, listed as a victim in the report, then came back inside and asked someone to call 911. Another witness who came to pick up an Uber order said she observed a man pull into a parking space before another vehicle pulled into the space in front of them. She said the man was staring while he walked to the door, and when she looked away and got out of her vehicle to pick up the order, the man began yelling. The witness said that while exiting Pollo Tropical, the man was following someone out, calling them names and lunging toward them. She said she observed something in the man's hand and continued to lunge. The witness said the man was so close to the other person that they were almost touching before she saw the other person pull out a firearm and shoot. A witness picking up a DoorDash order said Harris came into Pollo Tropical yelling at another man over a parking space. The witness said the man exited to get his order, and Harris continued to yell, telling the man to 'come outside.' The witness said Harris held the door open and then approached the man before he heard a gunshot. The witness said the man stated that Harris 'ran up on him with a knife.' Officers recovered a 9mm handgun from the scene. The Port St. Lucie Police Department confirmed with WPTV that Harris, despite being the victim of the incident, faces charges of battery and aggravated battery with a deadly weapon.

entry.title: Amendment 3 could shift property-tax costs onto Florida renters, report warns
entry.summary: A tax break for Florida homeowners could bring a bigger bill for renters next door, according to a new report examining Amendment 3. The report released by the Florida Housing Coalition estimates that if local governments raise property-tax rates to replace revenue lost under the amendment, annual taxes would increase by an average of $406 per apartment and $1,081 per single-family rental home in 2028. Watch more from Forrest Saunders on the report Amendment 3 could shift property-tax costs onto Florida renters, report warns Jared Walczak, the tax-policy analyst who wrote the report, said much of that expense could ultimately be passed on to tenants through higher rents. Renters pay taxes, they just don't write the check, Walczak said. Amendment 3 would increase the homestead exemption for non-school property taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, with inflation adjustments beginning in 2029. The exemption reduces the property value on which taxes are calculated for qualifying primary residences. School district property taxes would remain unchanged. Rental properties do not qualify for the homestead exemption. Local governments facing lost revenue could respond by cutting spending, increasing property-tax rates, raising other taxes or fees, or combining those approaches. Walczaks analysis models rate increases intended to replace lost revenue, subject to existing limits on those rates. While landlords would write the check, most of the burden would ultimately be borne by renters in the form of higher rent, he said. The estimates represent average increases in property-tax bills. How much of that cost reaches tenants would depend on rental-market conditions and local budget decisions. By 2031, the report estimates the additional annual property-tax burden would reach $544 per apartment and $1,471 per single-family rental home under the same approach. The amendment also includes a provision benefiting rental and other non-homestead properties: It would lower the annual cap on increases in assessed value from 10% to 5%. Walczak's report concludes that the benefit of the lower assessment cap would be outweighed by the modeled tax shift.Supporters, including Florida Realtors, argue that homeowners also need help with housing costs.“Everywhere you look, people are feeling the pinch of affordability, and Amendment 3 has the opportunity to return more money back to the taxpayer," said Margy Grant of Florida Realtors.The potential loss of local revenue has also drawn opposition from the Florida Sheriffs Association, which warns the amendment could squeeze funding for deputies and other public-safety needs.Miami-Dade Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz pushed back against those warnings in a statement posted on X.“Tax relief and public safety are not competing priorities,” she said.Cordero-Stutz urged government agencies, including sheriffs’ offices, to examine their spending and eliminate unnecessary costs while protecting essential law-enforcement resources.Gov. Ron DeSantis supports Amendment 3 and says future lawmakers will pursue targeted state grants to help maintain essential services. The proposed constitutional amendment needs at least 60% of the votes cast on it to pass.

entry.title: ‘Is this going to be the real one?’ Martin County families react after fourth bomb threat - WPEC
entry.summary: ‘Is this going to be the real one?’ Martin County families react after fourth bomb threat    WPEC
entry.article_text: Students returned to class as usual Wednesday after a 15-year-old Martin County High School student was accused of making a false bomb threat Tuesday, marking the fourth threat tied to the Stuart school in just over a week as parents voice growing concern. Families express concern after repeated threats: The repeated threats are taking a toll on some students and parents. CBS12 News spoke with freshman Maya and her mother, Liz, during school drop-off Wednesday morning. Maya described the response to one of the previous threats as frightening. The last bomb threat, it was crazy because, like a cop in Building Two, the alarm didn’t even go off, Maya said. A police officer had to go door to door and come get us and tell us to get out of the building. So, it was kind of like scary. Her mother said the string of threats has left her questioning what could happen each time she drops her daughter off at school. It is very concerning, Liz said. Every morning it’s like, should I bring her to school today? Is it going to be another one? Is this going to be the real one? District officials told CBS12 News counselors are readily available to support students if they are nervous from the ongoing issue. Student arrested in latest threat: The latest threat was reported Tuesday morning. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office said 15-year-old sophomore Noah Taylor used FortifyFL, Florida’s school safety reporting system, to submit a report claiming bombs were inside a boys bathroom and would go off during third period. The school resource deputy determined the threat was not credible. Investigators said surveillance video and interviews with students led them to Taylor. Deputies said Taylor later admitted making the false report because Taylor wanted to get out of his third-period class. Taylor was arrested and charged with making a false report concerning the planting of a bomb, a second-degree felony. Sheriff John Budensiek said Taylor is not believed to be connected to the three previous threats involving Martin County High School. Three earlier threats still under investigation: The Sheriff’s Office continues to investigate the other three threats. Budensiek said investigators traced the first threat to someone in Russia. The other two investigations remain active. The sheriff has warned students that false threats can carry serious and lasting consequences, including criminal charges and possible school discipline. For families such as Maya and Liz, the concern now is whether the threats will stop. The advice I give to my daughter is to stay calm. She’s very smart and quick to think, and I tell her to do what God is telling her right away. Follow the rules and what the teachers tell you, but you have to react how you feel in that moment. I know they’re not allowed to use their phones, but I really don’t care if you need to make a phone call in an emergency, just do it," said Liz. Maya said what initially felt unusual has started to feel more routine after so many incidents. A lot of people were screaming and calling their parents. Then, when they got home, they were looking on Facebook because Facebook has everything. We all talked about it and who we think is doing it. Everyone was saying it was Russia or something, but I don’t know," said Maya. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office continues working to determine who is responsible for the three unresolved threats. Martin County High School released the following statement: The safety and security of our students and staff remains our top priority. We appreciate the swift response and coordination of the Martin County Sheriff's Office, our School Resource Officers, and the District's Safety and Security Team, whose efforts allowed yesterday's false FortifyFL report involving Martin County High School to be quickly investigated, determined to be unfounded, and ultimately resolved with an arrest. Because the report was confirmed to be false, there is no additional law enforcement presence on campus related to this incident. Our two School Resource Officers remain on campus, and additional patrols continue as part of our normal daily safety operations. We also want to be clear: false threats and false reports are not pranks. They create fear, disrupt the educational environment, divert critical law enforcement resources, and carry serious disciplinary and criminal consequences. Individuals who make false reports should expect to be held fully accountable, exactly as how it unfolded yesterday. We understand these threats can cause fear and distress, and when we talk about student safety, we want them to feel safe as well. We will be providing additional services and staff during the school day, including School Social Service Workers and School Counselors, and we encourage students who need support to talk with them. We continue to encourage students, staff, and families to report legitimate safety concerns. Every report is taken seriously and investigated thoroughly because protecting our students and staff will always come first.

entry.title: Martin County High School student, 15, arrested for bomb threat made to 'get out of class,' sheriff says - WPTV
entry.summary: Martin County High School student, 15, arrested for bomb threat made to 'get out of class,' sheriff says    WPTV
entry.article_text: A 15-year-old Martin County High School student was arrested Tuesday and charged with a felony after officials say he confessed to sending a fake bomb threat through the Fortify Florida app, telling investigators he "was just tired of being in class," according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. The incident is the fourth threat leveled against the school in just a week and a half.WATCH: Martin County High student arrested for allegedly making fake bomb threatThe arrest comes as the school district is only six weeks into the academic year, and authorities are sending a clear message that all threats, even those intended as pranks, will be met with severe consequences.Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said the school's resource officer received the threat around 9 a.m. Tuesday."The tip said, 'I was walking by the boys bathroom, and they were saying there is bombs in the school and that they are going to blow up in third period today,'" Budensiek said, reading from the alert. The tipster also claimed to hear about a bomb in a trash can and fireworks in backpacks.Investigators immediately reviewed security camera footage and were able to quickly trace the electronic submission of the tip back to a 15-year-old student on campus.When first confronted, the student, who WPTV is not naming due to his age, denied any involvement."Initially, he denied knowing what had taken place," Budensiek said. "Alibied for himself, saying that maybe somebody else sent the tip."However, after further questioning, the student confessed, according to the sheriff. "He gave the explanation... as he just wanted to get out of third-period class," the sheriff said.While an arrest has been made in Tuesday's case, Sheriff Budensiek confirmed it is not connected to three other recent threats against the school."The initial threat came in, we know it came in through Russia," Budensiek said. "And then the last two, we're still investigating, and we could potentially be making some more arrests on that case."Budensiek issued a stern warning to any student who might consider making a similar threat as a joke."This really is catastrophic for your life," he said. "This individual's been arrested for a felony. He's been transported to DYS in Fort Pierce. He's going to have strong repercussions from the school, if not expulsion... and it will affect his ability to get jobs down the road. While it may come across as a joke, we have to take these serious."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

We understand these threats can cause fear and distress, and when we talk about student safety, we want them to feel safe as well. We will be providing additional services and staff during the school day, including School Social Service Workers and School Counselors, and we encourage students who need support to talk with them. We continue to encourage students, staff, and families to report legitimate safety concerns. entry.title: Stolen Broward deputy's car found on I-95 in St. Lucie County, woman arrested - cw34.com
entry.summary: Stolen Broward deputy's car found on I-95 in St. Lucie County, woman arrested    cw34.com
entry.article_text: A Fort Lauderdale woman is facing multiple charges after authorities located a stolen Broward Sheriff's Office patrol vehicle along Interstate 95 in St. Lucie County Tuesday night. According to the Broward Sheriff's Office, shortly after 9 p.m., Broward County Regional Communications received a report that a marked BSO vehicle had been stolen from the public parking area of the Public Safety Building in Fort Lauderdale. Investigators, working with the Florida Highway Patrol, Port St. Lucie Police Department and St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, tracked the vehicle to the northbound lanes of Interstate 95 near Gatlin Boulevard in Port St. Deputies then spotted a woman nearby wearing an outer ballistic vest bearing Broward Sheriff's Office insignia. She was detained and identified as Shannon Marie Dillon, 42, of Fort Lauderdale. Lucie police said officers quickly established a perimeter after learning the suspect may have had access to a firearm. "The reason why the perimeter was established was because information was given to us that the female who had stolen the patrol vehicle had access to a firearm," Port St. Lucie Police spokesperson Brandon Martinez said. "PSLPD deployed both our K-9 unit and our drone resources." Drone video obtained by CBS12 News shows law enforcement officers from multiple agencies surrounding the stolen patrol vehicle along Interstate 95 before Dillon was arrested. Body camera video shows deputies ordering Dillon to get on the ground before she was taken into custody without incident. Dillon was booked into the St. Lucie County Jail and faces charges of grand theft of law enforcement equipment, unlawful use of a police badge or law enforcement vehicle, unlawful possession of four or fewer identification items, possession or use of drug paraphernalia, possession of a weapon or ammunition by a convicted felon, driving while license suspended, and resisting an officer without violence. She also faces Broward County charges of grand theft of law enforcement equipment from an authorized emergency vehicle and grand theft, according to investigators. The Broward County Sheriff's Office issued a statement crediting the coordination between agencies for bringing the incident to a safe end. The great coordination between all the agencies involved brought this incident to a peaceful conclusion. Nothing is missing from the vehicle. The deputy was on duty, and he reported his mark unit missing. The Internal Affairs Unit is investigating the incident to determine exactly what happened and if any agency policy was violated. See also: Can Florida police pull you over for a license plate frame? What the new law says Investigators with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office and the Broward Sheriff's Office are still working the case.

entry.summary: The Florida Panthers preseason is underway, and one of the biggest storylines is new acquisition Brady Tkachuk a star in his own right and the younger brother of Panthers forward Matthew Tkachuk. Brady, the former captain of the Ottawa Senators, sat down with WPTV anchor and Panthers 360 host Mike Trim to talk about joining South Florida's roster. WATCH: Brady Tkachuk joins Panthers, says family bond with brother Matthew makes South Florida special Brady Tkachuk interview with WPTV Panthers Anchor Mike Trim When asked how it feels to be in South Florida, Brady kept it simple. 'It's pretty special. It's been awesome down here so far,' Brady said. Beyond hockey, Brady said the opportunity to raise his family near his brother's is something he does not take lightly. 'You know, our families, it's just, you know, our kids growing up together and, uh, you know, for my kids seeing, um, you know, Matthew and Ellie a lot and then the same thing for, for Millie seeing us that just gonna be so special that you know we're not going to take a second for granted,' Brady said. As for comparisons to his older brother Matthew widely regarded as one of the game's elite players Brady deflected any suggestion that he has the edge. 'He's, he's the biggest motivator. Just see how great that he is that, you know, if I'm to be half the player that he is, I'd be, I'd be very lucky,' Brady said. entry.title: Coco Gauff will be a player-owner for the Florida franchise in the new season of World Team Tennis
entry.summary: Coco Gauff will be a player-owner for the Florida franchise that will compete in the new season of World Team Tennis. The two-time Grand Slam singles champion is scheduled to play in the Florida Flamingos Racquet Club's home matches on Dec. 14 and 15. The team will play in Amerant Bank Arena in Sunrise, home of the NHL's Florida Panthers. Gauff grew up in Delray Beach, Florida. 'I'm looking forward to playing at home in front of my family and friends in South Florida,' Gauff said Thursday in a statement. 'Its not often, as a tennis player, that we get to compete as part of a team, so Im excited for the new experience, not only for myself but, even more importantly, for the fans.' The Flamingos were one of the original franchises when World Team Tennis began in 1974 as a way of having a mixed-gender team format for tennis, with Hall of Famer Billie Jean King among the founders. It returns in December with the other teams based in New York and Toronto. U.S. Open semifinalists Frances Tiafoe and Jessica Pegula will be teammates for New York Empire Racquet Club, while the Toronto North Racquet Club features Canadian players Denis Shapovalov, Leylah Fernandez, Victoria Mboko and Gabriel Diallo. Gauff's teammates include Tommy Paul, Learner Tien, Iva Jovic, Brandon Nakashima and Eva Lys. The league will have a new match format featuring four singles sets (a mens and womens No. 1 and No. 2), and a mixed doubles super tiebreaker. Each team will start two men and two women.

entry.title: Central Elementary students get hands-on learning about environment through Guy Harvey Conservation School
entry.summary: Central Elementary School in Okeechobee is now the only public school in the county to be named a Guy Harvey Conservation School . The program is giving students hands-on learning in environmental conservation through science, technology, engineering, arts and math (STEAM). For Central Elementary, the partnership connects students to the natural world around them while helping them understand the importance of protecting Florida's waterways, wildlife and ecosystems. WATCH BELOW: Okeechobee's Central Elementary named Guy Harvey Conservation School Central Elementary in Okeechobee named a Guy Harvey Conservation School Fifth graders at the school are already getting a deep dive into environmental conservation, learning about topics like sharks and shark anatomy. WPTV reporter Christy Waite listened to students who say the projects are inspiring them to consider careers in STEAM. 'I would love to work with animals and teach kids what you learned in school,' one fifth grader said. Principal Jennifer Radcliff said the school's location near Lake Okeechobee gives students a special connection to nature. 'We live in a beautiful place here in Okeechobee and we want to make sure students know how to preserve this,' Radcliff said. Becoming a Guy Harvey Conservation School is a campus-wide effort. Teachers like Mrs. Biesiadecki will attend special training sessions throughout the year to bring new conservation lessons into the classroom. 'I wanted to be a marine biologist, but I became a science teacher. I get the best of both worlds because I can bring the ocean into my classroom,' Biesiadecki said. She is impressed and happy to see more girls interested in science and wildlife and hopes it encourages them to pursue careers in STEAM. Students will have the opportunity to dissect the sharks, something teachers and staff say they didn't get to do until middle or high school. The program also goes beyond the classroom by offering grants to support field trips and classroom supplies. entry.title: West Palm Beach GreenMarket returns Oct. 3 with global flavors, legacy vendors
entry.summary: The West Palm Beach GreenMarket is returning to the downtown waterfront for its 32nd season, and for many vendors, the market represents more than a Saturday tradition. It has become a launching pad for local business growth across Palm Beach County. This season's theme, 'The World, Right Here,' highlights international flavors and cultures represented throughout the market, which returns Saturday, Oct. 3, to the Great Lawn at 100 N. Clematis St. WATCH BELOW: West Palm Beach GreenMarket returns with global flavors West Palm Beach GreenMarket Returns With Global Flavors 'It's the world right here,' said Kaitlynn Kenney with the City of West Palm Beach Community Events team. Several vendors featured during WPTVs 'Shining A Light' segment shared how the GreenMarket helped expand their businesses from weekend booths to permanent storefronts. Mauricio Sanchez of Sanvel Coffee said the company sources coffee directly from Colombia before roasting it locally each week. 'Our coffee is sourced directly in Colombia,' Sanchez said. 'We roast here every week.' Sanvel Coffee began at the GreenMarket and has since expanded into two brick-and-mortar locations in Wellington and Riviera Beach. French bakery Caf Marseille has experienced similar growth after building a customer base at the market. 'A lot of our customer base are customers that we actually met through the GreenMarket,' owner Jean Marseille said. 'So it's been tremendous for us.' The bakery recently opened its permanent caf location after first introducing customers to its pastries at the waterfront market. Luv's Kitchen Seasoning also brings international inspiration to the market with seasonings influenced by Jamaican flavors and cooking traditions. 'We've got 12 different blends, all natural, ready-to-use complete seasoning blends,' owner Lavina Joyner said. 'All you've got to do is sprinkle and cook.' Palm Beach Cider Donuts, one of the market's longtime staples, has been part of the GreenMarket for more than two decades. 'We've been a vendor for over 25 years,' owner Travis Oimoen said. The business now operates a storefront on Northlake Boulevard while continuing its popular GreenMarket tradition each season. City officials say the GreenMarket draws between 10,000 and 15,000 visitors on average Saturdays and remains one of downtown West Palm Beachs most popular weekly attractions. entry.title: Palm Beach County commissioners unanimously approve moratorium on new hyperscale AI data centers
entry.summary: Palm Beach County commissioners unanimously approved a one-year moratorium on the construction of new hyperscale AI data centers Thursday, completing the final vote in a process that began this summer. WATCH PREVIOUS COVERAGE BELOW: Palm Beach County commissioners reject Project Tango AI data center after nearly 12 hours of debate This is an issue WPTV has been following closely for several months. The moratorium adds a definition for a large-scale data center use to the Palm Beach County Unified Land Development Code and establishes a temporary halt on new facilities that meet that definition. The county's zoning commission recommended approval of the measure in August . The temporary ban gives county officials and staff time to research and draft comprehensive regulations for the fast-growing industry, which has faced increasing public scrutiny. A study from the University of Pennsylvania indicates that approximately 60% of Americans oppose data centers being built in their communities, a significant increase from earlier this year. The moratorium follows the commission's rejection of Project Tango, a controversial data center expansion proposal near the Arden community, back in July. Residents and commissioners cited concerns that the project could negatively affect nearby homes and Saddle View Elementary School. The county's action aligns with a national trend, as other local and state governments implement similar moratoriums to better understand and manage AI-related development. What comes next During a meeting earlier this year, commissioners and zoning staff discussed a range of potential rules that could be implemented following the one-year study period.
