entry.article_text: Kyler Murray and the Minnesota Vikings' offense would've appreciated a touchdown for their progress down the stretch, but there was only one way to truly secure this victory.T.J. Hockenson fittingly took the winning slide.The Vikings stayed undefeated with more dominance by their defense and five field goals from Will Reichard, sidestepping their early passing game problems to beat the winless Miami Dolphins 15-10 on Sunday.Hockenson tied a career high with 13 receptions for 119 yards on 13 targets from Murray, including the game-sealing 8-yard catch on third-and-5 from the 10. The eighth-year tight end was wide open and could've coasted into the end zone, but he wisely slid in front of the goal line to drain the clock to the two-minute warning."Once you get the first down, you've got to get down," said Hockenson, who had his highest yardage total since Week 10 of the 2023 season. I saw that goal line and I wanted it, but it's for the betterment of the team that we ended on offense."With the Dolphins out of timeouts, the Vikings had Murray take three straight kneel-downs to move to 4-0 for the second time in three years — despite going without a touchdown in two games."If we want to score, we should do it earlier," Vikings coach Kevin O'Connell said.Murray finished 27 for 37 for 247 yards without a turnover, but he took four sacks for 34 yards against a Dolphins defense that had none in the first three games and was often tentative and unsteady in the pocket until Hockenson helped him open up the field with a handful of clutch and difficult catches.The Dolphins, who are 0-4 for the first time since starting 0-7 in 2019 in their first season under then-coach Brian Flores, were crushed by a combination of unforced mistakes — including nine penalties for 55 yards.New Dolphins quarterback Malik Willis went just 9 for 17 for 85 yards, losing a fumble during one of the two sacks by Dallas Turner. The four teams the Dolphins have faced in coach Jeff Hafley's first year are 15-1."You hate the feeling of continuing to get better without actually gaining wins on the win column, but as we see, we're going out there and competing," Willis said.Willis thought he had escaped the relentless Vikings pass rush to float a 68-yard touchdown pass to Chris Bell early in the second quarter, but Bell was flagged for illegal touching after stepping out of bounds as he moved to get open.The Vikings had 11 penalties for 85 yards, but they dodged one when Ivan Pace Jr. had a call for roughing the kicker waved off by the video replay assist system's determination that he tipped Bradley Pinion's punt and therefore didn't commit a penalty.After netting just 76 yards on 21 plays in the first half and failing to finish any possession across midfield, the Dolphins finally found a couple of creases in Minnesota's suffocating defense directed by Flores.Ollie Gordon, in an elevated role following the season-ending knee injury to star running back De'Vone Achane, ripped off a career-best 53-yard run on third-and-5 to set up Riley Patterson's 27-yard field goal. Gordon, who ended the game with 100 yards rushing, had a 12-yard touchdown run on the next drive to pull the Dolphins within 12-10.Reichard, who stretched the NFL's longest active streak to 31 consecutive made field goals, drew a loud roar when he was shown on the videoboard during the two-minute warning. Murray, on the other hand, heard some mild rounds of boos as the unproductive possessions began to pile up.But the Vikings had the ball for 14 of 15 minutes in the fourth quarter, accumulating eight first downs.Aaron Jones also carried another heavy load with 20 carries for 94 yards and four receptions for 34 yards, with the Vikings missing star wide receiver Justin Jefferson (ankle) for the first time since Week 12 of the 2023 season and running back Jordan Mason (thumb) for the third game in a row."That door will get kicked down soon," Murray said.The Vikings played most of the second half without two of their best blockers. Left guard Donovan Jackson (knee) was sidelined in the first quarter and left tackle Christian Darrisaw (neck) was hurt in the second after going head-first into the pile at the end of a run. Darrisaw returned after halftime, only to be pulled again as a precaution for a concussion evaluation following a second hit.Dolphins: Host Cincinnati next Sunday.Vikings: Play at New Orleans next Sunday.

entry.title: 'I'm forced to live in this filth': Jensen Beach residents frustrated by recurring septic backups after storms - WFLX
entry.summary: 'I'm forced to live in this filth': Jensen Beach residents frustrated by recurring septic backups after storms    WFLX
entry.article_text: WPTV is looking into drainage and septic issues on the Treasure Coast. Neighbor Daniel Fletchall reached out to our news team about septic issues in his community on Northwest Sunset Boulevard in Jensen Beach. WATCH BELOW: 'I'm forced to live in this filth': Neighbors demand septic solution Fletchall said after a heavy rain, he and his neighbors' septic backs up and comes up into their yards "The sewage water from the septic tank will actually make its way up out of the tank and into my yard," said Fletchall. "It smells back here, and I can't let my dog out." Fletchall said they can't even flush their toilets for days. "I got to go down to Home Depot or go to the mall to use the bathroom," said Fletchall. Fletchall added he can't shower or wash his clothes. "Thankfully, my parents live nearby, so I can go take a shower," said Fletchall. "But it's just not happening here.” Fletchall isn't the only one affected by this issue. Neighbors like Christie Berger are also having septic issues every time there's heavy rain. "I go to McDonald's to use the bathroom if I have to," Berger said. Neighbor Rachelle Kukan said it's becoming unacceptable. "I wish I could just kind of pick up and move because this is such a problem and it's so serious to me that I would leave if I could," said Kukan. Fletchall said he had septic companies come out to fix the drainage in his yard. Elevating the septic tank, Fletchall said, would be costly, and even then he's been told it might not solve the problem. Fletchall said he'd like the Martin County staff to extend the sewer lines into his neighborhood. "I'm forced to live in this filth, and I still pay the taxes every year to have things done around the county, but I’m not getting any help here," said Fletchall. WPTV reached out to Martin County about any solutions. Staff said the neighborhood on Northwest Sunset Boulevard is on the list to get septic-to-sewer conversions, but no date has been set yet. Staff said they're looking at ways to potentially move the neighborhood up on the list of systems to convert.

entry.title: I-TEAM: A widow maps brain cancer cases in St. Lucie County — some just doors apart - cbs12.com
entry.summary: I-TEAM: A widow maps brain cancer cases in St. Lucie County — some just doors apart    cbs12.com
entry.article_text: Matt Elliott wants to know whether his brain cancer could be connected to other diagnoses on the Treasure Coast. He also knows he may not live long enough to get an answer. It might take them years to even figure out what the hell’s going on around here, Elliott said. I can’t expect myself to be around at the end of it. Lucie County have raised similar questions for years, pointing to diagnoses just houses apart and, in some cases, among unrelated residents of the same home decades apart. In June, I-Team reporter Katie Bente revisited families’ search for answers. In this second part of her investigation, Bente went street by street with a widow tracking the diagnoses and pressing health officials for updated findings. A few houses apart For Stephanie Ankiel , one stop on the drive through Fort Pierce brings the questions back to her own family. She pointed to her late husband’s childhood home, then another home a few houses away where she said a resident was diagnosed in 2025 with the same type of brain tumor. This is the house my late husband grew up in, Ankiel said. He was diagnosed with the same exact thing as that gentleman in 2025. Both men were initially diagnosed with oligodendroglioma, a different type of brain tumor from glioblastoma . Ankiel said her husband Mark Cunningham’s cancer later progressed to glioblastoma. A few streets away, she identified another home where she said two unrelated residents developed glioblastoma decades apart. This is the house where we’ve had two glioblastoma cases, 20 years apart, no family relation, she said. Elsewhere along the route, Ankiel pointed to neighboring homes where she said a woman and an 18-year-old had been diagnosed with brain cancer. The I-Team is withholding exact addresses to protect families’ privacy. PART 1: Brain cancer diagnoses leave St. Lucie County families searching for answers, again Ankiel helps patients through the Brain Cancer Foundation of the Treasure Coast , including a child who is just 3. She has spent years mapping where patients lived and looking for possible connections. Three additional brain cancer cases were confirmed in August alone in the areas families are tracking. Those diagnoses and the proximity of patients’ homes do not establish a cancer cluster or a common cause. But Ankiel wants officials to examine the range of brain cancers represented on her map, beyond glioblastoma alone. Regardless if it’s Glio at this point, we have too much brain cancer in this area. CDC guidance allows consideration of different cancer types when evidence suggests shared causes or exposures. No such connection has been established among the cases families are tracking. What the state studied and what is new The Florida Department of Health’s 2019 review examined glioblastoma diagnoses from 1998 through 2017 in ZIP codes 34952, 34982 and 34983. It found no statistically significant increase and did not designate a cancer cluster. That review did not include later diagnoses and focused on glioblastoma rather than the range of brain tumors represented on Ankiel’s map. Her husband’s initial diagnosis is one reason she wants officials to examine that broader picture. The I-Team asked whether the department had analyzed cases diagnosed since 2017 and what would trigger new environmental testing. Lucie County Health Officer Clint Sperber said officials have been reviewing cancer registry data and environmental influences. Our latest analysis, which includes data through 2023, shows no indication of higher rates in St. Lucie County or in the specific zip codes people have asked about, Sperber wrote. Lucie’s rates are in line with nearby counties and with the state as a whole. The updated report was not available when he responded. Sperber said officials were finishing a summary to release online. His response did not explain how the analysis handled tumors initially classified as another type and later diagnosed as glioblastoma, or whether other brain cancers were examined separately. It also did not specify what would trigger additional environmental testing. No environmental factor questioned by families has been established as a cause of these cancers. A call for another look Rep. Brian Mast said he has again asked the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to examine the concerns and provide the data behind its conclusions. You need to give us the receipts, Mast said. Give us the data of where these took place, how many of them took place. The CDC said state and local health departments lead examinations of unusual cancer patterns. It confirmed that it assisted Florida’s investigation in 2018, but did not specifically address whether it had received Mast’s latest request or would open a new review. In a statement to the I-Team, a CDC spokesperson said: CDC is prepared to provide additional assistance upon the Florida Department of Health’s request. Making the most of the time left Elliott was diagnosed this year with glioblastoma, an aggressive, fast-growing grade 4 brain cancer. The former bar manager described struggling to speak after surgery and initially believing his diagnosis was an isolated case. Meeting other local patients changed that. I thought I was the only one, he said. He has decided not to continue treatment, choosing to spend his remaining time with friends and family, going to the beach and swimming. While he wants investigators to find answers, he is focused on the life he still has. I’m not going to be that person that lives to be 65, 70, 80 years old, Elliott said. But I get to hang out with my friends. I get to go take a swim, have some fun.

entry.summary: Fort Pierce man faces aggravated assault charge after incident involving U-Haul    WPBF
entry.article_text: A Fort Pierce man is facing an aggravated assault charge after two tow trucks were hit with a U-Haul truck. On Thursday, Fort Pierce Police officers responded to the 5400 block of Jamboree Drive, east of Interstate 95, regarding a report of a U-Haul box truck crashing into two vehicles. Officers learned that the U-Haul had been parked in violation of homeowner association restrictions, and the contracted tow company was attempting to remove it. During the tow attempt, the person intervened, police said. A second tow truck was positioned behind the U-Haul to prevent it from leaving. After the person refused to pay a drop fee, he entered the U-Haul, backed off the tow truck and struck the tow truck parked behind him, police said. He then continued to drive forward and reverse repeatedly until he freed the U-Haul from between the two vehicles, police said. The person drove down the street, where responding officers located him shortly afterward. No injuries were reported. The U-Haul was towed and the man was taken to the St. Police didn't identify him. entry.title: Is it legal? Trump promises Medicare and ACA checks without Congress ahead of midterm elections
entry.summary: President Trump announced that more than 20 million seniors on Medicare will soon receive a direct deposit of nearly $100, drawing Democratic criticism and questions about whether the payments made without congressional approval are legal. 'I am pleased to announce over 20 million seniors on Medicare will still be receiving a deposit of nearly $100 directly into their bank accounts,' Trump said. RELATED STORY | Trump announces $500 refunds for nearly 1 million 'Obamacare' enrollees Trump said the money will come from the Medicare Improvement Fund. A White House fact sheet says most eligible seniors will receive $90 via direct deposit in early October. Those without direct deposit will receive a check. The Medicare payment is not the only check the administration is cutting. Last month, Trump announced refunds to some people enrolled in Affordable Care Act health plans, saying they had been previously overcharged. 'Nearly 1 million hardworking Americans in 30 states will soon be getting refunds of $500 each,' Trump said. On the campaign trail, Trump has also promised more money if Republicans win in the November midterm elections. IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | $5K reality check: Experts say Trump's promise of midterm checks would strain the economy So far, no legal challenge has resulted in a court blocking either the $500 ACA refunds or the $90 Medicare payments, though Democrats have been sharply critical of both. 'If you want to BUY midterm votes, maybe start by not gutting everyone's health care in the first place,' Oregon Sen. Ron Wyden said, referring to the $500 ACA checks. Also drawing scrutiny on Capitol Hill is Trump's use of taxpayer dollars to pay for commercials this campaign season. The White House says the spending is legal, but others disagree. Complaints have been filed with the FCC and broadcasters, though no judge has yet blocked the commercials from airing.

entry.title: 17-year-old dies after shooting near Garcia's Boat Ramp in Indian River County
entry.summary: A 17-year-old died after being shot near a boat ramp in Indian River County late Friday night, according to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office. Deputies responded to reports of a juvenile shot in the 3700 block of County Road 512, near Garcia's Boat Ramp, at approximately 11:24 p.m. WATCH: 17-year-old dies after shooting near Garcia's Boat Ramp 17-year-old dies after shooting near Garcia's Boat Ramp in Indian River County The sheriff's office said deputies found the 17-year-old and began lifesaving measures until Indian River County Fire Rescue arrived. entry.title: Back to Basics Angel Program seeks help to provide holiday gifts for 10,000 Palm Beach County children
entry.summary: While many people are just beginning to think about the holidays, volunteers with Back to Basics are already hard at work making sure thousands of Palm Beach County children have gifts to open this Christmas. The nonprofit's annual Angel Program provides new sneakers, socks, underwear, and a toy to children in need throughout the county. Each year, the organization serves more than 10,000 children through the effort. Sign Up For An Angel . 'We work directly with the schools to provide gifts for kids in need throughout Palm Beach County,' said Kelly Enriquez, executive director for Back to Basics. 'We provide new sneakers, socks, underwear, and a toy for all of them.' Because of the large number of children served, preparations begin months before the holiday season arrives. Some gifts are already being sorted and wrapped as volunteers work to get ahead of the demand. 'The biggest part of our program is we can depend on the community to adopt these children,' Kelly said. 'About 7,000 will go out to the community each year and the rest of them we do in-house.' The organization is encouraging local residents, businesses and civic groups to participate by adopting children, donating gifts or volunteering their time. Back to Basics is also celebrating another successful community initiative. The nonprofit recently completed its annual school uniform drive, which provided approximately 20,000 uniforms to students at more than 60 elementary and middle schools throughout Palm Beach County. 'We serve over 60 schools here in Palm Beach County,' said board member Mike O'Dell. 'Many of the children who go to school are required to have uniforms, and they just don't have the financial wherewithal to do that.' Volunteers say community support is essential to the success of both programs and helps ensure local children have the resources they need to thrive both in school and during the holiday season. 'You're helping those in need, and this is a great way to have your children learn the generosity and the joy of giving,' Santa Claus joked during WPTV's Shining A Light visit. As the holiday season approaches, Back to Basics hopes more people will step forward to help make Christmas brighter for thousands of Palm Beach County children.

entry.summary: Flood safety tips shared as Indiantown residents prepare for more rain    WPEC
entry.article_text: Indiantown residents remain concerned about flooding after heavy rain left streets covered in water last week, with more rain and storms in the forecast for this week. CBS12 crews captured video of vehicles driving through standing water on roadways in parts of the village. Residents say flooding can quickly become expensive when water affects homes and property. The sad part is, if you don’t have insurance or anything like that you’re just stuck, your stuck with the bill, said Mary Brown, a Booker Park resident. The flooding has renewed questions about the more than $2 million drainage and roadway project in Booker Park. The project began in 2022 to help reduce flooding, but residents say heavy rain is still leaving some streets underwater. Village leaders have said they are working with Martin County on longer-term drainage solutions, including the possible repair or replacement of broken pipes. The next Indiantown Village Council meeting is Thursday night. With more rain possible this week, Martin County Fire Rescue and the Florida Department of Health in Martin County have tips available online for residents to plan ahead and avoid driving or walking through floodwater. You can CLICK HERE to view the entire list. Officials say water on a roadway may be deeper or more contaminated than it appears. Drivers who encounter a flooded road should turn around rather than attempt to drive through it. Martin County Fire Rescue responds to flooding-related emergencies, including when a vehicle becomes stuck in floodwater. Residents should call 911 during an emergency. For ongoing drainage problems or flooded roadways, residents can submit a report through Martin County’s online Request for Service system . The county asks residents to include the specific address or location and details about the issue, such as standing water, a blockage or a low spot near a drainage structure. CLICK HERE to submit a request. Health officials also advise residents whose wells flood to use bottled or boiled water until the well can be tested.

entry.title: I-TEAM: A widow maps brain cancer cases in St. Lucie County — some just doors apart - WPEC
entry.summary: I-TEAM: A widow maps brain cancer cases in St. Lucie County — some just doors apart    WPEC
entry.article_text: Matt Elliott wants to know whether his brain cancer could be connected to other diagnoses on the Treasure Coast. He also knows he may not live long enough to get an answer. It might take them years to even figure out what the hell’s going on around here, Elliott said. I can’t expect myself to be around at the end of it. Lucie County have raised similar questions for years, pointing to diagnoses just houses apart and, in some cases, among unrelated residents of the same home decades apart. In June, I-Team reporter Katie Bente revisited families’ search for answers. In this second part of her investigation, Bente went street by street with a widow tracking the diagnoses and pressing health officials for updated findings. A few houses apart For Stephanie Ankiel , one stop on the drive through Fort Pierce brings the questions back to her own family. She pointed to her late husband’s childhood home, then another home a few houses away where she said a resident was diagnosed in 2025 with the same type of brain tumor. This is the house my late husband grew up in, Ankiel said. He was diagnosed with the same exact thing as that gentleman in 2025. Both men were initially diagnosed with oligodendroglioma, a different type of brain tumor from glioblastoma . Ankiel said her husband Mark Cunningham’s cancer later progressed to glioblastoma. A few streets away, she identified another home where she said two unrelated residents developed glioblastoma decades apart. This is the house where we’ve had two glioblastoma cases, 20 years apart, no family relation, she said. Elsewhere along the route, Ankiel pointed to neighboring homes where she said a woman and an 18-year-old had been diagnosed with brain cancer. The I-Team is withholding exact addresses to protect families’ privacy. PART 1: Brain cancer diagnoses leave St. Lucie County families searching for answers, again Ankiel helps patients through the Brain Cancer Foundation of the Treasure Coast , including a child who is just 3. She has spent years mapping where patients lived and looking for possible connections. Three additional brain cancer cases were confirmed in August alone in the areas families are tracking. Those diagnoses and the proximity of patients’ homes do not establish a cancer cluster or a common cause. But Ankiel wants officials to examine the range of brain cancers represented on her map, beyond glioblastoma alone. Regardless if it’s Glio at this point, we have too much brain cancer in this area. CDC guidance allows consideration of different cancer types when evidence suggests shared causes or exposures. No such connection has been established among the cases families are tracking. What the state studied and what is new The Florida Department of Health’s 2019 review examined glioblastoma diagnoses from 1998 through 2017 in ZIP codes 34952, 34982 and 34983. It found no statistically significant increase and did not designate a cancer cluster. That review did not include later diagnoses and focused on glioblastoma rather than the range of brain tumors represented on Ankiel’s map. Her husband’s initial diagnosis is one reason she wants officials to examine that broader picture. The I-Team asked whether the department had analyzed cases diagnosed since 2017 and what would trigger new environmental testing. Lucie County Health Officer Clint Sperber said officials have been reviewing cancer registry data and environmental influences. Our latest analysis, which includes data through 2023, shows no indication of higher rates in St. Lucie County or in the specific zip codes people have asked about, Sperber wrote. Lucie’s rates are in line with nearby counties and with the state as a whole. The updated report was not available when he responded. Sperber said officials were finishing a summary to release online. His response did not explain how the analysis handled tumors initially classified as another type and later diagnosed as glioblastoma, or whether other brain cancers were examined separately. It also did not specify what would trigger additional environmental testing. No environmental factor questioned by families has been established as a cause of these cancers. A call for another look Rep. Brian Mast said he has again asked the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to examine the concerns and provide the data behind its conclusions. You need to give us the receipts, Mast said. Give us the data of where these took place, how many of them took place. The CDC said state and local health departments lead examinations of unusual cancer patterns. It confirmed that it assisted Florida’s investigation in 2018, but did not specifically address whether it had received Mast’s latest request or would open a new review. In a statement to the I-Team, a CDC spokesperson said: CDC is prepared to provide additional assistance upon the Florida Department of Health’s request. Making the most of the time left Elliott was diagnosed this year with glioblastoma, an aggressive, fast-growing grade 4 brain cancer. The former bar manager described struggling to speak after surgery and initially believing his diagnosis was an isolated case. Meeting other local patients changed that. I thought I was the only one, he said. He has decided not to continue treatment, choosing to spend his remaining time with friends and family, going to the beach and swimming. While he wants investigators to find answers, he is focused on the life he still has. I’m not going to be that person that lives to be 65, 70, 80 years old, Elliott said. But I get to hang out with my friends. I get to go take a swim, have some fun.

entry.title: Wrong-way driver arrested, faces DUI manslaughter charge after deadly I-95 crash
entry.summary: A wrong-way driver sparked a deadly three-vehicle crash early Sunday morning on I-95 in West Palm Beach, killing one person and seriously injuring two others, according to the Florida Highway Patrol (FHP). The crash happened around 5:30 a.m. Sunday on the northbound lanes of I-95 near Palm Beach Lakes Boulevard. Investigators say a GMC Sierra pickup truck was traveling south in the inside lane of northbound I-95, driving the wrong way as it approached Palm Beach Lakes Boulevard. A Palm Beach County Sheriff's deputy spotted the vehicle traveling the wrong way and paced it at about 60 to 65 mph before losing sight of it shortly before the crash. A Dodge Grand Caravan was traveling north in the inside lane when its driver, later identified as Angelo Genova, 68, of West Palm Beach, attempted to swerve right to avoid the oncoming pickup but was unable to avoid a collision. Following the initial impact, the pickup rotated and came to rest in the inside northbound lane. The van spun across the roadway from west to east. A Cadillac El Dorado was traveling north behind the van and was unable to avoid the wreckage. The Cadillac then struck the rear of the van, according to FHP. Genova was pronounced dead at the scene. The wrong-way driver, identified in an arrest report as Edwin Castro, 26, of West Palm Beach, and the Cadillac driver suffered serious injuries and were transported to St. Mary's Medical Center for treatment. FHP said the driver of the Cadallic suffered incapacitating injuries. According to the arrest report, deputies and troopers observed that Castro showed signs of impairment after the crash, including a strong odor of alcohol, bloodshot eyes and slurred speech. Hospital toxicology results showed Castro's blood alcohol level was 0.239, nearly three times Florida's legal limit of 0.08, investigators said. Castro was arrested and charged with DUI causing death, vehicular homicide, DUI causing serious bodily injury, reckless driving causing serious bodily injury, two counts of DUI causing property damage or injury and two counts of reckless driving causing property damage or injury. He was also cited for driving the wrong way on the interstate. The arrest report also states that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement told investigators that Castro had a final order of removal after a denied asylum claim from Guatemala. entry.title: Altercation at tow yard leads to shooting, Martin County Sheriff's Office says - WPBF
entry.summary: Altercation at tow yard leads to shooting, Martin County Sheriff's Office says    WPBF
entry.article_text: Two women are in custody in Martin County after a shooting at a tow yard led to a police chase and a violent crash Friday afternoon. “I have more questions than I have answers,” Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said. Budensiek said the incident began around 1 p.m. when two women arrived at Gary’s Towing and Recovery, 4405 SE Cove Road, near Stuart, to retrieve a car that had been towed earlier that morning. While they were there, two other individuals showed up to claim the same vehicle. “They got into some type of argument about the belongings in the car, which, by the way, the only thing in the car really was a couple of guns,” Budensiek said. The sheriff said one of the original women then grabbed a gun and began shooting. No one was injured, but bullets struck trailers in the yard. “It’s just crazy how it went down,” said Gary Reed, the owner of Gary’s Towing and Recovery. Reed, who was not present during the shooting, said his employee called him, screaming for help. And I’m running as fast as I can,” Reed said. https://www.facebook.com/MartinCountySheriffsOffice/posts/pfbid0enPBfuxCWxva9Ce6vmU7hGP3nKdhfidsLzp1e7zxkZ58uSYxB3KhHPTdVi9kagZnl By the time deputies and Reed arrived at the scene, all four individuals involved had fled. The sheriff said the accused shooter had taken the car they were disputing, but deputies located her shortly later on Cove Road near U.S. She attempted to flee but was quickly arrested. Investigators identified her as Jade Rondon, 23, from Miami. The other woman she was with has been identified as Valerie Valdes, 22, also from Miami. Budensiek said she was taken into custody after causing a violent collision on U.S. “Why she was driving at a high rate of speed, why she was weaving out of traffic, we’re not sure. We didn’t even know for sure that that car was involved at that time,” Budensiek said. The sheriff said investigators are working to answer these questions and plan to obtain search warrants for the suspects’ cars and phones. He hopes to have more answers by next week. Rondon already is facing two counts of aggravated assault with a firearm, discharging a firearm in public, aggravated fleeing and eluding, driving while license suspended, felony criminal mischief. Valdes has been cited for operating an unregistered motor vehicle and four counts of reckless driving with injuries. Because the incident was a half-mile from Murray Middle School, MCSO activated an active-shooter response and placed the school on lockout. Detectives with the sheriff's office's Criminal Investigations Division and crime scene personnel are processing the scene and interviewing multiple witnesses. Investigators said the shooting appears to be an isolated incident and there is no threat to the public. No information about a possible suspect or what led up to the shooting has been released. Anyone with information is asked to call the Indian River County Sheriff's Office at 772-569-6700 or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 1-800-273-TIPS. The investigation remains active.

entry.title: 2 killed, including a high school student, in Florida school bus crash, sheriff says
entry.summary: A 10th-grade student and another person were killed after a multi-vehicle crash involving a school bus happened Monday morning in Central Florida. Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd said during a morning news conference that the crash happened around 6 a.m., when a Chevrolet Malibu veered over the center line of a road and hit a Winter Haven High School bus traveling in the opposite direction. There were 37 students on board. The impact of the collision ripped the tire off the bus and caused it to crash head-on into an oncoming Jeep before rolling over off the side of Winter Haven Road. The sheriff said the driver of the Jeep had died. At least five other people involved in the crash were hospitalized, according to authorities. 'It was a horrible crash,' Judd said. 'It was a terrible, tragic morning. We had a beautiful 10th grade girl lose her life.' The city of Winter Haven is located about 51 miles east of Tampa and 47 miles southwest of Orlando. This story was originally published by Leilyn Torres and Anthony Romano with the Scripps News Group in Tampa.

entry.title: I-TEAM: A widow maps brain cancer cases in St. Lucie County - some just doors apart - WPEC
entry.summary: I-TEAM: A widow maps brain cancer cases in St. Lucie County - some just doors apart    WPEC
entry.article_text: Matt Elliott wants to know whether his brain cancer could be connected to other diagnoses on the Treasure Coast. He also knows he may not live long enough to get an answer. It might take them years to even figure out what the hell’s going on around here, Elliott said. I can’t expect myself to be around at the end of it. Lucie County have raised similar questions for years, pointing to diagnoses just houses apart and, in some cases, among unrelated residents of the same home decades apart. In June, I-Team reporter Katie Bente revisited families’ search for answers. In this second part of her investigation, Bente went street by street with a widow tracking the diagnoses and pressing health officials for updated findings. A few houses apart For Stephanie Ankiel , one stop on the drive through Fort Pierce brings the questions back to her own family. She pointed to her late husband’s childhood home, then another home a few houses away where she said a resident was diagnosed in 2025 with the same type of brain tumor. This is the house my late husband grew up in, Ankiel said. He was diagnosed with the same exact thing as that gentleman in 2025. Both men were initially diagnosed with oligodendroglioma, a different type of brain tumor from glioblastoma . Ankiel said her husband Mark Cunningham’s cancer later progressed to glioblastoma. A few streets away, she identified another home where she said two unrelated residents developed glioblastoma decades apart. This is the house where we’ve had two glioblastoma cases, 20 years apart, no family relation, she said. Elsewhere along the route, Ankiel pointed to neighboring homes where she said a woman and an 18-year-old had been diagnosed with brain cancer. The I-Team is withholding exact addresses to protect families’ privacy. PART 1: Brain cancer diagnoses leave St. Lucie County families searching for answers, again Ankiel helps patients through the Brain Cancer Foundation of the Treasure Coast , including a child who is just 3. She has spent years mapping where patients lived and looking for possible connections. Three additional brain cancer cases were confirmed in August alone in the areas families are tracking. Those diagnoses and the proximity of patients’ homes do not establish a cancer cluster or a common cause. But Ankiel wants officials to examine the range of brain cancers represented on her map, beyond glioblastoma alone. Regardless if it’s Glio at this point, we have too much brain cancer in this area. CDC guidance allows consideration of different cancer types when evidence suggests shared causes or exposures. No such connection has been established among the cases families are tracking. What the state studied and what is new The Florida Department of Health’s 2019 review examined glioblastoma diagnoses from 1998 through 2017 in ZIP codes 34952, 34982 and 34983. It found no statistically significant increase and did not designate a cancer cluster. That review did not include later diagnoses and focused on glioblastoma rather than the range of brain tumors represented on Ankiel’s map. Her husband’s initial diagnosis is one reason she wants officials to examine that broader picture. The I-Team asked whether the department had analyzed cases diagnosed since 2017 and what would trigger new environmental testing. Lucie County Health Officer Clint Sperber said officials have been reviewing cancer registry data and environmental influences. Our latest analysis, which includes data through 2023, shows no indication of higher rates in St. Lucie County or in the specific zip codes people have asked about, Sperber wrote. Lucie’s rates are in line with nearby counties and with the state as a whole. The updated report was not available when he responded. Sperber said officials were finishing a summary to release online. His response did not explain how the analysis handled tumors initially classified as another type and later diagnosed as glioblastoma, or whether other brain cancers were examined separately. It also did not specify what would trigger additional environmental testing. No environmental factor questioned by families has been established as a cause of these cancers. A call for another look Rep. Brian Mast said he has again asked the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to examine the concerns and provide the data behind its conclusions. You need to give us the receipts, Mast said. Give us the data of where these took place, how many of them took place. The CDC said state and local health departments lead examinations of unusual cancer patterns. It confirmed that it assisted Florida’s investigation in 2018, but did not specifically address whether it had received Mast’s latest request or would open a new review. In a statement to the I-Team, a CDC spokesperson said: CDC is prepared to provide additional assistance upon the Florida Department of Health’s request. Making the most of the time left Elliott was diagnosed this year with glioblastoma, an aggressive, fast-growing grade 4 brain cancer. The former bar manager described struggling to speak after surgery and initially believing his diagnosis was an isolated case. Meeting other local patients changed that. I thought I was the only one, he said. He has decided not to continue treatment, choosing to spend his remaining time with friends and family, going to the beach and swimming. While he wants investigators to find answers, he is focused on the life he still has. I’m not going to be that person that lives to be 65, 70, 80 years old, Elliott said. But I get to hang out with my friends. I get to go take a swim, have some fun.

entry.title: 'I get chewed to death': St. Lucie County tackles mosquito breeding after heavy rain - WPBF
entry.summary: 'I get chewed to death': St. Lucie County tackles mosquito breeding after heavy rain    WPBF
entry.article_text: Lucie County mosquito control are working to stop mosquitoes from breeding after recent rain created standing water. In a residential neighborhood near U.S. 1 and Fort Pierce, mosquito control teams treated swales and used a backpack blower to distribute larvicide. Officials said the rain has increased standing water, which allows mosquito eggs to hatch. "So relative to last year, mosquito calls have been pretty reduced, but at any moment’s notice following a lot of rain, we can have a huge strike in population, so it's important to be on top of our game," said Daniel Tuzzolino, senior entomologist at St. Lucie County Mosquito Control. DENGUE FEVER: Dengue fever case in Palm Beach County prompts mosquito control action Kenneth Fusco, a nearby resident, shared his experience with the mosquito problem. "If I go out in my front yard and start to do anything, you get bit. I have an island behind me with some cats. If I go over there, I have to wear long pants because I get chewed to death," Fusco said. He added, "Park the truck and leave it for 20 minutes and leave it in front of my house, please!" Crews are also monitoring reports of dengue fever and West Nile virus in surrounding counties. They are asking residents to empty or remove containers holding water to prevent mosquito breeding. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates "We are really doubling down and making sure that the people of St. Lucie County know the importance of tipping and tossing because anything that you do to remove potential environment for those dangerous mosquitoes really helps reduce the likelihood that we have transmission in this county," Tuzzolino said. Thursday's heavy rain also caused erosion and a washout along Indian River Drive, where crews were completing a shoulder repair project designed to protect the roadway during heavy rain events. More rain is expected, which could lead to additional standing water and, Tuzzolino said, "A lot more mosquitoes! A lot more mosquitoes!" If you are dealing with a mosquito problem near your home, contact St. Lucie County mosquito control at 772-462-1962 or email mosquito@stlucieco.org. entry.title: Discover The Palm Beaches to host 2-day hospitality and tourism job fair in Lake Worth Beach & Greenacres
entry.summary: Residents looking for work in Palm Beach County's tourism and hospitality industry will have two opportunities this month to connect with employers ahead of the busy tourism season. Discover The Palm Beaches (DTPB), the county's destination marketing organization, announced it will host its 5th Annual Hospitality and Tourism Job Fair on Oct. 9 and Oct. 15, bringing together employers from across the region. The free event is open to everyone and will feature full-time and part-time job opportunities in hotels, restaurants, attractions, entertainment venues, retail businesses and other tourism-related organizations. The first job fair will be held from 8:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. on Friday, Oct. 9, at Palm Beach State College's Lake Worth campus Public Safety Building, located at 4200 S. Congress Ave. The second event is scheduled for 8:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. on Thursday, Oct. 15, at the City of Greenacres Community Center, 501 Swain Blvd. According to DTPB, Palm Beach County's tourism industry supports nearly 95,000 local jobs and continues to be one of the area's largest economic drivers. 'A strong tourism industry depends on a strong workforce,' said Heather Andrews, senior vice president of commercial strategy and destination stewardship for DTPB. 'This job fair brings together leading employers and talented local residents, creating connections that strengthen careers, support businesses and contribute to the continued success of The Palm Beaches.' Available positions include front desk, food and beverage, operations, sales, marketing and management roles. Many employers are offering competitive benefits, paid time off and opportunities for advancement, organizers said. The job fair comes amid continued growth in Palm Beach County's tourism sector. DTPB said The Palm Beaches welcomed a record 6.09 million visitors during the first half of 2026, a 6.4% increase compared to the same period last year. Spanish and Creole translators will be available at both events to help job seekers connect with prospective employers. Applicants can pre-register for the event on the Palm Beach's website and are encouraged to dress professionally and bring their resume. entry.title: New I-95 Oslo Road interchange opens in Indian River County over a year ahead of schedule
entry.summary: Governor Ron DeSantis was in Indian River County on Monday to celebrate the completion of a new I-95 interchange at Oslo Road, a $100 million project state officials say will improve traffic flow, emergency response times and freight movement. The interchange, which opened about a year ahead of schedule , marks the first new I-95 interchange built in Indian River County in nearly 50 years. 'This is going to bring a new critical connection to I-95 for a part of the state that has changed quite a bit,' DeSantis said. According to the governor, drivers using Oslo Road to access I-95 can expect travel times to be cut roughly in half. 'This will ultimately save some lives because time is of the essence in some of these situations,' DeSantis said. 'Every single second counts when it comes to saving lives, and this is going to reduce the time it takes for first responders to get to incidents substantially,' Perdue said. entry.title: I-TEAM: A widow maps brain cancer cases in St. Lucie County - some just doors apart - WPEC
entry.summary: I-TEAM: A widow maps brain cancer cases in St. Lucie County - some just doors apart    WPEC
entry.article_text: Matt Elliott wants to know whether his brain cancer could be connected to other diagnoses on the Treasure Coast. He also knows he may not live long enough to get an answer. It might take them years to even figure out what the hell’s going on around here, Elliott said. I can’t expect myself to be around at the end of it. Lucie County have raised similar questions for years, pointing to diagnoses just houses apart and, in some cases, among unrelated residents of the same home decades apart. In June, I-Team reporter Katie Bente revisited families’ search for answers. In this second part of her investigation, Bente went street by street with a widow tracking the diagnoses and pressing health officials for updated findings. A few houses apart For Stephanie Ankiel , one stop on the drive through Fort Pierce brings the questions back to her own family. She pointed to her late husband’s childhood home, then another home a few houses away where she said a resident was diagnosed in 2025 with the same type of brain tumor. This is the house my late husband grew up in, Ankiel said. He was diagnosed with the same exact thing as that gentleman in 2025. Both men were initially diagnosed with oligodendroglioma, a different type of brain tumor from glioblastoma . Ankiel said her husband Mark Cunningham’s cancer later progressed to glioblastoma. A few streets away, she identified another home where she said two unrelated residents developed glioblastoma decades apart. This is the house where we’ve had two glioblastoma cases, 20 years apart, no family relation, she said. Elsewhere along the route, Ankiel pointed to neighboring homes where she said a woman and an 18-year-old had been diagnosed with brain cancer. The I-Team is withholding exact addresses to protect families’ privacy. PART 1: Brain cancer diagnoses leave St. Lucie County families searching for answers, again Ankiel helps patients through the Brain Cancer Foundation of the Treasure Coast , including a child who is just 3. She has spent years mapping where patients lived and looking for possible connections. Three additional brain cancer cases were confirmed in August alone in the areas families are tracking. Those diagnoses and the proximity of patients’ homes do not establish a cancer cluster or a common cause. But Ankiel wants officials to examine the range of brain cancers represented on her map, beyond glioblastoma alone. Regardless if it’s Glio at this point, we have too much brain cancer in this area. CDC guidance allows consideration of different cancer types when evidence suggests shared causes or exposures. No such connection has been established among the cases families are tracking. What the state studied and what is new The Florida Department of Health’s 2019 review examined glioblastoma diagnoses from 1998 through 2017 in ZIP codes 34952, 34982 and 34983. It found no statistically significant increase and did not designate a cancer cluster. That review did not include later diagnoses and focused on glioblastoma rather than the range of brain tumors represented on Ankiel’s map. Her husband’s initial diagnosis is one reason she wants officials to examine that broader picture. The I-Team asked whether the department had analyzed cases diagnosed since 2017 and what would trigger new environmental testing. Lucie County Health Officer Clint Sperber said officials have been reviewing cancer registry data and environmental influences. Our latest analysis, which includes data through 2023, shows no indication of higher rates in St. Lucie County or in the specific zip codes people have asked about, Sperber wrote. Lucie’s rates are in line with nearby counties and with the state as a whole. The updated report was not available when he responded. Sperber said officials were finishing a summary to release online. His response did not explain how the analysis handled tumors initially classified as another type and later diagnosed as glioblastoma, or whether other brain cancers were examined separately. It also did not specify what would trigger additional environmental testing. No environmental factor questioned by families has been established as a cause of these cancers. A call for another look Rep. Brian Mast said he has again asked the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to examine the concerns and provide the data behind its conclusions. You need to give us the receipts, Mast said. Give us the data of where these took place, how many of them took place. The CDC said state and local health departments lead examinations of unusual cancer patterns. It confirmed that it assisted Florida’s investigation in 2018, but did not specifically address whether it had received Mast’s latest request or would open a new review. In a statement to the I-Team, a CDC spokesperson said: CDC is prepared to provide additional assistance upon the Florida Department of Health’s request. Making the most of the time left Elliott was diagnosed this year with glioblastoma, an aggressive, fast-growing grade 4 brain cancer. The former bar manager described struggling to speak after surgery and initially believing his diagnosis was an isolated case. Meeting other local patients changed that. I thought I was the only one, he said. He has decided not to continue treatment, choosing to spend his remaining time with friends and family, going to the beach and swimming. While he wants investigators to find answers, he is focused on the life he still has. I’m not going to be that person that lives to be 65, 70, 80 years old, Elliott said. But I get to hang out with my friends. I get to go take a swim, have some fun.

entry.article_text: WPTV learned there are 13 license plate reader cameras in St. Lucie County that don't have permits, according to county staff.Wednesday, Sept. 30, was the deadline the Florida Department of Transportation gave municipalities to remove the license plate readers from state-controlled roads.WATCH BELOW: Unpermitted license plate readers found in St. Lucie CountyNow WPTV is pressing city leaders about why the cameras are there, who they belong to, and what is happening to the cameras now.On Thursday, WPTV spoke to Ricky Mathura, who works at a gas station off Orange Avenue and 25th Street in Fort Pierce, where one of the unpermitted license plate readers was found."I don't know why it's there," said Mathura. Lucie County Communications Director Erick Gill said they're trying to find that out."We don't know who they belong to," Gill said. "They were just put in our right-of-way."The county says there's 53 permitted license plate readers on their right-of-ways and gave WPTV a list with all the locations of the unpermitted license plate readers staff found.RELATED: FDOT revokes permits for automated license plate readers"We were surprised, you know, that were that many out there,” said Gill.The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office told WPTV they claimed three of them but are working to find out why they weren't permitted.Gill said county staff is actively working to identify the owners of the other readers and taped notices on the cameras for the owners to take them down within 30 days.Once the 30 days are up, Gill said staff will remove the readers safely."We'll begin the process of either removing them if we feel like we can safely remove them without damaging the equipment and endangering our staff, or at least covering up so the cameras can't capture any surveillance," Gill said.

entry.title: Gov. DeSantis to hold press conference in Vero Beach - WPBF
entry.summary: Gov. DeSantis to hold press conference in Vero Beach    WPBF
entry.article_text: The new I-95 interchange at Oslo Road is now open for drivers in Indian River County, a year ahead of schedule. Ron DeSantis, joined by Florida Department of Transportation Secretary Jared Perdue, held a press conference at 11 a.m. in Vero Beach on Monday announcing the completion of the nearly $100 million project. "This is the first new interchange built in this area, in almost 50 years, so this is going to bring new critical connection to I-95 for a part of the state that has changed quite a bit," DeSantis said. DeSantis said the new interchange is expected to reduce congestion on nearby interchanges like Indrio Road and State Road 60, cutting drive times in half. It also aims to improve emergency response efforts and movement along Florida's supply chain. "With the number of daily vehicles on the corridor still expected to grow between now and 2045 significantly, the Oslo Road interchange sets a clear example of how Florida delivers infrastructure that improves quality of life today while building more capacity for the future," DeSantis said. According to FDOT, work began back in August 2023 and was projected to be completed by spring 2027. "We actually implemented voluntary acceleration on this project," Perdue said. "Thank you to Halley Engineering Contractors and team for bringing an idea forward that actually enabled us to finish this project an entire year — to be exact, 400 days — ahead of schedule." While this new interchange is now complete, Perdue said work isn't done just yet on the Treasure Coast, as there are nearly a billion dollars of transportation investment planned for the area that FDOT will continue to work on and finish as quickly as possible. entry.article_text: Parents, students and grandparents gathered outside the Okeechobee County School Board on Monday, demanding greater accountability over bullying concerns after a 14-year-old student said relentless harassment pushed her to a breaking point.Signs lined the street as protesters chanted "no more bullying" and "hold bullies accountable," rallying around 14-year-old Estrella Ventura Meras, a student at Okeechobee Achievement Academy.Last week, WPTV reported on a video showing Estrella jumping from the window of a moving school bus. WPTV is not showing the video.Estrella told WPTV she jumped to escape students who had been bullying her since the start of the school year. She said she later went home and attempted to take her own life."I thank God he gave me another chance to live," Estrella said, holding back tears.Her mother, Estela Meras, said she found her daughter pale and lying next to a pill bottle. She said Estrella had left behind a note saying she was tired."What if I hadn't found her there lying in bed?" Meras said as she became emotional. Now, Estrella and her mother are calling for change."I just hope there's justice and the students responsible," said Estela Meras. "Everybody was on the bus laughing about her instead of helping her. If it was me, I would have been helping somebody."Estrella told WPTV she repeatedly reported the alleged bullying to teachers and administrators at Okeechobee Achievement Academy but said nothing changed. Her mother said she also previously raised concerns about bullying involving her daughter and now wants the district to reevaluate how it handles those reports.Other families at Monday's protest told WPTV they have also raised concerns about bullying at Okeechobee Achievement Academy and believe more needs to be done. "Somebody has to take some accountability somewhere," protester Maria Rodriguez said. Okeechobee County Schools said it shares parents' belief that "bullying has no place in our schools" and that every student deserves to feel safe, supported and heard.The district said the allegations involving Estrella remain under investigation. Citing federal student privacy law, district officials said they could not publicly discuss details of the investigation, education records or any potential student discipline.The district said schools are responsible for investigating bullying allegations reported by students and parents. If a family believes a school has failed to act on a complaint, district officials said the family should contact the district office so administrators can review both the allegations and the school's response."We take allegations that reports have gone unaddressed seriously," district spokesperson Dr. Joseph Stanley said in a statement to WPTV.Under School Board Policy 5.321, bullying reports can be made verbally, in writing or anonymously, and no specific reporting form is required. The policy calls for separate, confidential interviews and a review of evidence, with investigative procedural steps to be completed within a maximum of 10 school days, according to the district.The district said the policy also requires parents to be promptly notified when an investigation begins and requires a written report and recommendations for corrective action. It also includes provisions for counseling, intervention and follow-up measures intended to protect students.The district told WPTV that Okeechobee Achievement Academy has completed investigations into four other reports of alleged bullying during the current school year. Those cases involved four alleged victims and nine alleged perpetrators.None of the four complaints was substantiated as bullying, according to the district. Those cases are separate from the investigation involving Estrella, which remains open.However, the district stressed that an allegation being unsubstantiated as "bullying" does not necessarily mean no inappropriate behavior occurred. Florida law defines bullying as "systematically and chronically inflicting physical hurt or psychological distress" on one or more students. The district said a single incident generally does not meet that definition on its own, although one incident could reveal a broader pattern. Conduct that does not legally qualify as bullying could also constitute harassment or another violation requiring intervention or discipline.District officials said cooperation from students and parents is important during investigations because details about incidents, witnesses, previous reports and other evidence can help investigators determine what happened. The district said limited participation can restrict the information available to investigators but does not prevent officials from reviewing the evidence they can obtain.Despite calls from some parents for changes, Okeechobee County Schools said it believes its existing policies comply with Florida law and provide a thorough framework for responding to bullying allegations. The district said no procedural, staffing, disciplinary or policy changes are currently under consideration in response to the concerns raised by families.Instead, officials said their focus is on consistently implementing existing requirements, conducting thorough investigations and taking appropriate action based on the evidence.For Estrella's mother and the families who stood alongside her Monday, however, the protest was about making sure their concerns are heard before another child reaches a breaking point."All we want is answers for Estrella," Rodriguez said.

entry.article_text: No arrests have been made in the shooting death of a 17-year-old at a teen meetup near Garcia's Boat Ramp in Indian River County, with a self-defense claim expected in the case, Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers announced Monday.WATCH BELOW: Sheriff Eric Flowers give update on shooting death of teen"We got kids out here losing their lives chasing likes and shares on social media," Flowers said.The shooting occurred late Friday night when approximately 100 teens, ranging in age from 14 to 19, gathered at Garcia's Boat Ramp in the 3700 block of County Road 512, the sheriff said. Deputies had broken up a similar group earlier that evening before the crowd moved to the boat ramp."The 17-year-old, and a group of his friends, are approaching a truck, and there are two people, both 18 years old, inside of that truck. The 17-year-old opens the door, and he starts to punch," Flowers said. "He's going to punch on the people that are inside of that truck. That shot is the shot that ultimately killed 17-year-old in this case."The teen's friends drove him away from the scene, east on County Road 512, while calling 911 and a dispatcher told them to stop at Fellsmere City Hall, where emergency crews performed CPR, the sheriff said. He was taken to Sebastian River Medical Center and later flown to Holmes Regional Medical Center in Melbourne, where he died from his injuries.The two individuals in the truck were identified using the sheriff's office's Flock technology, the sheriff said. Flowers said both have been cooperative with investigators, surrendering the weapon used in the shooting and the truck. Additional individuals involved in the incident have also been identified through Flock, though some remain unidentified. Investigators also recovered other weapons from the vehicle in which the 17-year-old was transported from the scene.WATCH: 17-year-old dies after shooting near Garcia's Boat RampFlowers said a warrant will be submitted in the case, but it will be up to the state to determine whether charges are filed."There have been no arrests on this case at this time, because the preliminary investigation shows that the 17-year-old was opening the door to attempt to fight with the two that were inside of the vehicle. They had a history of fighting," Flowers said. "Self defense plays a part in these, and when these kids go out and videotape these fights, and now guns are involved, there's going to be more of this." Names of those involved are not being released as the investigation continues, the sheriff said.Investigators believe at least four fights occurred at the boat ramp on the night of the shooting. Multiple shell casings and rounds were recovered from the scene.During Monday's news conference, Flowers released video of the shooting, noting the footage had already circulated widely on social media and that the victim's mother had seen it. One of the 18-year-olds involved in the shooting attends Vero Beach High School.The sheriff said teen meetups like the one at Garcia's Boat Ramp are coordinated through Snapchat, making them difficult for law enforcement to track in advance."When it's Snapchat, it's basically a private conversation," Flowers said. "But it quickly can escalate to over 100, 150, 200 people there."Flowers said the meetups, which have included alcohol, fighting, and firearms, have been taking place for years across Indian River County, Okeechobee, and surrounding areas, but that social media has intensified the danger."Now we're adding guns and alcohol into the mix, and we're adding social media into the mix, and so what we're seeing is an escalation of each one of these," Flowers said. There's guns, and those two just don't mix. And now add in the fuel of the fire of social media, and now we have a 17-year-old dead."The sheriff said teens at these gatherings are motivated in part by a desire for online attention."The kids like to fight, and they like to videotape it, and they like to get their likes and shares because of that," Flowers said. Parents, you see these videos. You do not want your teens out at these meetups."With Vero Beach High School's homecoming game scheduled for Friday and the dance on Saturday, Flowers said additional deputies will be on duty. Meanwhile, the sheriff urged parents to monitor their children's whereabouts and report any information about planned meetups to the sheriff's office."Parents, if your kids are telling you that they're headed out to one of these meetups, ask them where they're going. Ask, find out the details. Share that with us," Flowers said.He recommended parents use location-sharing apps such as Life360 to track their children and said a child appearing to be in a remote or unusual location can be an indicator that a meetup is taking place.The investigation remains active. Flowers said anyone who witnessed any of the events that night, including the shooting itself, and has not yet spoken to investigators is urged to come forward."I can tell you, our investigation is not even remotely over, and if we are able to identify people that were involved in this, from underage drinking to fighting, hurting other people," Flowers said. " If they did something wrong, they're going to have to be accountable for that."Anyone with information is asked to call the Indian River County Sheriff's Office at 772-569-6700 or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 1-800-273-TIPS.

entry.title: I-TEAM: A widow maps brain cancer cases in St. Lucie County - some just doors apart - WPEC
entry.summary: I-TEAM: A widow maps brain cancer cases in St. Lucie County - some just doors apart    WPEC
entry.article_text: Matt Elliott wants to know whether his brain cancer could be connected to other diagnoses on the Treasure Coast. He also knows he may not live long enough to get an answer. It might take them years to even figure out what the hell’s going on around here, Elliott said. I can’t expect myself to be around at the end of it. Lucie County have raised similar questions for years, pointing to diagnoses just houses apart and, in some cases, among unrelated residents of the same home decades apart. In June, I-Team reporter Katie Bente revisited families’ search for answers. In this second part of her investigation, Bente went street by street with a widow tracking the diagnoses and pressing health officials for updated findings. A few houses apart For Stephanie Ankiel , one stop on the drive through Fort Pierce brings the questions back to her own family. She pointed to her late husband’s childhood home, then another home a few houses away where she said a resident was diagnosed in 2025 with the same type of brain tumor. This is the house my late husband grew up in, Ankiel said. He was diagnosed with the same exact thing as that gentleman in 2025. Both men were initially diagnosed with oligodendroglioma, a different type of brain tumor from glioblastoma . Ankiel said her husband Mark Cunningham’s cancer later progressed to glioblastoma. A few streets away, she identified another home where she said two unrelated residents developed glioblastoma decades apart. This is the house where we’ve had two glioblastoma cases, 20 years apart, no family relation, she said. Elsewhere along the route, Ankiel pointed to neighboring homes where she said a woman and an 18-year-old had been diagnosed with brain cancer. The I-Team is withholding exact addresses to protect families’ privacy. PART 1: Brain cancer diagnoses leave St. Lucie County families searching for answers, again Ankiel helps patients through the Brain Cancer Foundation of the Treasure Coast , including a child who is just 3. She has spent years mapping where patients lived and looking for possible connections. Three additional brain cancer cases were confirmed in August alone in the areas families are tracking. Those diagnoses and the proximity of patients’ homes do not establish a cancer cluster or a common cause. But Ankiel wants officials to examine the range of brain cancers represented on her map, beyond glioblastoma alone. Regardless if it’s Glio at this point, we have too much brain cancer in this area. CDC guidance allows consideration of different cancer types when evidence suggests shared causes or exposures. No such connection has been established among the cases families are tracking. What the state studied and what is new The Florida Department of Health’s 2019 review examined glioblastoma diagnoses from 1998 through 2017 in ZIP codes 34952, 34982 and 34983. It found no statistically significant increase and did not designate a cancer cluster. That review did not include later diagnoses and focused on glioblastoma rather than the range of brain tumors represented on Ankiel’s map. Her husband’s initial diagnosis is one reason she wants officials to examine that broader picture. The I-Team asked whether the department had analyzed cases diagnosed since 2017 and what would trigger new environmental testing. Lucie County Health Officer Clint Sperber said officials have been reviewing cancer registry data and environmental influences. Our latest analysis, which includes data through 2023, shows no indication of higher rates in St. Lucie County or in the specific zip codes people have asked about, Sperber wrote. Lucie’s rates are in line with nearby counties and with the state as a whole. The updated report was not available when he responded. Sperber said officials were finishing a summary to release online. His response did not explain how the analysis handled tumors initially classified as another type and later diagnosed as glioblastoma, or whether other brain cancers were examined separately. It also did not specify what would trigger additional environmental testing. No environmental factor questioned by families has been established as a cause of these cancers. A call for another look Rep. Brian Mast said he has again asked the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to examine the concerns and provide the data behind its conclusions. You need to give us the receipts, Mast said. Give us the data of where these took place, how many of them took place. The CDC said state and local health departments lead examinations of unusual cancer patterns. It confirmed that it assisted Florida’s investigation in 2018, but did not specifically address whether it had received Mast’s latest request or would open a new review. In a statement to the I-Team, a CDC spokesperson said: CDC is prepared to provide additional assistance upon the Florida Department of Health’s request. Making the most of the time left Elliott was diagnosed this year with glioblastoma, an aggressive, fast-growing grade 4 brain cancer. The former bar manager described struggling to speak after surgery and initially believing his diagnosis was an isolated case. Meeting other local patients changed that. I thought I was the only one, he said. He has decided not to continue treatment, choosing to spend his remaining time with friends and family, going to the beach and swimming. While he wants investigators to find answers, he is focused on the life he still has. I’m not going to be that person that lives to be 65, 70, 80 years old, Elliott said. But I get to hang out with my friends. I get to go take a swim, have some fun.

entry.title: DeSantis opens new I-95 interchange in Indian River County, a year early - WPEC
entry.summary: DeSantis opens new I-95 interchange in Indian River County, a year early    WPEC
entry.article_text: Ron DeSantis opened the new I-95 interchange at Oslo Road in Indian River County on Monday, calling it a critical connection for drivers, emergency crews and the region’s growing population. The roughly $100 million project opened one year ahead of schedule , according to the governor’s office and the Florida Department of Transportation. This is the first new interchange built in this area in almost 50 years, DeSantis said. It’s going to bring [a] new critical connection [to] I-95 for a part of the state that has changed quite a bit. The new exit is expected to ease congestion at nearby Indrio Road and State Road 60 interchanges, DeSantis said. Drivers traveling from Oslo Road to I-95 can expect their travel times to be cut in half, he added. With the number of daily vehicles on the corridor still expected to grow between now and 2045 significantly, the Oslo Road interchange sets a clear example of how Florida delivers infrastructure that improves quality of life today while building more capacity for the future, DeSantis said. The governor also said the direct interstate connection will help emergency crews respond faster in southern Indian River County. See also: Two killed, including 10th-grade girl, after rollover school bus crash in Polk County We anticipate that just for the local community on a normal basis, for local, like non-hurricane-type emergencies, that the emergency response time will be reduced by up to 56%, DeSantis said. That will ultimately save some lives, of course, because time is of the essence in some of these situations. FDOT Secretary Jared Perdue said the project was completed 400 days early through what the agency calls voluntary acceleration, which lets contractors propose ways to speed construction and share in the savings. This is going to reduce the time it takes for first responders to get to incidents substantially, Perdue said. We’re really excited about that, to include cutting commute time in half and so many other benefits. DeSantis said FDOT also acquired land near the interchange for a dedicated gopher tortoise habitat. He said the site will be the only relocation area of its kind in Southeast Florida. Florida [is] showing that it’s possible to do the projects that we need done while also buttressing environmental stewardship, DeSantis said. Perdue said nearly $1 billion in transportation investment is planned for the Treasure Coast region.

entry.title: Indian River County sheriff investigates whether fatal shooting of teen at boat ramp was self-defense
entry.summary: A 17-year-old was killed in a shooting Friday night at Garcia's Boat Ramp in Indian River County, and investigators are examining whether the shooting was an act of self-defense , according to Sheriff Eric Flowers. WATCH: WPTV'S Coverage of Teen killed in Garcia's Boat Ramp shooting 17-Year-Old Killed at Indian River County Boat Ramp; Sheriff Investigating Self-Defense Claim The shooting happened during a confrontation at the popular waterfront gathering spot, which authorities say has become a frequent meetup location for teenagers. According to Flowers, investigators reviewed video that showed the 17-year-old opening the door of a truck and throwing punches at people inside before a shot was fired. 'The 17-year-old opens the door, and he starts to punch. He's going to punch the people that are inside of that truck,' Flowers said during a news conference. 'One shot is fired. That shot is the shot that ultimately killed the 17-year-old in this case.' Video released by the Indian River County Sheriff's Office shows the confrontation moments before the shooting. Flowers said social media has played a role in drawing large groups of teens to locations like Garcia's Boat Ramp and warned that the presence of firearms is increasing the risks associated with those gatherings. 'We got kids out here losing their lives chasing likes and shares on social media,' Flowers said. 'Now we're adding guns into the mix, and we're adding social media into the mix, and so what we're seeing is an escalation of each one of these.' Authorities said both the shooter and the driver of the truck have cooperated with investigators, turning over the firearm and the vehicle involved in the incident. As of Monday, no arrests had been made. 'It's gonna be up to the state on whether charges are ultimately filed, but I can tell you, self-defense plays a part in these,' Flowers said. The investigation remains active. The sheriff is asking anyone with video footage or information about the shooting, as well as future teen meetup events, to contact investigators. Flowers also urged parents to know where their children are and suggested location-tracking tools as one way to help keep them safe.

He’s going to punch the people that are inside of that truck. That shot is the shot that ultimately killed (the) 17-year-old in this case,” Flowers said. No arrests have been made. They turned over the truck. They’ve been talking to our detectives all weekend. They’re still here talking to us now,” Flowers said. “So, it’s going to be up to the state on whether charges are ultimately filed. But I can tell you, self-defense plays a part in these.” Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Flowers said large gatherings involving teenagers have been a growing concern for law enforcement and often begin through social media platforms such as Snapchat. “This has been going on for a long time, but now we’re adding guns into the mix and we’re adding social media into the mix,” Flowers said. “And so what we’re seeing is an escalation of each one of these.” As of Monday, Bah had been identified publicly by his family.
