entry.article_text: No arrests have been made in the shooting death of a 17-year-old at a teen meetup near Garcia's Boat Ramp in Indian River County, with a self-defense claim expected in the case, Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers announced Monday. WATCH BELOW: Sheriff Eric Flowers give update on shooting death of teen "We got kids out here losing their lives chasing likes and shares on social media," Flowers said. The shooting occurred late Friday night when approximately 100 teens, ranging in age from 14 to 19, gathered at Garcia's Boat Ramp in the 3700 block of County Road 512, the sheriff said. Deputies had broken up a similar group earlier that evening before the crowd moved to the boat ramp. "The 17-year-old, and a group of his friends, are approaching a truck, and there are two people, both 18 years old, inside of that truck. The 17-year-old opens the door, and he starts to punch," Flowers said. "He's going to punch on the people that are inside of that truck. That shot is the shot that ultimately killed 17-year-old in this case." The teen's friends drove him away from the scene, east on County Road 512, while calling 911 and a dispatcher told them to stop at Fellsmere City Hall, where emergency crews performed CPR, the sheriff said. He was taken to Sebastian River Medical Center and later flown to Holmes Regional Medical Center in Melbourne, where he died from his injuries. The two individuals in the truck were identified using the sheriff's office's Flock technology, the sheriff said. Flowers said both have been cooperative with investigators, surrendering the weapon used in the shooting and the truck. Additional individuals involved in the incident have also been identified through Flock, though some remain unidentified. Investigators also recovered other weapons from the vehicle in which the 17-year-old was transported from the scene. WATCH: 17-year-old dies after shooting near Garcia's Boat Ramp Flowers said a warrant will be submitted in the case, but it will be up to the state to determine whether charges are filed. "There have been no arrests on this case at this time, because the preliminary investigation shows that the 17-year-old was opening the door to attempt to fight with the two that were inside of the vehicle. They had a history of fighting," Flowers said. "Self defense plays a part in these, and when these kids go out and videotape these fights, and now guns are involved, there's going to be more of this." Names of those involved are not being released as the investigation continues, the sheriff said. Investigators believe at least four fights occurred at the boat ramp on the night of the shooting. Multiple shell casings and rounds were recovered from the scene. During Monday's news conference, Flowers released video of the shooting, noting the footage had already circulated widely on social media and that the victim's mother had seen it. One of the 18-year-olds involved in the shooting attends Vero Beach High School. The sheriff said teen meetups like the one at Garcia's Boat Ramp are coordinated through Snapchat, making them difficult for law enforcement to track in advance. "When it's Snapchat, it's basically a private conversation," Flowers said. "But it quickly can escalate to over 100, 150, 200 people there." Flowers said the meetups, which have included alcohol, fighting, and firearms, have been taking place for years across Indian River County, Okeechobee, and surrounding areas, but that social media has intensified the danger. "Now we're adding guns and alcohol into the mix, and we're adding social media into the mix, and so what we're seeing is an escalation of each one of these," Flowers said. There's guns, and those two just don't mix. And now add in the fuel of the fire of social media, and now we have a 17-year-old dead." Region Indian River County The sheriff said teens at these gatherings are motivated in part by a desire for online attention. "The kids like to fight, and they like to videotape it, and they like to get their likes and shares because of that," Flowers said. Parents, you see these videos. You do not want your teens out at these meetups." With Vero Beach High School's homecoming game scheduled for Friday and the dance on Saturday, Flowers said additional deputies will be on duty. Meanwhile, the sheriff urged parents to monitor their children's whereabouts and report any information about planned meetups to the sheriff's office. "Parents, if your kids are telling you that they're headed out to one of these meetups, ask them where they're going. Ask, find out the details. Share that with us," Flowers said. He recommended parents use location-sharing apps such as Life360 to track their children and said a child appearing to be in a remote or unusual location can be an indicator that a meetup is taking place. The investigation remains active. Flowers said anyone who witnessed any of the events that night, including the shooting itself, and has not yet spoken to investigators is urged to come forward. "I can tell you, our investigation is not even remotely over, and if we are able to identify people that were involved in this, from underage drinking to fighting, hurting other people," Flowers said. " If they did something wrong, they're going to have to be accountable for that." Anyone with information is asked to call the Indian River County Sheriff's Office at 772-569-6700 or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 1-800-273-TIPS.

entry.title: DeSantis opens new I-95 interchange in Indian River County, a year early - WPEC
entry.summary: DeSantis opens new I-95 interchange in Indian River County, a year early    WPEC
entry.article_text: Ron DeSantis opened the new I-95 interchange at Oslo Road in Indian River County on Monday, calling it a critical connection for drivers, emergency crews and the region’s growing population. The roughly $100 million project opened one year ahead of schedule , according to the governor’s office and the Florida Department of Transportation. This is the first new interchange built in this area in almost 50 years, DeSantis said. It’s going to bring [a] new critical connection [to] I-95 for a part of the state that has changed quite a bit. The new exit is expected to ease congestion at nearby Indrio Road and State Road 60 interchanges, DeSantis said. Drivers traveling from Oslo Road to I-95 can expect their travel times to be cut in half, he added. With the number of daily vehicles on the corridor still expected to grow between now and 2045 significantly, the Oslo Road interchange sets a clear example of how Florida delivers infrastructure that improves quality of life today while building more capacity for the future, DeSantis said. The governor also said the direct interstate connection will help emergency crews respond faster in southern Indian River County. See also: Two killed, including 10th-grade girl, after rollover school bus crash in Polk County We anticipate that just for the local community on a normal basis, for local, like non-hurricane-type emergencies, that the emergency response time will be reduced by up to 56%, DeSantis said. That will ultimately save some lives, of course, because time is of the essence in some of these situations. FDOT Secretary Jared Perdue said the project was completed 400 days early through what the agency calls voluntary acceleration, which lets contractors propose ways to speed construction and share in the savings. This is going to reduce the time it takes for first responders to get to incidents substantially, Perdue said. We’re really excited about that, to include cutting commute time in half and so many other benefits. DeSantis said FDOT also acquired land near the interchange for a dedicated gopher tortoise habitat. He said the site will be the only relocation area of its kind in Southeast Florida. Florida [is] showing that it’s possible to do the projects that we need done while also buttressing environmental stewardship, DeSantis said. Perdue said nearly $1 billion in transportation investment is planned for the Treasure Coast region.

entry.title: I-TEAM: A widow maps brain cancer cases in St. Lucie County - some just doors apart - WPEC
entry.summary: I-TEAM: A widow maps brain cancer cases in St. Lucie County - some just doors apart    WPEC
entry.article_text: Matt Elliott wants to know whether his brain cancer could be connected to other diagnoses on the Treasure Coast. He also knows he may not live long enough to get an answer. It might take them years to even figure out what the hell’s going on around here, Elliott said. I can’t expect myself to be around at the end of it. Lucie County have raised similar questions for years, pointing to diagnoses just houses apart and, in some cases, among unrelated residents of the same home decades apart. In June, I-Team reporter Katie Bente revisited families’ search for answers. In this second part of her investigation, Bente went street by street with a widow tracking the diagnoses and pressing health officials for updated findings. A few houses apart For Stephanie Ankiel , one stop on the drive through Fort Pierce brings the questions back to her own family. She pointed to her late husband’s childhood home, then another home a few houses away where she said a resident was diagnosed in 2025 with the same type of brain tumor. This is the house my late husband grew up in, Ankiel said. He was diagnosed with the same exact thing as that gentleman in 2025. Both men were initially diagnosed with oligodendroglioma, a different type of brain tumor from glioblastoma . Ankiel said her husband Mark Cunningham’s cancer later progressed to glioblastoma. A few streets away, she identified another home where she said two unrelated residents developed glioblastoma decades apart. This is the house where we’ve had two glioblastoma cases, 20 years apart, no family relation, she said. Elsewhere along the route, Ankiel pointed to neighboring homes where she said a woman and an 18-year-old had been diagnosed with brain cancer. The I-Team is withholding exact addresses to protect families’ privacy. PART 1: Brain cancer diagnoses leave St. Lucie County families searching for answers, again Ankiel helps patients through the Brain Cancer Foundation of the Treasure Coast , including a child who is just 3. She has spent years mapping where patients lived and looking for possible connections. Three additional brain cancer cases were confirmed in August alone in the areas families are tracking. Those diagnoses and the proximity of patients’ homes do not establish a cancer cluster or a common cause. But Ankiel wants officials to examine the range of brain cancers represented on her map, beyond glioblastoma alone. Regardless if it’s Glio at this point, we have too much brain cancer in this area. CDC guidance allows consideration of different cancer types when evidence suggests shared causes or exposures. No such connection has been established among the cases families are tracking. What the state studied and what is new The Florida Department of Health’s 2019 review examined glioblastoma diagnoses from 1998 through 2017 in ZIP codes 34952, 34982 and 34983. It found no statistically significant increase and did not designate a cancer cluster. That review did not include later diagnoses and focused on glioblastoma rather than the range of brain tumors represented on Ankiel’s map. Her husband’s initial diagnosis is one reason she wants officials to examine that broader picture. The I-Team asked whether the department had analyzed cases diagnosed since 2017 and what would trigger new environmental testing. Lucie County Health Officer Clint Sperber said officials have been reviewing cancer registry data and environmental influences. Our latest analysis, which includes data through 2023, shows no indication of higher rates in St. Lucie County or in the specific zip codes people have asked about, Sperber wrote. Lucie’s rates are in line with nearby counties and with the state as a whole. The updated report was not available when he responded. Sperber said officials were finishing a summary to release online. His response did not explain how the analysis handled tumors initially classified as another type and later diagnosed as glioblastoma, or whether other brain cancers were examined separately. It also did not specify what would trigger additional environmental testing. No environmental factor questioned by families has been established as a cause of these cancers. A call for another look Rep. Brian Mast said he has again asked the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to examine the concerns and provide the data behind its conclusions. You need to give us the receipts, Mast said. Give us the data of where these took place, how many of them took place. The CDC said state and local health departments lead examinations of unusual cancer patterns. It confirmed that it assisted Florida’s investigation in 2018, but did not specifically address whether it had received Mast’s latest request or would open a new review. In a statement to the I-Team, a CDC spokesperson said: CDC is prepared to provide additional assistance upon the Florida Department of Health’s request. Making the most of the time left Elliott was diagnosed this year with glioblastoma, an aggressive, fast-growing grade 4 brain cancer. The former bar manager described struggling to speak after surgery and initially believing his diagnosis was an isolated case. Meeting other local patients changed that. I thought I was the only one, he said. He has decided not to continue treatment, choosing to spend his remaining time with friends and family, going to the beach and swimming. While he wants investigators to find answers, he is focused on the life he still has. I’m not going to be that person that lives to be 65, 70, 80 years old, Elliott said. But I get to hang out with my friends. I get to go take a swim, have some fun.

entry.title: I-Team investigates Florida rules for seatbelts on school buses after fatal crash in Winter Haven
entry.summary: A deadly school bus crash in Polk County is raising new questions about how students are protected inside Florida school buses and why state law still falls short of federal safety recommendations. One student, a 10th grader on her way to Winter Haven High School, was killed Monday morning when a school bus carrying 39 people was involved in a crash. The circumstances surrounding the crash remain under investigation, including what happened outside the bus and what took place inside it. Watch report from Katie Lagrone School bus seatbelts 'We have one fatality of a beautiful high school girl. It's just heartbreaking,' Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd said during a morning news briefing. Investigators have not released details about how many students were wearing seat belts, what type of restraints were in use, or whether the belts played a role in the outcome of the crash. Florida requires seat belts, but not the type federal investigators recommend Florida law requires school buses built since 2001 to be equipped with seat belts. However, students are not required to wear them, and state law does not require the more protective lap-and-shoulder belts recommended by federal safety investigators. Instead, many Florida school buses continue to use standard lap belts. The federal recommendation followed an investigation by investigative reporter Katie LaGrone more than a decade ago. In 2012, a St. Lucie County school bus collided with a semi-truck, killing 9-year-old Aaron Beauchamp. Aaron was wearing the bus's standard lap belt at the time of the crash. Several years later, investigators with the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) examined that crash and studied how different types of seat belts affect student safety. The agency's testing showed significant differences between standard lap belts and lap-and-shoulder restraints. Simulations demonstrated that lap-and-shoulder belts provide greater protection by better controlling a passenger's movement during a crash. As a result, the NTSB recommended that all school buses nationwide be equipped with lap-and-shoulder belts. Federal recommendation to Florida went unanswered The NTSB specifically urged Florida to change state law to require lap-and-shoulder belts on new large school buses. entry.title: 'All we want is answers': Okeechobee parents demand action on bullying after 14-year-old jumps from school bus
entry.summary: Parents, students and grandparents gathered outside the Okeechobee County School Board on Monday, demanding greater accountability over bullying concerns after a 14-year-old student said relentless harassment pushed her to a breaking point. Signs lined the street as protesters chanted 'no more bullying' and 'hold bullies accountable,' rallying around 14-year-old Estrella Ventura Meras, a student at Okeechobee Achievement Academy. WATCH BELOW: Parents demand action after girl jumps from school bus Parents demand action on bullying after girl jumps from school bus Last week, WPTV reported on a video showing Estrella jumping from the window of a moving school bus. WPTV is not showing the video. Estrella told WPTV she jumped to escape students who had been bullying her since the start of the school year. She said she later went home and attempted to take her own life. 'I thank God he gave me another chance to live,' Estrella said, holding back tears. Her mother, Estela Meras, said she found her daughter pale and lying next to a pill bottle. She said Estrella had left behind a note saying she was tired. 'What if I hadn't found her there lying in bed?' Meras said as she became emotional. Now, Estrella and her mother are calling for change. 'I just hope there's justice and the students responsible,' said Estela Meras. 'Everybody was on the bus laughing about her instead of helping her. If it was me, I would have been helping somebody.' Estrella told WPTV she repeatedly reported the alleged bullying to teachers and administrators at Okeechobee Achievement Academy but said nothing changed. Her mother said she also previously raised concerns about bullying involving her daughter and now wants the district to reevaluate how it handles those reports. Other families at Monday's protest told WPTV they have also raised concerns about bullying at Okeechobee Achievement Academy and believe more needs to be done. 'Somebody has to take some accountability somewhere,' protester Maria Rodriguez said. District says Estrella's case remains under investigation Okeechobee County Schools said it shares parents' belief that 'bullying has no place in our schools' and that every student deserves to feel safe, supported and heard. The district said the allegations involving Estrella remain under investigation. If it was me, I would have been helping somebody."Estrella told WPTV she repeatedly reported the alleged bullying to teachers and administrators at Okeechobee Achievement Academy but said nothing changed. Her mother said she also previously raised concerns about bullying involving her daughter and now wants the district to reevaluate how it handles those reports.Other families at Monday's protest told WPTV they have also raised concerns about bullying at Okeechobee Achievement Academy and believe more needs to be done. "Somebody has to take some accountability somewhere," protester Maria Rodriguez said. Okeechobee County Schools said it shares parents' belief that "bullying has no place in our schools" and that every student deserves to feel safe, supported and heard.The district said the allegations involving Estrella remain under investigation. Citing federal student privacy law, district officials said they could not publicly discuss details of the investigation, education records or any potential student discipline.The district said schools are responsible for investigating bullying allegations reported by students and parents. If a family believes a school has failed to act on a complaint, district officials said the family should contact the district office so administrators can review both the allegations and the school's response."We take allegations that reports have gone unaddressed seriously," district spokesperson Dr. Joseph Stanley said in a statement to WPTV.Under School Board Policy 5.321, bullying reports can be made verbally, in writing or anonymously, and no specific reporting form is required. The policy calls for separate, confidential interviews and a review of evidence, with investigative procedural steps to be completed within a maximum of 10 school days, according to the district.The district said the policy also requires parents to be promptly notified when an investigation begins and requires a written report and recommendations for corrective action. It also includes provisions for counseling, intervention and follow-up measures intended to protect students.The district told WPTV that Okeechobee Achievement Academy has completed investigations into four other reports of alleged bullying during the current school year. Those cases involved four alleged victims and nine alleged perpetrators.None of the four complaints was substantiated as bullying, according to the district. Those cases are separate from the investigation involving Estrella, which remains open.However, the district stressed that an allegation being unsubstantiated as "bullying" does not necessarily mean no inappropriate behavior occurred. Florida law defines bullying as "systematically and chronically inflicting physical hurt or psychological distress" on one or more students. The district said a single incident generally does not meet that definition on its own, although one incident could reveal a broader pattern. Conduct that does not legally qualify as bullying could also constitute harassment or another violation requiring intervention or discipline.District officials said cooperation from students and parents is important during investigations because details about incidents, witnesses, previous reports and other evidence can help investigators determine what happened. The district said limited participation can restrict the information available to investigators but does not prevent officials from reviewing the evidence they can obtain.Despite calls from some parents for changes, Okeechobee County Schools said it believes its existing policies comply with Florida law and provide a thorough framework for responding to bullying allegations. The district said no procedural, staffing, disciplinary or policy changes are currently under consideration in response to the concerns raised by families.Instead, officials said their focus is on consistently implementing existing requirements, conducting thorough investigations and taking appropriate action based on the evidence.For Estrella's mother and the families who stood alongside her Monday, however, the protest was about making sure their concerns are heard before another child reaches a breaking point."All we want is answers for Estrella," Rodriguez said.

entry.title: Discover The Palm Beaches to host 2-day hospitality and tourism job fair in Lake Worth Beach & Greenacres
entry.summary: Residents looking for work in Palm Beach County's tourism and hospitality industry will have two opportunities this month to connect with employers ahead of the busy tourism season. Discover The Palm Beaches (DTPB), the county's destination marketing organization, announced it will host its 5th Annual Hospitality and Tourism Job Fair on Oct. 9 and Oct. 15, bringing together employers from across the region. WATCH: 2-day hospitality, tourism job fair taking place this month 2-day hospitality, tourism job fair taking place this month in Palm Beach County The free event is open to everyone and will feature full-time and part-time job opportunities in hotels, restaurants, attractions, entertainment venues, retail businesses and other tourism-related organizations. The first job fair will be held from 8:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. on Friday, Oct. 9, at Palm Beach State College's Lake Worth campus Public Safety Building, located at 4200 S. Congress Ave. The second event is scheduled for 8:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. on Thursday, Oct. 15, at the City of Greenacres Community Center, 501 Swain Blvd. According to DTPB, Palm Beach County's tourism industry supports nearly 95,000 local jobs and continues to be one of the area's largest economic drivers. 'A strong tourism industry depends on a strong workforce,' said Heather Andrews, senior vice president of commercial strategy and destination stewardship for DTPB. 'This job fair brings together leading employers and talented local residents, creating connections that strengthen careers, support businesses and contribute to the continued success of The Palm Beaches.' Available positions include front desk, food and beverage, operations, sales, marketing and management roles. Many employers are offering competitive benefits, paid time off and opportunities for advancement, organizers said. The job fair comes amid continued growth in Palm Beach County's tourism sector. DTPB said The Palm Beaches welcomed a record 6.09 million visitors during the first half of 2026, a 6.4% increase compared to the same period last year. Spanish and Creole translators will be available at both events to help job seekers connect with prospective employers. Applicants can pre-register for the event on the Palm Beach's website and are encouraged to dress professionally and bring their resume. entry.article_text: A 17-year-old died after being shot near a boat ramp in Indian River County late Friday night, according to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office. Deputies responded to reports of a juvenile shot in the 3700 block of County Road 512, near Garcia's Boat Ramp, at approximately 11:24 p.m. WATCH: 17-year-old dies after shooting near Garcia's Boat Ramp The sheriff's office said deputies found the 17-year-old and began lifesaving measures until Indian River County Fire Rescue arrived. entry.title: Indian River County sheriff investigates whether fatal shooting of teen at boat ramp was self-defense - WFLX
entry.summary: Indian River County sheriff investigates whether fatal shooting of teen at boat ramp was self-defense    WFLX
entry.article_text: A 17-year-old was killed in a shooting Friday night at Garcia's Boat Ramp in Indian River County, and investigators are examining whether the shooting was an act of self-defense , according to Sheriff Eric Flowers. WATCH: WPTV'S Coverage of Teen killed in Garcia's Boat Ramp shooting The shooting happened during a confrontation at the popular waterfront gathering spot, which authorities say has become a frequent meetup location for teenagers. According to Flowers, investigators reviewed video that showed the 17-year-old opening the door of a truck and throwing punches at people inside before a shot was fired. "The 17-year-old opens the door, and he starts to punch. He's going to punch the people that are inside of that truck," Flowers said during a news conference. That shot is the shot that ultimately killed the 17-year-old in this case." Video released by the Indian River County Sheriff's Office shows the confrontation moments before the shooting. Flowers said social media has played a role in drawing large groups of teens to locations like Garcia's Boat Ramp and warned that the presence of firearms is increasing the risks associated with those gatherings. "We got kids out here losing their lives chasing likes and shares on social media," Flowers said. "Now we're adding guns into the mix, and we're adding social media into the mix, and so what we're seeing is an escalation of each one of these." Authorities said both the shooter and the driver of the truck have cooperated with investigators, turning over the firearm and the vehicle involved in the incident. As of Monday, no arrests had been made. "It's gonna be up to the state on whether charges are ultimately filed, but I can tell you, self-defense plays a part in these," Flowers said. The investigation remains active. The sheriff is asking anyone with video footage or information about the shooting, as well as future teen meetup events, to contact investigators. Flowers also urged parents to know where their children are and suggested location-tracking tools as one way to help keep them safe.

Flowers said investigators believe the meetup was part of a growing trend of teens gathering at remote locations arranged through Snapchat , where fights are recorded and shared online. "We got kids out here losing their lives chasing likes and shares on social media," he said. "We've got kids out here losing their lives trying to go viral on social media." He said there may have been as many as four fights at the boat ramp that night, and investigators are still working to identify people who were there. "They had a history of fighting," Flowers said. "This has been an ongoing thing." The sheriff urged parents to ask their children whether they attended the meetup and encouraged anyone who witnessed the shooting or recorded it to contact investigators. "It's not safe," Flowers said. There's guns, and those two just don't mix. And now add in the fuel of the fire of social media, and now we have a 17-year-old dead." In a statement, the Indian River School District gave its condolences to the teen's family: The School District of Indian River County is heartbroken by this young person’s death. Our hearts are with his family, friends, and the students and staff who knew and cared about him. Grief support was in place over the weekend, including counselors at Sebastian River High School’s Homecoming Dance, and continues today as students and staff return to school. Our teams will remain available in the days ahead, offering care and responding to the needs of those affected. A spokesperson for SDIRC said the student had recently withdrawn from Sebastian River High School to be home schooled.

entry.title: Mother of teen killed during party at Indian River County boat ramp disputes shooter's claim of self-defense - WPBF
entry.summary: Mother of teen killed during party at Indian River County boat ramp disputes shooter's claim of self-defense    WPBF
entry.article_text: The mother of a 17-year-old boy shot and killed during a party Friday night at a boat ramp in Indian River County said she believes her son was protecting others when he was killed. She has identified her son as Sulliman Bah. Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers held a news conference about the shooting Monday afternoon. He said there were about 1,000 teenagers gathered at Garcia's Boat Ramp, just south of Fellsmere. Flowers showed two videos of the shooting from different angles. The videos start with Bah approaching a white pickup truck. "Seventeen-year-old opens the door, and he starts to punch. He's going to punch on the people that are inside of that truck. One shot is fired," Flowers said. The sheriff said the shot was fired by the passenger in the truck, killing Bah. Flowers stated that Bah had a history with the two 18-year-olds in the truck, noting that they had fought before. The 18-year-olds told investigators they had the gun to protect themselves. "At this time, it looks as though there will be a self-defense claim," Flowers said. Bah’s mother, however, disputes the self-defense claim. In a text message to WPBF 25 News reporter Ari Hait, she said, "Sulliman was a defender of his friends. Always protecting the underdog, and I believe he was trying to save the crowd from that gun that he knew was about to be used...He was there to protect his friends from the thugs that had previously threatened him and many others multiple times." She added that she does not see her son throwing a punch in the video. "If anything, I believe he was attempting to push the gun away," she said. The sheriff has not released the identities of the two 18-year-olds in the truck but said they are cooperating with investigators. No arrests have been made so far. "It's going to be up to the state on whether charges ultimately will be filed. But I can tell you self-defense plays a part in these," Flowers said. The sheriff emphasized that the investigation is ongoing and urged anyone who attended the party to contact his office. entry.article_text: Indiantown residents remain concerned about flooding after heavy rain left streets covered in water last week, with more rain and storms in the forecast for this week. CBS12 crews captured video of vehicles driving through standing water on roadways in parts of the village. Residents say flooding can quickly become expensive when water affects homes and property. The sad part is, if you don’t have insurance or anything like that you’re just stuck, your stuck with the bill, said Mary Brown, a Booker Park resident. The flooding has renewed questions about the more than $2 million drainage and roadway project in Booker Park. The project began in 2022 to help reduce flooding, but residents say heavy rain is still leaving some streets underwater. Village leaders have said they are working with Martin County on longer-term drainage solutions, including the possible repair or replacement of broken pipes. The next Indiantown Village Council meeting is Thursday night. With more rain possible this week, Martin County Fire Rescue and the Florida Department of Health in Martin County have tips available online for residents to plan ahead and avoid driving or walking through floodwater. You can CLICK HERE to view the entire list. Officials say water on a roadway may be deeper or more contaminated than it appears. Drivers who encounter a flooded road should turn around rather than attempt to drive through it. Martin County Fire Rescue responds to flooding-related emergencies, including when a vehicle becomes stuck in floodwater. Residents should call 911 during an emergency. For ongoing drainage problems or flooded roadways, residents can submit a report through Martin County’s online Request for Service system . The county asks residents to include the specific address or location and details about the issue, such as standing water, a blockage or a low spot near a drainage structure. CLICK HERE to submit a request. Health officials also advise residents whose wells flood to use bottled or boiled water until the well can be tested.

entry.article_text: Video above: News and weather for Monday, October 5, 2026 A Port St. Lucie resident accused of theft at a Palm Beach County apartment complex more than two years ago entered a plea agreement. According to court documents in Palm Beach County, Ashley R. Clayton, 38, pleaded guilty on Monday, Oct. 5, to money laundering, organized scheme to defraud and making false entry in book of business entity. Clayton agreed to the plea agreement on Sept. Clayton was sentenced to five years of probation for each charge, but will serve the penalties at the same time, credited with 12 days of time served in Palm Beach County jail, ordered to pay court costs and complete community service. As part of the plea agreement, Clayton and the victim will determine the amount of restitution Clayton owes to the property management company of the apartment complex. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Clayton is banned from performing any financial transaction for any business or person and was ordered to complete mental health and substance abuse evaluations. According to a Riviera Beach Police Department report, Clayton was an employee at Berkeley Landing Apartments located at 3100 Broadway for three months. On June 13, 2024, a regional manager for the apartment complex told police that Clayton was the community manager who oversaw payments for rent, deposits, application fees, background checks, credit checks and compliance application process for the apartment complex. It was determined that Clayton was collecting money by having residents use Zelle, which allows users to electronically transfer money. The residents’ money went to Clayton’s banking account. Some residents even gave Clayton blank money orders. The police report said Clayton sent residents a letter on apartment complex letterhead stating, “They are currently working on making sure all payment ledgers are up-to-date. We are asking that rent payments be made in the form of money orders until further notice.” The apartment complex did not give Clayton permission to send the letter. Clayton was fired but returned to the property and returned 20 money orders totaling $14,798.22 to the apartment complex management. entry.title: I-TEAM: A widow maps brain cancer cases in St. Lucie County - some just doors apart - WPEC
entry.summary: I-TEAM: A widow maps brain cancer cases in St. Lucie County - some just doors apart    WPEC
entry.article_text: Matt Elliott wants to know whether his brain cancer could be connected to other diagnoses on the Treasure Coast. He also knows he may not live long enough to get an answer. It might take them years to even figure out what the hell’s going on around here, Elliott said. I can’t expect myself to be around at the end of it. Lucie County have raised similar questions for years, pointing to diagnoses just houses apart and, in some cases, among unrelated residents of the same home decades apart. In June, I-Team reporter Katie Bente revisited families’ search for answers. In this second part of her investigation, Bente went street by street with a widow tracking the diagnoses and pressing health officials for updated findings. A few houses apart For Stephanie Ankiel , one stop on the drive through Fort Pierce brings the questions back to her own family. She pointed to her late husband’s childhood home, then another home a few houses away where she said a resident was diagnosed in 2025 with the same type of brain tumor. This is the house my late husband grew up in, Ankiel said. He was diagnosed with the same exact thing as that gentleman in 2025. Both men were initially diagnosed with oligodendroglioma, a different type of brain tumor from glioblastoma . Ankiel said her husband Mark Cunningham’s cancer later progressed to glioblastoma. A few streets away, she identified another home where she said two unrelated residents developed glioblastoma decades apart. This is the house where we’ve had two glioblastoma cases, 20 years apart, no family relation, she said. Elsewhere along the route, Ankiel pointed to neighboring homes where she said a woman and an 18-year-old had been diagnosed with brain cancer. The I-Team is withholding exact addresses to protect families’ privacy. PART 1: Brain cancer diagnoses leave St. Lucie County families searching for answers, again Ankiel helps patients through the Brain Cancer Foundation of the Treasure Coast , including a child who is just 3. She has spent years mapping where patients lived and looking for possible connections. Three additional brain cancer cases were confirmed in August alone in the areas families are tracking. Those diagnoses and the proximity of patients’ homes do not establish a cancer cluster or a common cause. But Ankiel wants officials to examine the range of brain cancers represented on her map, beyond glioblastoma alone. Regardless if it’s Glio at this point, we have too much brain cancer in this area. CDC guidance allows consideration of different cancer types when evidence suggests shared causes or exposures. No such connection has been established among the cases families are tracking. What the state studied and what is new The Florida Department of Health’s 2019 review examined glioblastoma diagnoses from 1998 through 2017 in ZIP codes 34952, 34982 and 34983. It found no statistically significant increase and did not designate a cancer cluster. That review did not include later diagnoses and focused on glioblastoma rather than the range of brain tumors represented on Ankiel’s map. Her husband’s initial diagnosis is one reason she wants officials to examine that broader picture. The I-Team asked whether the department had analyzed cases diagnosed since 2017 and what would trigger new environmental testing. Lucie County Health Officer Clint Sperber said officials have been reviewing cancer registry data and environmental influences. Our latest analysis, which includes data through 2023, shows no indication of higher rates in St. Lucie County or in the specific zip codes people have asked about, Sperber wrote. Lucie’s rates are in line with nearby counties and with the state as a whole. The updated report was not available when he responded. Sperber said officials were finishing a summary to release online. His response did not explain how the analysis handled tumors initially classified as another type and later diagnosed as glioblastoma, or whether other brain cancers were examined separately. It also did not specify what would trigger additional environmental testing. No environmental factor questioned by families has been established as a cause of these cancers. A call for another look Rep. Brian Mast said he has again asked the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to examine the concerns and provide the data behind its conclusions. You need to give us the receipts, Mast said. Give us the data of where these took place, how many of them took place. The CDC said state and local health departments lead examinations of unusual cancer patterns. It confirmed that it assisted Florida’s investigation in 2018, but did not specifically address whether it had received Mast’s latest request or would open a new review. In a statement to the I-Team, a CDC spokesperson said: CDC is prepared to provide additional assistance upon the Florida Department of Health’s request. Making the most of the time left Elliott was diagnosed this year with glioblastoma, an aggressive, fast-growing grade 4 brain cancer. The former bar manager described struggling to speak after surgery and initially believing his diagnosis was an isolated case. Meeting other local patients changed that. I thought I was the only one, he said. He has decided not to continue treatment, choosing to spend his remaining time with friends and family, going to the beach and swimming. While he wants investigators to find answers, he is focused on the life he still has. I’m not going to be that person that lives to be 65, 70, 80 years old, Elliott said. But I get to hang out with my friends. I get to go take a swim, have some fun.

entry.title: DeSantis opens new I-95 interchange in Indian River County, a year early - WPEC
entry.summary: DeSantis opens new I-95 interchange in Indian River County, a year early    WPEC
entry.article_text: Ron DeSantis opened the new I-95 interchange at Oslo Road in Indian River County on Monday, calling it a critical connection for drivers, emergency crews and the region’s growing population. The roughly $100 million project opened one year ahead of schedule , according to the governor’s office and the Florida Department of Transportation. This is the first new interchange built in this area in almost 50 years, DeSantis said. It’s going to bring [a] new critical connection [to] I-95 for a part of the state that has changed quite a bit. The new exit is expected to ease congestion at nearby Indrio Road and State Road 60 interchanges, DeSantis said. Drivers traveling from Oslo Road to I-95 can expect their travel times to be cut in half, he added. With the number of daily vehicles on the corridor still expected to grow between now and 2045 significantly, the Oslo Road interchange sets a clear example of how Florida delivers infrastructure that improves quality of life today while building more capacity for the future, DeSantis said. The governor also said the direct interstate connection will help emergency crews respond faster in southern Indian River County. See also: Two killed, including 10th-grade girl, after rollover school bus crash in Polk County We anticipate that just for the local community on a normal basis, for local, like non-hurricane-type emergencies, that the emergency response time will be reduced by up to 56%, DeSantis said. That will ultimately save some lives, of course, because time is of the essence in some of these situations. FDOT Secretary Jared Perdue said the project was completed 400 days early through what the agency calls voluntary acceleration, which lets contractors propose ways to speed construction and share in the savings. This is going to reduce the time it takes for first responders to get to incidents substantially, Perdue said. We’re really excited about that, to include cutting commute time in half and so many other benefits. DeSantis said FDOT also acquired land near the interchange for a dedicated gopher tortoise habitat. He said the site will be the only relocation area of its kind in Southeast Florida. Florida [is] showing that it’s possible to do the projects that we need done while also buttressing environmental stewardship, DeSantis said. Perdue said nearly $1 billion in transportation investment is planned for the Treasure Coast region. Indian River County Commissioner Joseph Flescher recounted his reaction when he first heard about the opening. "When I got the phone call, I said, ' We're not near completion. I had been here just two weeks ago. We were nowhere near where we're at.' This team worked an incredible operation, said Flescher. Flescher also highlighted how important this new entrance ot I-95 is to the growing population across the county. This interchange is very much needed in the development of our county. And I don't mean the future development. I mean the current development, Flescher said.

entry.title: SLC seniors demand answers as Fort Pierce center prepares to close
entry.summary: A Fort Pierce senior center is expected to close, leaving some of the older adults who rely on it worried about losing a gathering place in their own community. The Council on Aging of St. Lucie confirmed the senior center at 1505 Orange Avenue in Fort Pierce is expected to close in the near future. The property is currently listed for sale for $2.2 million. The news came as a surprise to some seniors who use the center regularly, including 77-year-old Sandy Pietrewicz. She has relied on the center for nearly a decade. That's the community center that I go to for lunch and friendship and social activities with other elderly women, said Pietrewicz. After hearing the center could be closing, Pietrewicz said she and other seniors were left with questions about what would happen to the services they depend on. We were all talking about who we could contact, and I thought of WPTV immediately, she said. WPTV reporter Brooke Chau went to the center to get answers and hear directly from the seniors who use it. The Council on Aging said the closure will not mean an end to the services provided to seniors. You're going to get the same treatment. You're going to get the same love. You're going to get the same meals, said Trekina Smith with the Council on Aging. Once the property sells, seniors who currently use the Orange Avenue location are expected to transition to the Council on Aging's facility on Bayshore Boulevard in Port St. Lucie. The organization said transportation will be provided to help seniors get to the new location. But some seniors say the location itself is important. That makes us even angrier. We can't have something in our own community, Pietrewicz said. Geneira Lovett, who also uses the center, told WPTV that seniors in Fort Pierce want to be able to access services close to where they live. We live here, we want rights to do thing, besides trouble, Lovett said. The Council on Aging said it understands those concerns, but says change is necessary. For now, the Council on Aging says services at the Orange Avenue center are continuing. There is no finalized timeline for the closure because the transition is tied to the sale of the property. We understand the concerns, it's a change for us too. But hey, change comes, and you got to go with the change, Smith said. The organization said seniors will continue to have access to meals, activities, social opportunities and transportation once services move to the Port St. Lucie location.

entry.title: Newly renovated control room at Amerant Bank Arena brings Panthers games to life
entry.summary: It takes an army of 38 staff members to create all the video, replays, and entertainment fans enjoy at Florida Panthers games at Amerant Bank Arena. WPTV Florida Panthers Anchor and Panthers 360 Mike Trim went one-on-one with Mike Masino, vice president of entertainment and operations, who gave Trim a tour of the newly renovated control room and front-of-house operations. WATCH: Newly renovated control room at Amerant Bank Arena brings Panthers games to life New Amerant Bank Arena control room The front-of-house operations area serves as the hub of game-day activity. It houses the public address announcer, primary producer, music operations, a spotter, and a gold horn operator. Lighting operations and building lights are also managed from the same space, along with social media stations used for interactive fan games. 'Yeah, so this is our front-of-house operations area. This is where we have our public address announcer. We have our primary producer, music operations, our spotter, and our gold horn operator. We've got our lighting operations team as well as building lights. And then up here we have some of our fun stuff. We've got social media stations for some of our interactive games,' Mike Masino said. What is now one open workspace was once 3 separate rooms. 'This was actually 3 rooms,' Masino said. 'Flow communication becomes a lot easier. Direct line of sight is also helpful, and it actually created some more space for the operators,' Masino said. The tour also included the broadcast control room the engine room of the entire production. 'Now we've got the actual broadcast control room; this is where the real magic happens,' Masino said. Inside, Mark serves as the technical director, and Scott is the director. Masino compared the director's role to one familiar to those in television news. This is the house where we’ve had two glioblastoma cases, 20 years apart, no family relation, she said. Elsewhere along the route, Ankiel pointed to neighboring homes where she said a woman and an 18-year-old had been diagnosed with brain cancer. The I-Team is withholding exact addresses to protect families’ privacy. PART 1: Brain cancer diagnoses leave St. Lucie County families searching for answers, again Ankiel helps patients through the Brain Cancer Foundation of the Treasure Coast , including a child who is just 3. She has spent years mapping where patients lived and looking for possible connections. Three additional brain cancer cases were confirmed in August alone in the areas families are tracking. Those diagnoses and the proximity of patients’ homes do not establish a cancer cluster or a common cause. But Ankiel wants officials to examine the range of brain cancers represented on her map, beyond glioblastoma alone. Regardless if it’s Glio at this point, we have too much brain cancer in this area. CDC guidance allows consideration of different cancer types when evidence suggests shared causes or exposures. No such connection has been established among the cases families are tracking. What the state studied and what is new The Florida Department of Health’s 2019 review examined glioblastoma diagnoses from 1998 through 2017 in ZIP codes 34952, 34982 and 34983. It found no statistically significant increase and did not designate a cancer cluster. That review did not include later diagnoses and focused on glioblastoma rather than the range of brain tumors represented on Ankiel’s map. Her husband’s initial diagnosis is one reason she wants officials to examine that broader picture. The I-Team asked whether the department had analyzed cases diagnosed since 2017 and what would trigger new environmental testing. Lucie County Health Officer Clint Sperber said officials have been reviewing cancer registry data and environmental influences. Our latest analysis, which includes data through 2023, shows no indication of higher rates in St. Lucie County or in the specific zip codes people have asked about, Sperber wrote. Lucie’s rates are in line with nearby counties and with the state as a whole. The updated report was not available when he responded. Sperber said officials were finishing a summary to release online. His response did not explain how the analysis handled tumors initially classified as another type and later diagnosed as glioblastoma, or whether other brain cancers were examined separately. It also did not specify what would trigger additional environmental testing. No environmental factor questioned by families has been established as a cause of these cancers. A call for another look Rep. Brian Mast said he has again asked the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to examine the concerns and provide the data behind its conclusions. You need to give us the receipts, Mast said. Give us the data of where these took place, how many of them took place. The CDC said state and local health departments lead examinations of unusual cancer patterns. It confirmed that it assisted Florida’s investigation in 2018, but did not specifically address whether it had received Mast’s latest request or would open a new review. In a statement to the I-Team, a CDC spokesperson said: CDC is prepared to provide additional assistance upon the Florida Department of Health’s request. Making the most of the time left Elliott was diagnosed this year with glioblastoma, an aggressive, fast-growing grade 4 brain cancer. The former bar manager described struggling to speak after surgery and initially believing his diagnosis was an isolated case. Meeting other local patients changed that. I thought I was the only one, he said. He has decided not to continue treatment, choosing to spend his remaining time with friends and family, going to the beach and swimming. While he wants investigators to find answers, he is focused on the life he still has. I’m not going to be that person that lives to be 65, 70, 80 years old, Elliott said. But I get to hang out with my friends. I get to go take a swim, have some fun.

entry.summary: DeSantis opens new I-95 interchange in Indian River County, a year early    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Ron DeSantis opened the new I-95 interchange at Oslo Road in Indian River County on Monday, calling it a critical connection for drivers, emergency crews and the region’s growing population. The roughly $100 million project opened one year ahead of schedule , according to the governor’s office and the Florida Department of Transportation. This is the first new interchange built in this area in almost 50 years, DeSantis said. It’s going to bring [a] new critical connection [to] I-95 for a part of the state that has changed quite a bit. The new exit is expected to ease congestion at nearby Indrio Road and State Road 60 interchanges, DeSantis said. Drivers traveling from Oslo Road to I-95 can expect their travel times to be cut in half, he added. With the number of daily vehicles on the corridor still expected to grow between now and 2045 significantly, the Oslo Road interchange sets a clear example of how Florida delivers infrastructure that improves quality of life today while building more capacity for the future, DeSantis said. The governor also said the direct interstate connection will help emergency crews respond faster in southern Indian River County. See also: Two killed, including 10th-grade girl, after rollover school bus crash in Polk County We anticipate that just for the local community on a normal basis, for local, like non-hurricane-type emergencies, that the emergency response time will be reduced by up to 56%, DeSantis said. That will ultimately save some lives, of course, because time is of the essence in some of these situations. FDOT Secretary Jared Perdue said the project was completed 400 days early through what the agency calls voluntary acceleration, which lets contractors propose ways to speed construction and share in the savings. This is going to reduce the time it takes for first responders to get to incidents substantially, Perdue said. We’re really excited about that, to include cutting commute time in half and so many other benefits. DeSantis said FDOT also acquired land near the interchange for a dedicated gopher tortoise habitat. He said the site will be the only relocation area of its kind in Southeast Florida. Florida [is] showing that it’s possible to do the projects that we need done while also buttressing environmental stewardship, DeSantis said. Perdue said nearly $1 billion in transportation investment is planned for the Treasure Coast region. Indian River County Commissioner Joseph Flescher recounted his reaction when he first heard about the opening. "When I got the phone call, I said, ' We're not near completion. I had been here just two weeks ago. We were nowhere near where we're at.' This team worked an incredible operation, said Flescher. Flescher also highlighted how important this new entrance ot I-95 is to the growing population across the county. This interchange is very much needed in the development of our county. And I don't mean the future development. I mean the current development, Flescher said.

entry.article_text: WPTV is working to get answers to questions residents raised about a controversial Islamic center approved in Palm Beach County's Agricultural Reserve. After Friday's heated public meeting, many viewers reached out asking who is behind the project, how it was approved and what happens next.The proposed development would be located off Lyons Road and 152nd Place South in Delray Beach, on what is currently a dirt road and grassy field. The project includes a mosque, school and daycare.WATCH BELOW: Who's behind the Ag Reserve Islamic Center? Residents seek answersDuring Friday's meeting, several residents questioned who is involved with the project and where funding is coming from. One speaker told county leaders, "If credible documented evidence exists connecting specific individuals or organizations associated with this project to extremist organizations, residents deserve to know what authorities have investigated and determined. Who controls this organization? Who is financing this project? Where is the money coming from? And what security review has been conducted?"The project also drew protesters outside the meeting."Where are they from, who are they, were they vetted? Build it and they shall come," said a woman pushing back against the Islamic center, calling the developments part of a "Muslim takeover."Sachs pushed through the feedback from the crowd and said places of worship of all faiths go through a review process."Yes, an investigation was made into every house of worship, whether it is Christian, Jewish, Muslim, Hindu and we do have Hindu temples if anybody here is interested," Sachs said. there's an investigation made as to who owns it, who's going to run it, and whether or not they're going to abide by the rules of the county and the United States Constitution."Inside the meeting, a woman who identified herself as a Latina Muslim convert questioned the nature of the concerns being raised. Her comments drew a strong reaction from the crowd as some wanted to focus on traffic impacts and nearly caused the meeting to be shut down."I want to be safer again; will this development help my community to be safe? My mosque welcomes people of other faith to ask questions," she said.Questions about who is behind the project have remained a focal point for residents.The project consists of a 15-acre Islamic center featuring 5 acres for the mosque and 10 for the school and daycare along Lyons Road.County documents reviewed by WPTV appear to identify the applicant as the Islamic Center School of west Delray Beach. The organization also appears to own an additional 5 acres on the north side of 152nd Place South. Plans for that portion are uncertain.Seeking more context on the concerns raised at the meeting, WPTV spoke with former Rabbi David Steinhardt, who retired about 16 months ago after serving for more than 30 years as senior rabbi at B'nai Torah Congregation in Boca Raton. He also served as co-president of the Boca Raton Interfaith Clergy Association.When asked what his message would be to residents expressing concern about a mosque coming into the area and the impacts on the Jewish community, Steinhardt said, "No one's trying to take their place. The issue is how do we live together."He said fear often grows when people lack familiarity with one another."I think that when you don't know people, then you suspect people, and when you're suspicious, you fear people. And so when you fear people, then you don't necessarily act rationally. This is not a new group of people. These are people that have been in town for decades. We have worked together at the hospitals, in the courts, in business, in all different arenas of public uh public uh society. And in our community, we have shared in various efforts to bring peace to the world. And so, I know that community. I have been in conversation with that community and its leadership for decades."Steinhardt said he knows the president of the mosque approved for the site and said they are members of the Islamic Center of Boca Raton seeking a second mosque to provide better access for members."I don't know if it's a need, if it's a desire; that should be enough. Is there a need for the number of synagogues we have in our Community? I'm not sure, but there's a desire for more, and we all have the right to do that."WPTV also learned the project is represented by Brian Seymour with the Gunster law firm. A request for additional details has been sent, and WPTV is working to hear back.Another issue repeatedly raised Friday involved notification requirements. Several residents questioned why people living more than 500 feet from the site were not notified.The county's Planning and Zoning Division told WPTV that only property owners within 500 feet were notified because the project is located within the U/S, AGR and Glades tiers. Had the project been located within the Exurban and Rural tiers, a 1,000-foot notification radius would have applied.To see which growth tier a property falls under, open the Palm Beach County GIS Map Viewer. Once you're in the map, click the menu icon (the "pancake" in the upper corner), then use the "Search Layers" tool and type in "Managed Growth Tier System." That layer will show all of the county's designated growth tiers and allow you to see exactly where a property is located within the system.Palm Beach County Commissioner Maria Sachs is planning a second public meeting focused on projects in the Agricultural Reserve following feedback from Friday's meeting. Her staff told WPTV details are still being worked out.Sachs also told WPTV she is working with county staff to find an appropriate date to propose changes to the Unified Land Development Code regarding the Development Review Officer process for places of worship and governmental entities.The issue has become a focal point because several projects residents protested were approved through an administrative review process that has existed for years and allows certain government entities and houses of worship to move forward without direct approval from county commissioners."I think for the most part people had their voices heard, but what they said is they want to have a voice in what comes to development in this county. I respect that I hear them," Sachs said Friday.While the mosque was approved through the administrative process, the proposal for an Islamic school and daycare next door did require a vote by county commissioners.WPTV reviewed records from a 2023 county meeting and learned the project was approved by a 4-3 vote.Sachs, former Commissioner Michael Barnett and then-Commissioner Sara Baxter voted against the proposal, citing concerns that not enough input from residents had been collected.Vice Mayor Marci Woodward, Commissioner Maria Marino, Commissioner Gregg Weiss and former Commissioner Mack Bernard voted in favor of the project.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.summary: Mother of teen killed during party at Indian River County boat ramp disputes shooter's claim of self-defense    WPBF
entry.article_text: The mother of a 17-year-old boy shot and killed during a party Friday night at a boat ramp in Indian River County said she believes her son was protecting others when he was killed. She has identified her son as Sulliman Bah. Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers held a news conference about the shooting Monday afternoon. He said there were about 1,000 teenagers gathered at Garcia's Boat Ramp, just south of Fellsmere. Flowers showed two videos of the shooting from different angles. The videos start with Bah approaching a white pickup truck. "Seventeen-year-old opens the door, and he starts to punch. He's going to punch on the people that are inside of that truck. One shot is fired," Flowers said. The sheriff said the shot was fired by the passenger in the truck, killing Bah. Flowers stated that Bah had a history with the two 18-year-olds in the truck, noting that they had fought before. The 18-year-olds told investigators they had the gun to protect themselves. "At this time, it looks as though there will be a self-defense claim," Flowers said. Bah’s mother, however, disputes the self-defense claim. In a text message to WPBF 25 News reporter Ari Hait, she said, "Sulliman was a defender of his friends. Always protecting the underdog, and I believe he was trying to save the crowd from that gun that he knew was about to be used...He was there to protect his friends from the thugs that had previously threatened him and many others multiple times." She added that she does not see her son throwing a punch in the video. "If anything, I believe he was attempting to push the gun away," she said. The sheriff has not released the identities of the two 18-year-olds in the truck but said they are cooperating with investigators. No arrests have been made so far. "It's going to be up to the state on whether charges ultimately will be filed. But I can tell you self-defense plays a part in these," Flowers said. The sheriff emphasized that the investigation is ongoing and urged anyone who attended the party to contact his office. entry.summary: Five years later, Port St. Lucie police seek answers in 20-year-old woman’s killing    WPEC
entry.article_text: Five years after the shooting death of a 20-year-old woman, the Port St. Lucie Police Department is still seeking answers. Lucie police responded to reports of multiple gunshots near Southeast Green River Parkway and Southeast Charleston Drive. Police said Gabriella Gina Hanley was driving south on Southeast Green River Parkway in a black Kia Forte with her boyfriend, Darrick Mincey Jr., when another vehicle pulled alongside them and fired multiple rounds into their car. Officers and rescue personnel began life-saving measures after finding Hanley with multiple gunshot wounds. She was pronounced dead Oct. Mincey was also struck by gunfire but survived. See also: Teen identified after deadly Fellsmere shooting involving 100-plus teens Investigators found the Kia had 37 bullet impacts. Numerous 9mm cartridge casings were recovered, and forensic evidence indicated the bullets were fired from two separate rifles, police said. Five years later, detectives are continuing to conduct interviews and examine forensic and digital evidence. At the time of her death, Hanley left behind a 20-month-old baby. CBS12 reported in 2022 that investigators had identified three people of interest, but no charges were filed against them. entry.title: DeSantis opens new I-95 interchange in Indian River County, a year early - WPEC
entry.summary: DeSantis opens new I-95 interchange in Indian River County, a year early    WPEC
entry.article_text: Ron DeSantis opened the new I-95 interchange at Oslo Road in Indian River County on Monday, calling it a critical connection for drivers, emergency crews and the region’s growing population. The roughly $100 million project opened one year ahead of schedule , according to the governor’s office and the Florida Department of Transportation. This is the first new interchange built in this area in almost 50 years, DeSantis said. It’s going to bring [a] new critical connection [to] I-95 for a part of the state that has changed quite a bit. The new exit is expected to ease congestion at nearby Indrio Road and State Road 60 interchanges, DeSantis said. Drivers traveling from Oslo Road to I-95 can expect their travel times to be cut in half, he added. With the number of daily vehicles on the corridor still expected to grow between now and 2045 significantly, the Oslo Road interchange sets a clear example of how Florida delivers infrastructure that improves quality of life today while building more capacity for the future, DeSantis said. The governor also said the direct interstate connection will help emergency crews respond faster in southern Indian River County. See also: Two killed, including 10th-grade girl, after rollover school bus crash in Polk County We anticipate that just for the local community on a normal basis, for local, like non-hurricane-type emergencies, that the emergency response time will be reduced by up to 56%, DeSantis said. That will ultimately save some lives, of course, because time is of the essence in some of these situations. FDOT Secretary Jared Perdue said the project was completed 400 days early through what the agency calls voluntary acceleration, which lets contractors propose ways to speed construction and share in the savings. This is going to reduce the time it takes for first responders to get to incidents substantially, Perdue said. We’re really excited about that, to include cutting commute time in half and so many other benefits. DeSantis said FDOT also acquired land near the interchange for a dedicated gopher tortoise habitat. He said the site will be the only relocation area of its kind in Southeast Florida. Florida [is] showing that it’s possible to do the projects that we need done while also buttressing environmental stewardship, DeSantis said. Perdue said nearly $1 billion in transportation investment is planned for the Treasure Coast region. Indian River County Commissioner Joseph Flescher recounted his reaction when he first heard about the opening. "When I got the phone call, I said, ' We're not near completion. I had been here just two weeks ago. We were nowhere near where we're at.' This team worked an incredible operation, said Flescher. Flescher also highlighted how important this new entrance ot I-95 is to the growing population across the county. This interchange is very much needed in the development of our county. And I don't mean the future development. I mean the current development, Flescher said.

entry.title: Westlake considers school zone speed cameras near Seminole Ridge High School to improve student safety
entry.summary: The city of Westlake is considering installing speed enforcement cameras in a school zone near Seminole Ridge High School, a proposal that city leaders say would improve student safety. The topic is expected to come before the Westlake City Council during its meeting Tuesday at 6 p.m., as officials discuss a potential agreement with RedSpeed, the company that would provide the camera technology. WATCH BELOW: Westlake considers speed cameras near Seminole Ridge High Westlake considers speed cameras near Seminole Ridge High School According to Westlake City Manager Howard Brown Jr., the city has been discussing school zone speed cameras for about a year. A speed zone study conducted by the city found a need for additional enforcement in the area surrounding Seminole Ridge High School. 'Seminole Ridge High School will be the target area,' Brown said. City officials say the cameras would serve as an additional tool to address speeding drivers in the school zone. 'Some people are busy, and they are not paying attention that they are going through a school zone,' Brown said. Brown, who has a young child at home, said protecting children is a top priority. 'I have a little one at home. That's an area where we really want to protect our children and provide law enforcement with additional tools,' he said. Under the proposal, drivers caught traveling more than 10 mph over the posted speed limit on Seminole Pratt Whitney Road within the school zone would face a $100 citation. 'We are trying to break some of those bad driving habits,' Brown said. Not everyone is convinced the cameras are necessary. Westlake resident Nicole Haley said she worries speed cameras could worsen existing traffic congestion. 'I think it would back up traffic even more than it already is,' Haley said. Instead of adding cameras, Haley believes roadway improvements may be a better solution. 'I think integrating a roundabout like the one they have on Stribling would be better,' she said. If approved, the cameras could be operational before the end of the year. The city says there would also be a 30-day warning period before citations are issued. At this time, Seminole Ridge High School is the only school in the city being considered for speed camera enforcement. The speed camera discussion is one of several items on Tuesday night's council agenda. City officials have also indicated they will not move forward with license plate reader technology at this time. The meeting will be held at the Lodge

entry.title: Potential 2028 Democratic contenders set to discuss party’s future at post-midterms meeting
entry.summary: A group of potential 2028 Democratic presidential candidates is heading to Denver days after the midterms to discuss the partys future, in one of the partys first major gatherings following the election. Attendees will include former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and former US Ambassador to Japan Rahm Emanuel, as well as Sens. Ruben Gallego of Arizona, Chris Murphy of Connecticut, Raphael Warnock of Georgia and Elissa Slotkin of Michigan, according to an initial lineup shared first with CNN. The group of speakers also includes Govs. Mikie Sherrill of New Jersey and Abigail Spanberger of Virginia, plus several additional members of Congress. The Whats Next summit is being hosted from November 12-14 by Majority Democrats, an organization that launched last year to help Democrats win in more places. RELATED STORY | New midterm polling gives Democrats an edge in battleground states In staging the event less than two weeks after the midterms, where Democrats hope to retake the Senate and the House, the group is looking to move quickly to outline the lessons learned from the election that could be instructive going forward, including in the next White House race. This isnt a policy conference nor a talk shop on tactics, said Massachusetts Rep. Jake Auchincloss, chair of Majority Democrats, in a statement. Whats Next is timed for a unique moment after the midterms and before the presidential to debate a vision for the Democratic Party. Politicians who believe they have that vision should be on that stage. Organizers chose Denver partly because it is one of the cities under consideration to host the 2028 Democratic National Convention. The initial lineup also includes top party strategists such as David Axelrod, former senior adviser to President Barack Obama and a chief political analyst at CNN; Quentin Fulks, former principal deputy campaign manager for Kamala Harris in 2024; and Morris Katz, adviser to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | Trump claims Iran is waiting until after midterm elections to strike deal Majority Democrats is not the only organization holding an event in the immediate aftermath of the midterms in a bid to shape the partys future. Two days after the election, some of the partys most prominent strategists and commentators are set to converge in Washington, DC, for Crooked Con, which is hosted by the progressive media company Crooked Media.
